hr_labels <- list(implant ~ "Implant", age_10 ~ "Age (per 10 years)", sex ~ "Sex",
                  bmi_5 ~ "BMI (per 5 kg/m²)")

univariable_table <- cohort |>
  select(followup_years, revised, implant, age_10, sex, bmi_5, patient_id) |>
  tbl_uvregression(method = coxph, y = Surv(followup_years, revised), exponentiate = TRUE,
                   include = c(implant, age_10, sex, bmi_5),
                   method.args = list(cluster = patient_id),       # robust SEs, clustered on patient
                   label = hr_labels, pvalue_fun = label_style_pvalue(digits = 3))
multivariable_table <- clustered_model |>                   # robust SEs, for the bilateral patients
  tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE, label = hr_labels, pvalue_fun = label_style_pvalue(digits = 3))

tbl_merge(list(univariable_table, multivariable_table),

def hr_with_ci(model):
    """Each term's hazard ratio and 95% CI as text, like '3.19 (1.92 to 5.29)'."""
    rows = model.summary
    return (rows["exp(coef)"].map("{:.2f}".format) + " (" + rows["exp(coef) lower 95%"].map("{:.2f}".format)
            + " to " + rows["exp(coef) upper 95%"].map("{:.2f}".format) + ")")

univariable = []
for term in ["implant", "age_10", "sex", "bmi_5"]:
    one_predictor = CoxPHFitter().fit(cohort[["followup_years", "revised", term, "patient_id"]],
                                      duration_col="followup_years", event_col="revised", formula=term,
                                      cluster_col="patient_id",      # robust SEs, clustered on patient
                                      fit_options={"precision": 1e-12})
    univariable.append(hr_with_ci(one_predictor))

hr_table = pd.DataFrame({"Univariable HR (95% CI)": pd.concat(univariable),
                         "Multivariable HR (95% CI)": hr_with_ci(clustered_model)})   # robust SEs, for the bilateral patients

The Results start with the events: 81 revisions in 600 procedures (the first line of the implant model’s output), and 81 / 600 = 0.135, or 13.5%.

Methods: The association between implant and revision for any reason was estimated with Cox proportional hazards regression, with time from surgery as the time scale and implant A as the reference. Age, sex and body mass index were chosen in advance as covariates. Age entered the model as a linear term after a natural cubic spline showed no clear evidence of non-linearity. Proportional hazards were checked with scaled Schoenfeld residuals. In the Cox models, robust standard errors clustered on patient accounted for patients who had both sides replaced. A Fine-Gray model, treating death as a competing risk, was fitted as a sensitivity analysis.
Results: During follow-up, 81 of 600 procedures (13.5%) were revised. After adjustment for age, sex and body mass index, the hazard ratio for revision compared with implant A was 3.19 (95% CI 1.92 to 5.28) for implant C and 0.83 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.52) for implant B (test of proportional hazards, global p = 0.359). With death treated as a competing risk, the subdistribution hazard ratio for implant C was 3.09 (95% CI 1.86 to 5.14).

Before you submit, check that the paper states: - the number of patients, procedures and events - time zero and the event definition (page 13) - which covariates were adjusted for, and why - how continuous predictors were modeled, and how proportional hazards were checked - how bilateral patients and deaths were handled

title: 12 · Predict a value from several variables
text: Outcomes rarely depend on one thing. Heavier patients may take longer to operate on, but so may older ones, and knees take longer than hips. Multiple regression puts several predictors in one model, so each coefficient is that predictor’s effect with the others held fixed: adjusted for them. The regressions are the same four as on page 11, with more than one predictor.
crumbs: 12 · Predict a value from several variables

title: 12 · Predict a value from several variables
text:
Multiple linear regression
The question: Does BMI still predict operative time once age, sex and procedure are taken into account?

When to use it

The outcome is a measurement, and you want the effect of each of several predictors, adjusted for the others.
The assumptions of simple linear regression still apply: straight-line effects, independent patients, and residuals that are roughly normal with an even spread.
Choose the predictors before looking at the results, from what you know clinically. As a rule of thumb, allow at least 10 to 20 patients per predictor.
If an effect may bend → splines. If the outcome is yes/no → multiple logistic regression.



What the test really does
Multiple linear regression works like simple linear regression, with one coefficient for each predictor.

The model predicts each patient’s outcome by adding up the predictors, each multiplied by its own coefficient, plus an intercept.
As before, it measures each patient’s distance from that prediction (the residual) and finds the set of coefficients for which the sum of the squared residuals is as small as possible.
Each coefficient ends up describing only what its predictor adds once the others have explained what they can. BMI’s coefficient compares patients who differ in BMI but are alike in age, sex and procedure. That is what “adjusted” means.
Each coefficient gets its own standard error, confidence interval and p-value, read as in simple regression.

Once the model has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds BMI’s adjusted coefficient by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

Read the output
Each coefficient is the change in operative time for one unit of that predictor, with the other predictors held fixed:

bmi = 1.27: 1.27 more minutes per kg/m² (95% CI 1.06 to 1.49), for patients of the same age, sex and procedure.
age = 0.27: 0.27 more minutes per year of age (95% CI 0.15 to 0.39).
sexMale (R) or sex[T.Male] (Python) = −1.48: men took 1.48 minutes less than women, but the CI (−3.81 to 0.84) includes 0. Women are the reference group because “Female” comes first alphabetically.
procedureTKA = 6.74: TKAs took 6.74 minutes longer than THAs (95% CI 4.40 to 9.08).
Multiple R-squared = 0.27, adjusted R-squared = 0.26: the four predictors together explain about a quarter of the variation. The adjusted value is penalized for the number of predictors.
F-statistic, p < 0.001: the test that all four predictors together explain nothing.







Note🔍 Under the hood: an adjusted coefficient by hand






RPython



time_left <- resid(lm(op_time_min ~ age + sex + procedure, data = cohort))   # operative time, with what age, sex and procedure explain taken out
bmi_left <- resid(lm(bmi ~ age + sex + procedure, data = cohort))            # BMI, with what age, sex and procedure explain taken out
coef(lm(time_left ~ bmi_left))[["bmi_left"]]                                 # the slope between the two leftovers: BMI's adjusted coefficient

[1] 1.274412

coef(lm(op_time_min ~ bmi, data = cohort))[["bmi"]]                          # BMI on its own, for comparison

[1] 1.368005





time_left = smf.ols("op_time_min ~ age + sex + procedure", data=cohort).fit().resid   # operative time, with what age, sex and procedure explain taken out
bmi_left = smf.ols("bmi ~ age + sex + procedure", data=cohort).fit().resid            # BMI, with what age, sex and procedure explain taken out
print((time_left * bmi_left).sum() / (bmi_left ** 2).sum())                           # the slope between the two leftovers: BMI's adjusted coefficient

1.2744124172074565

print(smf.ols("op_time_min ~ bmi", data=cohort).fit().params["bmi"])                  # BMI on its own, for comparison

1.3680052814211734





Take out of both operative time and BMI everything that age, sex and procedure can explain, then fit a simple regression between what is left: its slope is 1.27, exactly the bmi coefficient of the full model. On its own, without adjustment, BMI’s slope is 1.37 (the last line).





Effect size and 95% CI
The adjusted coefficients with their 95% CIs are the effect sizes, with R² for the model as a whole. BMI’s coefficient fell only a little after adjustment, from 1.37 minutes per kg/m² on its own (the last line of the box above; page 11) to 1.27: age, sex and procedure explain little of BMI’s link with operative time.


How to report it

Methods: Operative time was modeled with multiple linear regression on BMI, age, sex and procedure, chosen before the analysis.
Results: Adjusted for age, sex and procedure, the coefficient for BMI was 1.27 minutes of operative time per kg/m² (95% CI 1.06 to 1.49; p < 0.001). The coefficient for TKA (vs THA) was 6.74 minutes (95% CI 4.40 to 9.08) and for age 0.27 minutes per year (95% CI 0.15 to 0.39). The model explained 27% of the variation in operative time (R² = 0.27).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: “adjusted” isn’t “caused”, and more predictors isn’t better



Adjusting removes the part of an effect explained by the variables in the model, not by the ones you left out or never measured, so an adjusted coefficient still isn’t proof of cause. Choose the predictors in advance and stop there: adding variables until something becomes significant, or dropping those that don’t (stepwise selection), gives results that won’t replicate.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: names for the same coefficients



Both programs use the first category alphabetically as the reference (Female, THA). R names the coefficients sexMale and procedureTKA; statsmodels names them sex[T.Male] and procedure[T.TKA] (T for “treatment” coding). The numbers are the same.

title: 12 · Predict a value from several variables
text:
Multiple nonlinear regression
The question: Do hips recover faster than knees after joint replacement?

When to use it

The curve’s shape is known, but its numbers may depend on other variables. Extend the recovery curve so that each of its numbers can differ between hips and knees, and fit one model with nonlinear least squares.
The shape isn’t known. Let a measured predictor’s effect bend with a spline: a flexible curve made of short cubic pieces joined smoothly at points called knots. A natural (or restricted) cubic spline is a straight line beyond the outer knots, which keeps it from flailing at the ends. Splines fit inside an ordinary linear, logistic or Cox model, and they’re the usual way to check whether a straight line is good enough.
If every effect is a straight line → multiple linear regression.



What the test really does
Both tools in this section are least-squares fits, like the ones on page 11.

A curve that differs between groups. Give each of the curve’s numbers two parts: its value for hips, and the difference for knees. The program then finds all six numbers at once, by making the squared distances between the scores and the two curves as small as possible.
Each difference comes with its own standard error and confidence interval, so the model shows directly how hips and knees differ.
A spline. Replace the single BMI column of a linear regression with a few columns built from BMI, which together can draw a smooth bend. The regression itself stays linear.
Compare the fit with and without the bend: an F test asks whether the squared residuals shrink by more than the extra coefficients would achieve by chance.



Look at the data first

RPython

  filter(!is.na(prom_score)) |>
  mutate(days = pmax(visit_days, 0),                        # pre-op visits count as day 0
         joint = if_else(instrument == "HOOS JR", "hip", "knee"),
         knee = as.numeric(joint == "knee"))                # 1 = knee, 0 = hip

Run it
Each of the curve’s three numbers gets a value for hips and a difference for knees: for a knee, plateau = plateau_hip + plateau_diff, and the same for start and tau.

RPython



recovery_by_joint <- function(days, knee, plateau_hip, plateau_diff, start_hip, start_diff, tau_hip, tau_diff) {
  plateau <- plateau_hip + plateau_diff * knee   # knee = 0 for hips, 1 for knees
  start <- start_hip + start_diff * knee
  tau <- tau_hip + tau_diff * knee
  plateau - (plateau - start) * exp(-days / tau)
}

def recovery_by_joint(x, plateau_hip, plateau_diff, start_hip, start_diff, tau_hip, tau_diff):
    days, knee = x
    plateau = plateau_hip + plateau_diff * knee   # knee = 0 for hips, 1 for knees

    tau = tau_hip + tau_diff * knee

Half of the eventual gain took about 37 days after a hip replacement and 56 days after a knee replacement, a difference of 19 days (95% CI 11 to 28). R prints the difference as 19.05 and its CI as 11.03 to 27.83; Python’s CI, computed from the standard error, is 10.6 to 27.5, which also rounds to 11 to 28.


How to report it

Methods: HOOS JR (hips) and KOOS JR (knees) were modeled against days since surgery with an exponential recovery curve whose start, plateau and time constant could differ between hips and knees, fitted by nonlinear least squares. Whether BMI’s effect on operative time was linear was checked by adding a natural cubic spline (3 degrees of freedom) and comparing the models with an F test.
Results: The difference in the time constant between knees and hips was 27.5 days (95% CI 15.9 to 40.1); half of the change was reached at about 56 days after knee replacement and 37 days after hip replacement. For BMI and operative time, comparing a spline with a straight line gave F = 0.58 (df = 2 and 593, p = 0.562).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: two questionnaires, and repeated scores



Hips answer HOOS JR and knees KOOS JR. A point on one isn’t guaranteed to equal a point on the other, so the differences in start and plateau mix up the joints with the questionnaires. The time constant is measured in days, not points, so it compares more fairly, as long as both questionnaires track recovery in a similar way. As on page 11, each joint contributes up to four related scores, so these CIs can’t be trusted: some may be too narrow and others too wide. A mixed model (page 16) handles that.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: splines and CIs




R’s ns() and Python’s cr() (from patsy, the formula library statsmodels uses) build the same natural cubic spline only when the knots match. ns(df = 3) puts knots at the 1/3 and 2/3 quantiles and at the minimum and maximum, so the Python code sets those explicitly. Other tools, like rms::rcs(), place the knots elsewhere and give slightly different curves. constraints='center' removes one column from patsy’s spline so that it doesn’t repeat the model’s intercept, as ns() does by default; both splines then use 3 degrees of freedom.
As on page 11, R’s confint() profiles the nonlinear fit, while the Python code uses estimate ± t × standard error, so the CIs differ slightly (τ difference: 15.3 to 39.7 days in Python).

text:
Multiple logistic regression
The question: Which factors predict return to sport at 12 months?

When to use it

The outcome is yes/no, and you want the odds ratio for each of several predictors, adjusted for the others.
The assumptions of simple logistic regression still apply, for every measured predictor.
Events limit predictors. A common rule of thumb is at least 10 patients in the smaller outcome group per predictor. Here 173 returned and 177 didn’t, so this model can afford about 17.
If the outcome is time until an event → Cox regression.



What the test really does
Multiple logistic regression works like simple logistic regression, with one coefficient for each predictor.

The model adds up the predictors, each multiplied by its own coefficient, to get each patient’s log odds of the outcome.
It tries out values for all the coefficients together and keeps the set under which the outcomes that really happened, taken together, were most likely.
Each coefficient describes what its predictor adds once the others are accounted for: e raised to the coefficient is the adjusted odds ratio.
A predictor with more than two categories gets one coefficient for each category except the first, which serves as the reference.

The more coefficients a model has to estimate, the more outcomes it needs in the smaller group: that is where the rule of thumb under “When to use it” comes from.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

acl <- read_csv("data/acl_cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(age_10 = age / 10)   # per 10 years

acl |>
  group_by(rts_12mo) |>
  summarise(n = n(), age = mean(age), tegner_preinjury = mean(tegner_preinjury),
            bptb_percent = 100 * mean(graft == "BPTB"))

text:
Cox regression
The question: Does implant C still carry a higher hazard of revision after adjusting for age, sex and BMI?

When to use it

The outcome is time until an event (revision), and you want each predictor’s hazard ratio, adjusted for the others.
Events limit predictors, as in logistic regression: about 10 events per predictor. 81 revisions allow about eight; implant (which uses two, B and C against A), age, sex and BMI use five.
Proportional hazards must hold for every predictor. Page 14 shows how to check it and covers Cox regression in full.



What the test really does
This is the Cox model of page 8 with more than one predictor.

Start at surgery and move forward in time. Each time a revision happens, look at who was still being followed just before it: the patients at risk.
Each predictor has its own hazard ratio. A patient’s hazard, compared with a reference patient, is the product of the hazard ratios that apply to them.
The model tries out values for all the hazard ratios together and keeps the set under which the revisions that really happened, taken together, were most likely.
Each hazard ratio then describes what its predictor adds once the others are accounted for: implant C against implant A, for patients of the same age, sex and BMI.

Adjusting matters when the groups differ in other ways. Compare the implants:

title: 10 · Quantify association between two variables
text: Two things measured on the same patients: femoral torsion on CT and on the modified Budin view, PROM improvement and satisfaction, ASA class and hypertension. The tests on this page don’t compare groups. They put one number on how strongly the two go together, with a 95% CI. If you want to predict one from the other, use regression (page 11).

title: 10 · Quantify association between two variables
text:
Pearson correlation
The question: How closely does femoral torsion on the modified Budin view track torsion on CT?

When to use it

Two measurements on the same patients, and you want one number for how closely they move together along a straight line.
Both are roughly normal, without extreme outliers, and the scatter plot looks like a cloud stretched along a line.
If either is skewed or ordinal, has outliers, or the points follow a curve → Spearman correlation.
If you want to predict one from the other, or adjust for other variables → linear regression.



What the test really does
Pearson’s r measures how closely the points follow a straight line.

For each patient, work out how far each of the two measurements is from its own mean, counted in standard deviations. A hip that lies 1 standard deviation above the mean on CT scores +1 on CT.
Multiply the two results for each patient. The product is positive when both measurements are on the same side of their means (both above or both below), and negative when they are on opposite sides.
Average the products over all the patients (dividing by n − 1). That average is r. When high goes with high and low with low, most products are positive and r is close to +1. When there is no straight-line relationship, positive and negative products cancel out and r is close to 0.
The test asks whether r is further from 0 than chance would explain. It turns r into a test statistic, t = r × √(n − 2) ÷ √(1 − r²), and t into a p-value.

Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds r and t by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

imaging <- read_csv("data/hip_preservation_imaging.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)   # one row per hip

ggplot(imaging, aes(torsion_ct_deg, torsion_budin_deg)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +   # see-through points show where they pile up
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +   # dashed line: the two methods read the same
  labs(x = "Femoral torsion on CT, degrees", y = "Femoral torsion on Budin view, degrees")











import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

imaging = pd.read_csv("data/hip_preservation_imaging.csv")   # one row per hip

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.scatter(imaging["torsion_ct_deg"], imaging["torsion_budin_deg"], alpha=0.6)   # see-through points show where they pile up
ax.axline((0, 0), slope=1, linestyle="--")   # dashed line: the two methods read the same
ax.set_xlabel("Femoral torsion on CT, degrees")
ax.set_ylabel("Femoral torsion on Budin view, degrees")
plt.show()











The points follow a straight line, with no extreme outliers, but a flatter one than the dashed line where the two methods would read the same: the Budin reading runs a little above CT at low torsion and below it at high torsion. (Torsion can be negative: the femur is then retroverted.)


Run it

RPython



torsion_corr <- cor.test(imaging$torsion_ct_deg, imaging$torsion_budin_deg)   # Pearson is the default
torsion_corr

Read the output

cor (R) or statistic (Python): Pearson’s r = 0.86. It runs from −1 (a perfect falling line) through 0 (no straight-line relationship) to +1 (a perfect rising line).
t = 14.7, df = 78: the test statistic and its degrees of freedom: 80 hips minus 2. Python doesn’t print it.
p < 0.001 (R prints p-value < 2.2e-16, the smallest value it shows; Python prints 3.0576926692219362e-24. Both are scientific notation for numbers far below 0.001): a correlation this strong would be very unlikely if torsion on CT and on the Budin view were unrelated.
95% CI 0.79 to 0.91.







Note🔍 Under the hood: r and t by hand






RPython



ct_sd_units <- (imaging$torsion_ct_deg - mean(imaging$torsion_ct_deg)) / sd(imaging$torsion_ct_deg)               # step 1: each CT value, in standard deviations from its mean
budin_sd_units <- (imaging$torsion_budin_deg - mean(imaging$torsion_budin_deg)) / sd(imaging$torsion_budin_deg)   # ... and each Budin value
r_by_hand <- sum(ct_sd_units * budin_sd_units) / (80 - 1)    # steps 2 and 3: multiply, add up, divide by n − 1 (80 hips)
r_by_hand

[1] 0.8576899

r_by_hand * sqrt(80 - 2) / sqrt(1 - r_by_hand^2)             # step 4: t

[1] 14.73238





import numpy as np

budin_sd_units = (imaging["torsion_budin_deg"] - imaging["torsion_budin_deg"].mean()) / imaging["torsion_budin_deg"].std()   # ... and each Budin value
r_by_hand = (ct_sd_units * budin_sd_units).sum() / (80 - 1)   # steps 2 and 3: multiply, add up, divide by n − 1 (80 hips)
print(r_by_hand)

0.8576898583915415

print(r_by_hand * np.sqrt(80 - 2) / np.sqrt(1 - r_by_hand ** 2))   # step 4: t

14.732384525508117





The by-hand r is 0.86 and the by-hand t is 14.7: the cor and t in R’s output. Python prints r as statistic and doesn’t print t.





Effect size and 95% CI
r is the effect size: r = 0.86 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.91). As a rough guide, 0.1 is small, 0.3 medium and 0.5 large. Squaring it gives the share of the variation in Budin torsion that goes with CT torsion: r² = 0.74, about three-quarters.


How to report it

Methods: The association between femoral torsion on CT and on the modified Budin view was measured with Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r).
Results: The correlation between femoral torsion on CT and on the modified Budin view was r = 0.86 (Pearson; 95% CI 0.79 to 0.91; p < 0.001; n = 80 hips).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: r only sees straight lines, isn’t cause, and isn’t agreement



A relationship that rises and then falls can have r close to 0, and one outlier can create or hide a correlation, so always look at the scatter plot first. And a correlation doesn’t say which causes which, or whether something else (age, sex) drives both. To adjust for other variables, use multiple regression.
A high r isn’t agreement. Two methods can rise and fall together and still read different angles. Here r = 0.86, yet the Budin reading was up to 12.9° away from CT, and 95% of the differences would be expected from −10.2° to 7.8° (the mean difference ± 1.96 standard deviations). Even those limits hide a trend: in the 8 hips with 25° or more on CT, the Budin reading averaged 7.0° lower. The code below computes these numbers. To ask whether one method can replace the other, use Bland-Altman limits.

[1] 8

mean(difference[high_ct])                             # their mean difference

12.899999999999999

title: 10 · Quantify association between two variables
text:
Spearman correlation
The question: Are patients whose HOOS JR or KOOS JR improved more from before surgery to 1 year also more satisfied?

When to use it

Two variables on the same patients, at least one of them ordinal (satisfaction from 1 to 5), skewed, or with outliers.
The relationship goes one way (always up, or always down) but needn’t be a straight line. Spearman’s ρ (rho) is Pearson’s r calculated on the ranks.
If both are roughly normal and the relationship is a straight line → Pearson correlation.



What the test really does
Spearman’s ρ is Pearson’s r with one change: it is calculated on ranks instead of the values themselves.

Rank the patients on the first variable, from lowest to highest. Tied values share the average of their ranks.
Do the same, separately, for the second variable.
Calculate Pearson’s r between the two sets of ranks. The result is ρ: close to +1 when patients who rank high on one variable also rank high on the other, close to −1 when the two rankings run in opposite directions, and close to 0 when they have nothing to do with each other.
The test asks whether ρ is further from 0 than chance would explain, and gives a p-value.

Because only the order counts, one outlier can’t dominate the result, and a relationship that rises along a curve can still give a ρ close to 1. Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds ρ by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

change <- proms |>
  filter(visit %in% c("preop", "1yr")) |>
  select(case_id, visit, prom_score) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit, values_from = prom_score) |>   # one row per case: preop and 1yr side by side
  mutate(improvement = `1yr` - preop) |>
  inner_join(select(cohort, case_id, satisfaction_1yr), by = "case_id") |>
  filter(!is.na(improvement), !is.na(satisfaction_1yr))          # both answers needed

nrow(change)   # procedures with both scores and a satisfaction answer

[1] 404

ggplot(change, aes(factor(satisfaction_1yr), improvement)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Satisfaction at 1 year (1 = very dissatisfied, 5 = very satisfied)", y = "Improvement, points")







change |>
  group_by(satisfaction_1yr) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_improvement = median(improvement))

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")
proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")

Effect size and 95% CI
ρ is the effect size. Neither cor.test() nor scipy gives its 95% CI, so R uses DescTools and Python uses the formula behind it (Fisher’s z transformation).

How to report it

Methods: The association between improvement in HOOS JR or KOOS JR from before surgery to 1 year and satisfaction at 1 year was measured with Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (ρ).
Results: Among 404 procedures with both scores and a satisfaction answer, the correlation between the change in HOOS JR or KOOS JR and satisfaction was ρ = 0.38 (Spearman; 95% CI 0.30 to 0.46; p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: two instruments in one number



Hip patients answer HOOS JR and knee patients KOOS JR. Both run from 0 to 100, but a point on one isn’t guaranteed to mean the same as a point on the other. Pooling them is fine for a first look; in a paper, analyze hips and knees separately or say why you pooled them.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: ties and the CI




With fewer than 1290 patients, R’s cor.test() tries an exact p-value. With ties it can’t compute one, so it warns and falls back to the usual approximation, the one scipy always uses. exact = FALSE asks for the approximation directly, without the warning.
Neither gives a CI for ρ. DescTools’ SpearmanRho() and the Python formula use the same method: Fisher’s z with a standard error of 1/√(n − 3).

title: 10 · Quantify association between two variables
text:
Contingency coefficients
The question: How strongly is ASA class linked with hypertension?

When to use it

Two categorical variables on the same patients. The chi-square test (page 8) asks whether they’re linked at all; a contingency coefficient says how strongly.
Phi (φ) is for 2 × 2 tables. Cramér’s V works for any table size and equals φ (without its sign) on a 2 × 2 table. Both run from 0 (no link) to 1 (each category of one predicts the other exactly).
Pearson’s contingency coefficient (C) is older. Its maximum is below 1 and depends on the table’s size (it is √((k − 1) ÷ k), where k is the smaller of the number of rows and the number of columns: √(1 ÷ 2) = 0.71 for a table with two columns), which makes it hard to read, so prefer V.
The chi-square p-value needs every expected count to be at least 5.



What the test really does
A contingency coefficient turns the chi-square statistic into a number between 0 and 1 that says how strong the link is.

Run the chi-square test. It compares the table you observed with the table you’d expect if the two variables were unrelated, and sums up the gap between them as χ².
χ² grows with the strength of the link, but also with the number of patients: double every count in the table and χ² doubles, although the link is no stronger.
Cramér’s V takes the sample size out: V = √(χ² ÷ (n × (k − 1))), where n is the number of patients and k is the smaller of the number of rows and the number of columns.
Pearson’s C uses a slightly different formula, C = √(χ² ÷ (χ² + n)), which can never reach 1.

Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” works out V and C by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

V = √(23.18 ÷ 600) = 0.20 and C = √(23.18 ÷ (23.18 + 600)) = 0.19, the numbers the functions in the next step print. Doubling every count doubles χ² to 46.36 but leaves V at 0.20: V measures the strength of the link, not the size of the study.





Effect size and 95% CI

RPython



effectsize::cramers_v(asa_hypertension, adjust = FALSE)   # see the R vs Python box

Cramer's V |       95% CI
-------------------------
0.20       | [0.12, 1.00]

- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].

Cramer's V (adj.) |       95% CI
--------------------------------
0.18              | [0.10, 1.00]

- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].

effectsize::pearsons_c(asa_hypertension)

Pearson's C |       95% CI
--------------------------
0.19        | [0.12, 1.00]

- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].





print(stats.contingency.association(asa_hypertension, method="cramer"))    # Cramér's V

0.19655916548428345

print(stats.contingency.association(asa_hypertension, method="pearson"))   # Pearson's C

0.19286868402903107





Cramér’s V = 0.20, a small-to-medium association (as a rough guide for tables with two rows or columns, 0.1 is small, 0.3 medium and 0.5 large). R also prints a one-sided 95% CI (0.12 to 1.00): V can’t be negative, so only its lower bound is informative. scipy doesn’t compute this CI. R’s second result, headed Cramer's V (adj.), is explained in the R vs Python box. Pearson’s C is 0.19 here, but its ceiling for this table is 0.71, not 1, so the same number means more than it seems: one more reason to report V.


How to report it

Methods: The association between ASA class and hypertension was tested with the chi-square test, with Cramér’s V as the effect size.
Results: Hypertension was present in 12 of 36 procedures (33.3%) in ASA 1 and 16 of 18 (88.9%) in ASA 4 (χ² = 23.2, df = 3, p < 0.001; Cramér’s V = 0.20, one-sided 95% CI 0.12 to 1.00).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: V gives the strength, not the pattern



Shuffling the rows of the table doesn’t change V, so V can’t say that hypertension rises steadily with ASA class. The row percentages show the pattern; put them in your Results. If the categories are ordered and you expect a trend, a test for trend can be more powerful than the plain chi-square test.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: Cramér’s V has two versions



effectsize’s cramers_v() and phi() apply a small-sample bias correction by default (here V = 0.18, the result headed Cramer's V (adj.) in the R tab), while scipy’s association() doesn’t. adjust = FALSE turns it off so the two match; whichever you use, say which in your Methods. On a 2 × 2 table, association(method="cramer") gives φ without its sign.

title: 8 · Compare three or more unmatched groups
text: Three or more groups of different patients: the four ASA classes, the three surgeons, three kinds of ACL graft, implants A, B and C. You could compare every pair of groups with the tests on page 6, but each extra test is another chance of a false positive. The tests on this page ask one question first: is there any difference among the groups at all? If the answer is yes, Which groups differ? explains the next step.
crumbs: 8 · Compare three or more unmatched groups

title: 8 · Compare three or more unmatched groups
text:
One-way ANOVA
The question: Does age at surgery differ across ASA classes 1 to 4?

When to use it

The outcome is a measurement, compared across three or more independent groups.
Within each group it’s roughly normal, or each group is reasonably large and not badly skewed (page 3).
The groups have similar spreads: as a rule of thumb, the largest SD is no more than about twice the smallest. If not, use Welch’s ANOVA (see the R vs Python box), especially when the group sizes are unequal.
If the outcome is skewed, bounded or ordinal → the Kruskal-Wallis test.



What the test really does
ANOVA compares the group means by comparing two kinds of variation. That is where its name comes from: analysis of variance.

Between the groups. Take the distance from each group’s mean to the overall mean (the mean of everyone), square it, and count it once for every patient in the group. Add these up: the sum of squares between the groups.
Within the groups. Take the distance from each patient’s value to the mean of their own group, square it, and add these up: the sum of squares within the groups. This is the noise: patients differ even when they are in the same group.
Divide each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom: the number of groups minus 1 for the first, the number of patients minus the number of groups for the second. The results are two variances, called mean squares.
Divide: F = mean square between ÷ mean square within. If every group had the same true mean, the group means would differ only as much as the noise makes them, and F would be close to 1. Turn F into a p-value: the chance of an F at least this large if every group really had the same mean.

Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds F by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(asa = factor(asa))   # ASA class is a group, not a number

ggplot(cohort, aes(asa, age)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "ASA class", y = "Age at surgery, years")

  group_by(asa) |>

1  Within  47599.066992  596    79.864206        NaN           NaN       NaN







Read the output

asa row: the variation between the group means. Df = 3 (four groups minus one), Sum Sq = 5727 (DF and SS in Python).
Residuals (R) or Within (Python): the variation of patients within their groups. Df = 596 (600 procedures, the sum of the n or count column above, minus four groups), Sum Sq = 47599.
Mean Sq (MS in Python): each Sum Sq divided by its Df. That gives 1908.9 between the groups (5727 ÷ 3; R rounded the 5727 it prints, Python shows 5726.69) and 79.9 within them (47599 ÷ 596).
F = 23.9: the first Mean Sq divided by the second, 1908.9 ÷ 79.9. If the groups had the same mean, F would be close to 1.
p < 0.001: ages this different across groups would be very unlikely if every ASA class had the same mean age. R prints the p-value as 1.28e-14 under Pr(>F), Python as 1.284107e-14 under p_unc. This is scientific notation: e-14 means “move the decimal point 14 places to the left”.
np2 = 0.107 (Python only): eta squared (η²), the share of all the variation that lies between the groups, 5727 ÷ (5727 + 47599). pingouin’s name stands for “partial eta squared”, which is the same number when there is only one grouping variable. The next step corrects it slightly.







Note🔍 Under the hood: F by hand






RPython



overall_mean <- mean(cohort$age)                                          # the mean age of all 600 procedures
class_means <- cohort |> group_by(asa) |> summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(age))
between_ss <- sum(class_means$n * (class_means$mean - overall_mean)^2)   # step 1: each class mean against the overall mean, once per procedure
within_ss <- sum((cohort$age - ave(cohort$age, cohort$asa))^2)           # step 2: each age against the mean of its own class, which ave() returns
between_ms <- between_ss / (4 - 1)                                        # step 3: divide by the degrees of freedom: 4 classes − 1 ...

The first two numbers are the Sum Sq column of the ANOVA table (SS in Python), 5727 and 47599; the next two are its Mean Sq column (MS), 1908.9 and 79.9. Their ratio is the F = 23.9 the test printed. The mean square within the groups is a variance, so its square root is an SD: √79.9 = 8.9 years, the typical spread of age within a class. That matches the SDs of about 9 in the table under “Look at the data first”.





Effect size and 95% CI
Omega squared (ω²) is the share of the variation in age that ASA class accounts for, corrected for the small upward bias of the simpler eta squared (η²). As a rough guide, 0.01 is small, 0.06 medium and 0.14 large.

---------------------------------

- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].





# omega squared from the ANOVA table: (SS between - df between × MS within) / (SS total + MS within)
ss_between, ss_within = age_anova.loc[0, "SS"], age_anova.loc[1, "SS"]

ω² = 0.10: ASA class accounts for about a tenth of the variation in age, a medium effect. R also prints a one-sided 95% CI (0.06 to 1.00): ω² can’t be negative, so only its lower bound is informative. scipy and pingouin don’t compute this CI. The ANOVA doesn’t say which classes differ: see Which groups differ?.


How to report it

Methods: Age was compared across ASA classes with one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), with omega squared (ω²) as the effect size.
Results: Mean age was 59.8 years (SD 8.7) in ASA 1 and 73.7 years (SD 9.3) in ASA 4 (one-way ANOVA, F(3, 596) = 23.9, p < 0.001; ω² = 0.10, one-sided 95% CI 0.06 to 1.00).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: ANOVA doesn’t tell you which groups differ



A significant ANOVA means at least one group mean differs from another, not that every group differs from every other. Don’t follow it with a string of unadjusted t tests: that brings back the false-positive problem the ANOVA was meant to avoid. Use a post-hoc test (page 15).








Tip🔀 R vs Python: classic or Welch’s ANOVA




Classic ANOVA assumes the groups have the same spread. R’s aov(), scipy’s f_oneway() and pingouin’s anova() all run it by default.
Welch’s ANOVA doesn’t assume equal spreads. R’s oneway.test() runs Welch’s version by default (add var.equal = TRUE for the classic one), the opposite of aov(). In Python use pg.welch_anova() or stats.f_oneway(..., equal_var=False).

title: 8 · Compare three or more unmatched groups
text:
Kruskal-Wallis test
The question: Does satisfaction 1 year after surgery differ between surgeons S1, S2 and S3?

When to use it

The outcome is ordinal (satisfaction from 1 to 5), skewed, or has a ceiling or floor, compared across three or more independent groups.
Like the Mann-Whitney test, it works on ranks: it asks whether values in some groups tend to be larger than in others.
With two groups it gives essentially the same result as the Mann-Whitney test.
If the outcome is a roughly normal measurement → one-way ANOVA.



What the test really does
The Kruskal-Wallis test does for three or more groups what the Mann-Whitney test does for two: it sets the scores aside and works with their order.

Line up all the scores from all the groups, from lowest to highest, and give each its position in the line: its rank. Tied scores share the average of their positions.
Work out the mean rank of each group.
If the groups didn’t differ, each group’s mean rank would be close to the mean of all the ranks, which is (n + 1) ÷ 2 for n scores.
The test statistic, H, measures how far the groups’ mean ranks are from that overall mean rank: each distance is squared and counted once for every patient in the group, then everything is added up and rescaled. H is 0 when all the mean ranks are equal, and larger the further apart they are. The larger H, the smaller the p-value.

Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds H by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

Both programs therefore divide it by a correction factor, here 0.84, which gives the H = 0.68 they printed.





Effect size and 95% CI
Epsilon squared (ε²) is the rank-based counterpart of ω²: the share of the variation in the ranks that the groups account for, from 0 to 1. It is H divided by (n − 1).

0.0013510047427243259





ε² = 0.001: H divided by n − 1 is 0.677 ÷ 501 = 0.00135. R prints it as 1.35e-03, which is scientific notation for the same number: the decimal point moves 3 places to the left. Surgeon accounts for essentially none of the variation in satisfaction. R’s one-sided CI runs from 0.00 to 1.00; it comes from a bootstrap, which is why the code sets a seed. scipy has no function for it.


How to report it

Methods: Satisfaction at 1 year (a 5-point ordinal scale) was compared across surgeons with the Kruskal-Wallis test, with epsilon squared (ε²) as the effect size.
Results: Of 600 procedures, 502 had a satisfaction score at 1 year: 192 of 232 for surgeon S1, 177 of 211 for S2 and 133 of 157 for S3. The median was 4 (IQR 4 to 5) for surgeon S1 and 5 (IQR 4 to 5) for surgeons S2 and S3 (Kruskal-Wallis H = 0.68, df = 2, p = 0.713; ε² = 0.001, one-sided 95% CI 0.00 to 1.00).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: missing answers aren’t random



Satisfaction is missing for 98 procedures (600 − 502). If unhappy patients were less likely to answer, every surgeon looks better than they are, and the comparison can be biased too. Always report how many answered in each group, as the Results above do, and consider whether non-response differs between groups. Here it barely does: 192 ÷ 232 = 83%, 177 ÷ 211 = 84% and 133 ÷ 157 = 85% of each surgeon’s procedures have a score.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: ties and the data format



Both kruskal.test() and stats.kruskal() correct H for ties, so they agree even with a 5-point scale full of tied scores. R takes a formula (outcome ~ group); scipy takes one list of values per group, which is why the Python code builds scores first.

title: 8 · Compare three or more unmatched groups
text:
Chi-square test
The question: Does return to sport 12 months after ACL reconstruction differ between bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB), hamstring and quadriceps tendon grafts?

When to use it

The outcome is categorical (here yes/no), compared across three or more independent groups: an r × c table.
Every expected count should be at least 5. If not, combine categories that make sense together, or use Fisher’s exact test, which R’s fisher.test() runs exactly on larger tables too. scipy’s stats.fisher_exact() accepts larger tables but estimates their p-value by random resampling, so it changes a little from run to run unless you give it a seed.
With two groups and a yes/no outcome → Fisher’s exact test.



What the test really does
The chi-square test compares the table you observed with the table you’d expect if return to sport had nothing to do with the graft. It works as it does for a 2 × 2 table (page 6), with more cells.

Work out the expected count for each of the six cells: row total × column total ÷ grand total. That is the count you’d see if every graft had the same rate of return to sport.
For each cell, take (observed − expected)² ÷ expected, then add up the six results. The sum is the test statistic, χ²: 0 when the table matches the expected counts exactly, and larger the further it is from them.
Turn χ² into a p-value with the chi-square distribution. This step is an approximation, and a poor one when expected counts are small. That is where the “at least 5” rule comes from.

The test gives one answer for the whole table: it doesn’t say which grafts differ. Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds χ² by hand.


Look at the data first
The ACL data hold one row per primary reconstruction; rts_12mo is 1 if the patient was back at their pre-injury sport 12 months after surgery.

RPython



library(tidyverse)

acl <- read_csv("data/acl_cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

rts_table <- table(
  graft    = factor(acl$graft, levels = c("BPTB", "hamstring", "quadriceps")),
  returned = factor(acl$rts_12mo, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("yes", "no"))
)

Effect size and 95% CI
Cramér’s V measures the strength of association in a table, from 0 (none) to 1 (perfect). It is √(χ² ÷ (n × (k − 1))), where n is the number of reconstructions and k the smaller of the number of rows and the number of columns: here √(22.24 ÷ (350 × 1)) = 0.25. For a table with 2 columns, about 0.1 is small, 0.3 medium and 0.5 large.

V = 0.25, between a small and a medium association (R’s second output, headed Cramer's V (adj.), is explained in the R vs Python box). R also prints a one-sided 95% CI, 0.16 to 1.00; scipy doesn’t compute one. For yes/no outcomes, the rate in each group (with its CI, as on page 4) is usually more informative than V. And remember what the test doesn’t tell you: which grafts differ (Which groups differ? below), or why. The grafts weren’t assigned at random, so a difference could come from the patients rather than the graft; page 12 shows how to adjust for other factors.


How to report it

Methods: Return to sport at 12 months was compared across graft types with the chi-square test, with Cramér’s V as the effect size.
Results: Return to sport at 12 months followed 84 of 129 BPTB reconstructions (65.1%), 67 of 154 hamstring reconstructions (43.5%) and 22 of 67 quadriceps reconstructions (32.8%) (χ² = 22.24, df = 2, p < 0.001; Cramér’s V = 0.25, one-sided 95% CI 0.16 to 1.00).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: no Yates’ correction here, and check the expected counts



Yates’ continuity correction (page 6) only applies to 2 × 2 tables, so both programs skip it for this 3 × 2 table. The expected-count rule still applies: Exercise 3 shows a table that breaks it, and what to do.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: two versions of Cramér’s V



effectsize’s cramers_v() applies a small-sample bias correction by default: that is R’s second output above, 0.24, headed Cramer's V (adj.). scipy’s association() doesn’t (0.25). We set adjust = FALSE in R so the two match. Either is acceptable; say which you report.

title: 8 · Compare three or more unmatched groups
text:
Cox regression
The question: Does the risk of revision differ between implants A, B and C?

When to use it

The outcome is time until an event (revision), compared across three or more independent groups.
The log-rank test extends to three or more groups and answers “do the curves differ?”. Cox regression also gives a hazard ratio for each group against a reference group, and can adjust for other variables.
It assumes each group’s hazard is a steady multiple of the reference group’s over time (proportional hazards). Page 14 shows how to check that and covers Cox regression in full.



What the test really does
Cox regression follows the groups over the whole follow-up, one revision at a time, as the log-rank test does. It also estimates how large the difference between the groups is.

Start at surgery and move forward in time. Each time a revision happens, look at who was still being followed just before it: the patients at risk.
Suppose the hazard with implant C were twice the hazard with implant A. Then, at that moment, each patient at risk with implant C would be twice as likely to be the one revised as each patient at risk with implant A.
The model tries out values for each implant’s hazard ratio against the reference group, and keeps the values under which the revisions that really happened, taken together, were most likely.
The overall test compares this best fit with a model in which every hazard ratio is 1, that is, no difference between the implants. The more the hazard ratios improve the fit, the larger the test statistic and the smaller the p-value.

The model only needs to know how the groups’ hazards compare, never the hazard itself. So it leaves open how the risk of revision changes over the years; it only assumes that the groups’ hazards stay in the same proportion (the third point under “When to use it”). A patient who leaves the study early is censored: they count among the patients at risk for as long as they were followed, and not after. Once the model has run, a box under “Read the output” works out each implant’s observed and expected revisions by hand.


Look at the data first

  ggsurvfit() +
  add_risktable() +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Years since surgery", y = "Revision-free survival")

RPython



revision_times <- sort(unique(cohort$followup_years[cohort$revised == 1]))    # every time at which a revision happened
expected <- sapply(c(A = "A", B = "B", C = "C"), function(group) {
  sum(sapply(revision_times, function(time) {
    at_risk <- cohort$followup_years >= time                                  # still followed just before this time
    revisions <- sum(cohort$followup_years == time & cohort$revised == 1)     # revisions at this time (usually 1)
    revisions * sum(at_risk & cohort$implant == group) / sum(at_risk)         # this implant's expected share of them
  }))                                                                         # added up over all the times
})
observed <- tapply(cohort$revised, cohort$implant, sum)
rbind(observed, expected, ratio = observed / expected)                        # observed, expected and their ratio, for each implant

for time in revision_times:
    at_risk = cohort["followup_years"] >= time                                            # still followed just before this time
    revisions = ((cohort["followup_years"] == time) & (cohort["revised"] == 1)).sum()     # revisions at this time (usually 1)
    for group in expected.index:
        expected[group] += revisions * (at_risk & (cohort["implant"] == group)).sum() / at_risk.sum()   # this implant's expected share, added up
observed = cohort.groupby("implant")["revised"].sum()

If all three implants carried the same risk, the 81 revisions would have been shared out as 34.0 (A), 30.0 (B) and 16.9 (C). Implant C had 38, more than twice its share; implants A and B had 25 and 18, fewer than theirs. The log-rank test, the “Score (logrank) test” line above, asks how unlikely gaps this large would be by chance. The ratio row divides observed by expected: 0.73 for A, 0.60 for B and 2.24 for C. Comparing these ratios gives a rough idea of the hazard ratios: 2.24 ÷ 0.73 = 3.1 for C against A, and 0.60 ÷ 0.73 = 0.8 for B against A. The Cox model estimates them properly, as 3.07 and 0.82.





Effect size and 95% CI
The hazard ratios with their 95% CIs are the effect sizes: implant C carried about three times the hazard of revision of implant A (3.07, 95% CI 1.85 to 5.09), while implant B didn’t differ clearly from A (0.82, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.50).


How to report it

Methods: Revision-free survival was compared across implants with Cox proportional hazards regression, with implant A as the reference.
Results: Compared with implant A, the hazard ratio for revision was 3.07 (95% CI 1.85 to 5.09) for implant C and 0.82 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.50) for implant B (likelihood ratio test for implant type, χ² = 27.6, df = 2, p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: the reference group shapes the story



Every hazard ratio here is relative to implant A, so the output doesn’t compare B with C directly. Choose the reference group on purpose (the standard implant, the largest group) and say which it is. And as on page 4, deaths here are treated as censored; page 13 covers competing risks.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: convergence and the reference group



Both programs use the first group alphabetically (A) as the reference and handle tied revision times with Efron’s method. lifelines’ default convergence rule stops a little early here, so we tighten it with fit_options={"precision": 1e-9}. This is the difference it makes:

title: 8 · Compare three or more unmatched groups
text:
Which groups differ?
The tests above answer “is there any difference among the groups?”. When the answer is yes, the next question is which groups differ from which. Comparing every pair with an ordinary test inflates the chance of a false positive. With four ASA classes there are six pairs (1 and 2, 1 and 3, 1 and 4, 2 and 3, 2 and 4, 3 and 4). Each test at the 5% level has a 95% chance of not raising a false alarm when nothing is going on. If the six tests were independent, all of them would stay quiet with probability 0.956 = 0.74. That leaves 1 − 0.74 = 0.26, roughly a one-in-four chance of at least one false alarm (page 15 works this out in code).
Post-hoc tests compare the pairs while keeping that overall error rate at 5%:



After
Use
Page




One-way ANOVA
Tukey’s HSD (Games-Howell if the spreads differ)
15


Kruskal-Wallis
Dunn’s test with Holm’s adjustment
15


Chi-square
Pairwise Fisher or chi-square tests with Holm’s adjustment
15


Cox regression
Hazard ratios against a chosen reference, or contrasts between groups
14



Tukey’s HSD controls false positives on its own, and so do Dunn’s test and other pairwise tests once Holm’s adjustment is applied, so none of them needs a significant overall test first. Decide before you see the data which comparisons you’ll make, and say so in your Methods (page 15).

title: 6 · Compare two unpaired groups
text: Two groups of different patients: a removable boot vs a cast in a trial, hamstring vs BPTB grafts, implant A vs implant C. This is the most common comparison in clinical research. If the same patients are measured twice, or patients were matched in pairs, use page 7 instead.

title: 6 · Compare two unpaired groups
text:
Unpaired t test
The question: Is the EFAS score 3 months after a midfoot injury different with a removable boot than with a cast?

When to use it

The outcome is a measurement, compared between two independent groups.
Within each group it’s roughly normal, or each group is large (about 30 or more) and not badly skewed (page 3).
A score that adds up several questions, such as the EFAS score (six questions scored 0 to 4, so 0 to 24), can be treated as a measurement when few patients sit at its floor or ceiling.
Use Welch’s version, which doesn’t assume the two groups have the same spread. It’s R’s default, but not Python’s (see the R vs Python box).
If the outcome is skewed, piles up at a floor or ceiling, or is ordinal → the Mann-Whitney test.



What the test really does
The t test asks one thing: is the difference between the two group means big compared with how much that difference would wobble from one sample to the next?

Take the difference between the two means.
Estimate the noise in that difference, its standard error. It shrinks when the groups are larger and grows when the scores are more spread out.
Divide: t = difference ÷ standard error. A t of 0 means no difference at all. A t beyond about ±2 means the difference is large compared with the noise.
Turn t into a p-value: the chance of a t at least this far from 0 if the two groups really had the same mean.

Welch’s version works out the standard error from each group’s own spread, so it doesn’t need the two spreads to be equal. Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds t by hand.


Look at the data first
The trial randomized 120 patients, 60 to each arm, and measured the EFAS score (European Foot and Ankle Society; 24 is the best) at 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months and 12 months.

  mutate(arm = factor(arm, levels = c("boot", "cast")))    # boot first: differences are boot minus cast

  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, ncol = 1) +

  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(efas), sd = sd(efas))          # the table from "Look at the data first"

efas_difference <- efas_by_arm$mean[1] - efas_by_arm$mean[2]    # step 1: the difference, boot minus cast
efas_se <- sqrt(sum(efas_by_arm$sd^2 / efas_by_arm$n))          # step 2: its standard error, √(SD²/n + SD²/n)
c(difference = efas_difference, standard_error = efas_se, t = efas_difference / efas_se)   # step 3: divide

    difference standard_error              t 
     3.5853270      0.5971968      6.0035939 





efas_difference = efas_boot.mean() - efas_cast.mean()                                      # step 1: the difference, boot minus cast
efas_se = (efas_boot.var() / len(efas_boot) + efas_cast.var() / len(efas_cast)) ** 0.5     # step 2: its standard error; var() is SD²
print(efas_difference, efas_se, efas_difference / efas_se)                                 # step 3: divide

3.585326953748007 0.5971967818851325 6.003593894847252





The difference of 3.6 points is 6.00 times its standard error of 0.60 points. That is the t = 6.00 the test printed.





Effect size and 95% CI

The mean difference with its CI is the effect size readers understand best: 3.6 points (95% CI 2.4 to 4.8). R prints the two means and leaves the subtraction to you (17.40 − 13.82 = 3.58); Python’s second line prints the difference, 3.585, and then the CI.
Hedges’ g expresses the difference in standard deviations, which lets you compare effects measured on different scales. As a rough guide, 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large.


RPython



effectsize::hedges_g(efas ~ arm, data = efas_3mo)

Hedges' g |       95% CI
------------------------
1.13      | [0.73, 1.52]

- Estimated using pooled SD.





g = pg.compute_effsize(efas_boot, efas_cast, eftype="hedges")
print(g)

1.130200311478461

print(pg.compute_esci(stat=g, nx=len(efas_boot), ny=len(efas_cast), eftype="hedges", decimals=3))   # its 95% CI

[0.727 1.534]





Hedges’ g is 1.13: the boot arm’s mean is more than one standard deviation higher, a large effect. Whether 3.6 points on a 24-point score matters to patients is a clinical question, not a statistical one.


How to report it

Methods: EFAS scores at 3 months were compared between the arms with Welch’s unpaired t test, in the patients seen at that visit.
Results: At 3 months, the mean EFAS score was 17.4 points (SD 2.9; n = 57) with a boot and 13.8 (SD 3.4; n = 55) with a cast (difference 3.6 points, 95% CI 2.4 to 4.8; Hedges’ g = 1.13, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.52; p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: don’t test the variances first



An old habit is to run a test of equal variances (such as Levene’s) and then choose Student’s or Welch’s t test depending on the result. Don’t: the two-step procedure distorts the p-value. Use Welch’s test from the start. When the variances really are equal, it gives almost the same answer as Student’s.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: Student’s or Welch’s?




The default differs. R’s t.test() runs Welch’s test unless you add var.equal = TRUE. scipy’s ttest_ind() runs Student’s test unless you add equal_var=False. Always set it explicitly in Python.
The order of the groups. R subtracts in the order of the factor levels (we put boot first); scipy subtracts the second argument from the first.
The CI for Hedges’ g. effectsize uses an exact method and pingouin an approximation, so the CIs can differ slightly (0.73 to 1.52 in R, 0.73 to 1.53 in Python). The estimates agree to five decimals: both correct g for small samples, effectsize with the exact formula and pingouin with the usual approximation. R’s table rounds g to 1.13; unrounded, R gives 1.130197 and Python 1.130200.

title: 6 · Compare two unpaired groups
text:
Mann-Whitney test
The question: Is pain 6 weeks after a midfoot injury different with a removable boot than with a cast?

When to use it

The outcome is skewed, has a ceiling or floor, or is ordinal, and you’re comparing two independent groups.
It asks whether values in one group tend to be larger than in the other: if you picked one patient from each group at random, how likely is the first to score higher?
It’s the same test as the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. R calls it wilcox.test().
If the outcome is roughly normal within each group → the unpaired t test.



What the test really does
The Mann-Whitney test ignores how far apart two scores are. It looks only at which one is higher.

Pair every patient in one group with every patient in the other.
In each pair, see who has the higher score. Count the pairs in which the first group’s patient is higher; a tie counts as half a pair. That count is the test statistic, U.
If the two groups were alike, the first group’s patient would be the higher one in about half of the pairs. The further U is from half of all the pairs, the smaller the p-value.

Software gets the same U faster. It sorts all the scores from both groups from lowest to highest and gives each one its position in that line, 1, 2, 3 and so on: its rank. Tied scores share the average of their positions. U then follows by simple arithmetic from the sum of one group’s ranks, which is why the test is also called a rank-sum test. The effect size step below counts the pairs for our data.


Look at the data first
The trial measured pain on a numeric rating scale (NRS) from 0 (no pain) to 10 (the worst pain imaginable), in whole numbers: an ordinal scale.

RPython



library(tidyverse)

trial <- read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)   # one row per patient and visit

pain_6wk <- trial |>
  filter(visit == "6wk", !is.na(pain_nrs)) |>              # patients seen at 6 weeks
  mutate(arm = factor(arm, levels = c("boot", "cast")))    # boot first: differences are boot minus cast

ggplot(pain_6wk, aes(pain_nrs)) +
  geom_bar() +                                             # one bar per whole score
  facet_wrap(~ arm, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(x = "Pain at 6 weeks (NRS, 0 = none, 10 = worst)", y = "Patients")







pain_6wk |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median = median(pain_nrs),
            q1 = quantile(pain_nrs, 0.25), q3 = quantile(pain_nrs, 0.75))

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  arm       n median    q1    q3
  <fct> <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 boot     58      4     3  4.75
2 cast     58      5     4  6   





import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pingouin as pg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

trial = pd.read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv")                       # one row per patient and visit
pain_6wk = trial[trial["visit"] == "6wk"].dropna(subset=["pain_nrs"])     # patients seen at 6 weeks
pain_boot = pain_6wk.loc[pain_6wk["arm"] == "boot", "pain_nrs"]

Four patients missed the 6-week visit (2 in each arm), so 116 of the 120 randomized patients are analyzed. Most scores sit between 2 and 6, and many patients share a score (ties). With whole numbers on an ordinal scale, medians are the fair summary: 4 points with a boot and 5 with a cast. (The table shows 58 patients in each arm, so 60 − 58 = 2 missed the visit in each.) The boot arm’s upper quartile, 4.75, isn’t a whole score: with its 58 scores in order, the quartile falls between the 43rd (a 4) and the 44th (a 5), and both programs place it three-quarters of the way between them.


Run it

RPython

                         exact = FALSE, correct = TRUE,   # see the R vs Python box

# pg.mwu() runs scipy's Mann-Whitney test and adds the rank-biserial effect size
pain_test = pg.mwu(pain_boot, pain_cast, method="asymptotic", use_continuity=True)   # see the R vs Python box
print(pain_test)

MWU  1074.5   two-sided  0.00066 -0.361177  0.319411







Read the output

W = 1074.5 (R) or U_val = 1074.5 (Python): the Mann-Whitney U statistic for the boot arm, the number of (boot, cast) pairs in which the boot patient reported more pain, counting ties as half. There are 58 × 58 = 3,364 pairs, so a U of 1,682 would mean no tendency either way. R calls it W.
p < 0.001: a difference like this would be unusual if pain had the same distribution in both arms.
difference in location −1.00, 95% CI −2.00 to −1.00 (R only): the Hodges-Lehmann estimate, below. R finds it by a numerical search, so it prints −1.000041 and the like; the last digits are noise.
RBC = −0.361 (Python): the rank-biserial effect size, below.
CLES = 0.319 (Python): the “common language effect size”, U divided by the number of pairs (1,074.5 ÷ 3,364). It is the chance that a randomly chosen boot patient reports more pain than a randomly chosen cast patient, counting a tie as half.



Effect size and 95% CI

The Hodges-Lehmann estimate is the median of the differences between every boot patient’s score and every cast patient’s score: a typical difference, in points.
The rank-biserial correlation (r) runs from −1 (every boot patient reported less pain than every cast patient) to +1 (the reverse). 0 means no tendency either way.


RPython

# Where r comes from: compare every boot patient with every cast patient (58 × 58 pairs)
pain_pairs <- outer(pain_6wk$pain_nrs[pain_6wk$arm == "boot"],   # every boot score ...
                    pain_6wk$pain_nrs[pain_6wk$arm == "cast"],   # ... minus every cast score

[1] 1074.5





# Hodges-Lehmann estimate: the median of every boot-minus-cast difference
def hodges_lehmann(x, y):
    return np.median(np.subtract.outer(np.asarray(x), np.asarray(y)))

print(hodges_lehmann(pain_boot, pain_cast))

-1.0

# scipy has no CI for it, so use a bootstrap: recompute it on 9999 resampled datasets.
# method="percentile": with whole-number scores, scipy's default method can't build this CI (see the R vs Python box)
hl_boot = stats.bootstrap((pain_boot.to_numpy(), pain_cast.to_numpy()), hodges_lehmann, vectorized=False,
                          method="percentile", rng=np.random.default_rng(2026))
print(hl_boot.confidence_interval)

ConfidenceInterval(low=np.float64(-2.0), high=np.float64(-1.0))

MWU   -0.361177
Name: RBC, dtype: float64

# Where r comes from: compare every boot patient with every cast patient (58 × 58 pairs)
pain_pairs = np.subtract.outer(pain_boot.to_numpy(), pain_cast.to_numpy())   # every boot score minus every cast score
print(pain_pairs.size)                                   # the number of pairs

3364

# Percentage of pairs in which the boot patient reported less pain, more pain, or the same pain
pair_shares = {"less": (pain_pairs < 0).mean(), "more": (pain_pairs > 0).mean(), "tied": (pain_pairs == 0).mean()}
print({name: round(100 * share) for name, share in pair_shares.items()})

{'less': 61, 'more': 25, 'tied': 14}

print((pain_pairs > 0).sum() + (pain_pairs == 0).sum() / 2)   # U by hand: pairs with more pain in the boot arm, ties count half

1074.5





With a boot, pain was typically 1 point lower (95% CI 2 points to 1 point lower), and r = −0.36. The last lines of the code show where r comes from. Of all 3,364 (boot, cast) pairs, the boot patient reported less pain in 61%, more in 25%, and 14% were tied. r is the difference between the “more” share and the “less” share: 0.25 − 0.61 = −0.36. U counts the same pairs, as the last line shows by hand: 1,074.5, the W (R) or U_val (Python) the test printed. And 1,074.5 ÷ 3,364 = 0.32, the “more” share plus half the tied share (0.25 + 0.07). With whole-number scores every difference between two patients is a whole number, so the Hodges-Lehmann estimate and its CI land on whole numbers too, and the estimate can sit on the edge of its own CI, as here.






Note🔍 Under the hood: why scipy’s default bootstrap gives nan here





scipy’s default bootstrap method (BCa) fine-tunes its interval by looking at how much the estimate changes when each patient is left out in turn. With whole-number scores, the Hodges-Lehmann estimate can only land on whole or half points, and here it doesn’t change at all:

RPython



boot_scores <- pain_6wk$pain_nrs[pain_6wk$arm == "boot"]
cast_scores <- pain_6wk$pain_nrs[pain_6wk$arm == "cast"]
# Leave each patient out in turn, and recompute the estimate without them
leave_one_out <- c(sapply(seq_along(boot_scores), function(i) median(outer(boot_scores[-i], cast_scores, "-"))),
                   sapply(seq_along(cast_scores), function(i) median(outer(boot_scores, cast_scores[-i], "-"))))
table(leave_one_out)                                     # how often each value came up

leave_one_out
 -1 
116 





# Leave each patient out in turn, and recompute the estimate without them
leave_one_out = ([hodges_lehmann(pain_boot.drop(i), pain_cast) for i in pain_boot.index]
                 + [hodges_lehmann(pain_boot, pain_cast.drop(i)) for i in pain_cast.index])
print(pd.Series(leave_one_out).value_counts())           # how often each value came up

-1.0    116
Name: count, dtype: int64





All 116 estimates are −1. BCa needs them to vary, so it returns nan with a warning; the percentile method doesn’t use them.





How to report it

Methods: Pain at 6 weeks (NRS 0 to 10, an ordinal scale) was compared between the arms with the Mann-Whitney test, in the patients seen at that visit, with the Hodges-Lehmann estimate of the difference and its 95% CI as the effect size.
Results: At 6 weeks, pain was a median of 4 points (IQR 3 to 4.75; n = 58) with a boot and 5 (IQR 4 to 6; n = 58) with a cast (Hodges-Lehmann difference −1 point, 95% CI −2 to −1; rank-biserial r = −0.36, 95% CI −0.53 to −0.17; p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: it isn’t a test of medians



The Mann-Whitney test asks whether one group’s values tend to be larger, not whether the medians differ. Two groups can have the same median and a significant Mann-Whitney test (if their shapes differ), or different medians and a non-significant one. Report the medians to describe the groups, but don’t write “the medians differed significantly”.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: Mann-Whitney defaults




Exact or approximate. With ties (as here) both programs use a normal approximation. Without ties, R computes an exact p-value for groups under 50, scipy only for very small groups. We set exact = FALSE in R and method="asymptotic" in Python so they always match.
Continuity correction. Both programs apply it by default for the approximation; we set it explicitly anyway.
The Hodges-Lehmann CI. R computes it by inverting the test; the Python code uses a bootstrap, a different method. With whole-number scores the estimate barely moves: leaving out any one patient still gives −1 (the box under “Effect size and 95% CI” shows it). scipy’s default bootstrap method (BCa) needs those leave-one-out estimates to vary, so here it returns nan with a warning. The percentile method (method="percentile") doesn’t need them. Here the two CIs agree (−2.00 to −1.00); on other data they can differ a little.
The CI for r. effectsize prints a 95% CI for the rank-biserial r. pingouin’s mwu() gives r (the RBC column) without one, so the CI in the Results sentence comes from R.

title: 6 · Compare two unpaired groups
text:
Fisher’s exact test and chi-square
The question: Does graft failure within 2 years of an ACL reconstruction differ between a hamstring graft and a bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) graft?

When to use it

The outcome is yes/no, compared between two independent groups: a 2 × 2 table.
Fisher’s exact test is valid for any sample size. The chi-square test is a large-sample approximation: use it only when every expected count is at least 5. When in doubt, use Fisher’s test.
If patients were followed for different lengths of time and the event can happen at any time → the log-rank test.



What the test really does
Both tests compare the table you observed with the table you’d expect if failure had nothing to do with the graft.
The chi-square test

Work out the expected count for each of the four cells: row total × column total ÷ grand total. That is the count you’d see if both grafts failed at the same overall rate.
For each cell, take (observed − expected)² ÷ expected, then add up the four results. The sum is the test statistic, χ²: 0 when the table matches the expected counts exactly, and larger the further it is from them.
Turn χ² into a p-value with the chi-square distribution. This step is an approximation, and a poor one when expected counts are small. That is where the “at least 5” rule comes from.

Fisher’s exact test needs no approximation. It keeps the row and column totals fixed and lists every table that could have those totals. It works out the exact probability of each one, then adds up the probabilities of all the tables that are no more likely than yours. That sum is the p-value.


Look at the data first
The ACL data hold one row per primary reconstruction. Everyone was followed for at least 2 years unless the graft failed first, so failure within 2 years (failure_2y) is known for every reconstruction. For two yes/no variables, “looking” means the 2 × 2 table, with the percentage in each group.

RPython



library(tidyverse)

acl <- read_csv("data/acl_cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
two_grafts <- acl |> filter(graft %in% c("hamstring", "BPTB"))   # the question compares two of the three grafts

# Put the comparison group first and the outcome "yes" first
failure_table <- table(
  graft  = factor(two_grafts$graft, levels = c("hamstring", "BPTB")),
  failed = factor(two_grafts$failure_2y, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("yes", "no"))
)
failure_table

           failed
graft       yes  no
  hamstring   6 148
  BPTB        6 123

prop.table(failure_table, margin = 1)    # row percentages: failures with each graft

           failed
graft              yes         no
  hamstring 0.03896104 0.96103896
  BPTB      0.04651163 0.95348837

Expected counts: what each cell would hold if failure were unrelated to the graft. All are at least 5, but only just (the smallest is 5.5), so the chi-square test is valid too.
X-squared = 0.0003, p-value = 0.986: the chi-square test, with Yates’ continuity correction, agrees.







Note🔍 Under the hood: chi-square by hand






RPython



chisq_observed <- failure_table
chisq_expected <- outer(rowSums(chisq_observed), colSums(chisq_observed)) / sum(chisq_observed)   # step 1: row total × column total ÷ grand total

    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  failure_table
X-squared = 0.098562, df = 1, p-value = 0.7536





import numpy as np

chisq_observed = failure_table.to_numpy()
chisq_expected = np.outer(chisq_observed.sum(axis=1), chisq_observed.sum(axis=0)) / chisq_observed.sum()   # step 1: row total × column total ÷ grand total
print(chisq_expected)

[[  6.53003534 147.46996466]
 [  5.46996466 123.53003534]]

print(((chisq_observed - chisq_expected) ** 2 / chisq_expected).sum())    # step 2: add up (observed − expected)² ÷ expected

0.09856165459872664

uncorrected = stats.chi2_contingency(failure_table, correction=False)       # the software, with Yates' correction switched off
print(uncorrected.statistic, uncorrected.pvalue)

0.09856165459872664 0.7535625801260732





The by-hand sum is 0.099, the same χ² the software gives once Yates’ correction is switched off (p = 0.754). The test above printed 0.0003 because, for a 2 × 2 table, R and scipy apply the correction unless told otherwise; the next box explains it.









Note🔍 Under the hood: Yates’ continuity correction





The chi-square test treats counts as if they could take any value, but counts are whole numbers. For a 2 × 2 table, Yates’ correction subtracts 0.5 from each |observed − expected| difference before squaring, which makes the p-value larger (more cautious). It’s meant to bring the p-value closer to Fisher’s, but it can overshoot, as here: each observed count is only about half a count from its expected count (6 failures against 6.5 and 5.5 expected), so the corrected statistic is almost 0 and p = 0.986, against Fisher’s 0.775. Both R’s chisq.test() and scipy’s chi2_contingency() apply it to 2 × 2 tables by default; without it (correct = FALSE, correction=False) p = 0.754. Either is acceptable if you say which you used; with small counts, prefer Fisher’s test.





Effect size and 95% CI
Two effect sizes, and it’s worth reporting both:

The risk difference: the difference between the two percentages, in percentage points. It’s what patients and clinicians understand. Its CI here is the simple “estimate ± 1.96 standard errors” interval, called a Wald CI: prop.test(..., correct = FALSE) in R, method="wald" in Python.
The odds ratio: the odds of failure with a hamstring graft divided by the odds with a BPTB graft. It’s what logistic regression reports (page 11), so it’s useful for comparing with other studies.


RPython



failure_fisher$estimate                  # odds ratio, hamstring vs BPTB

odds ratio 
 0.8316302 

failure_fisher$conf.int                  # its 95% CI

[1] 0.2163564 3.1962761

[1] 0.95

risk$estimate                            # failure rate with each graft: hamstring, then BPTB

How to report it

Methods: Graft failure within 2 years was compared between hamstring and BPTB grafts with Fisher’s exact test. Effect sizes are reported as risk differences with Wald 95% CIs and as odds ratios with exact 95% CIs.
