With only 12 failures, this study can’t tell. “No significant difference” is the honest wording; “hamstring and BPTB grafts fail equally often” isn’t.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: two different odds ratios



scipy’s fisher_exact() reports the simple sample odds ratio (a × d) / (b × c), 0.8311 here. R’s fisher.test() reports the conditional maximum-likelihood odds ratio, 0.8316, which goes with its exact CI. Use scipy.stats.contingency.odds_ratio(..., kind="conditional") to get R’s number and CI. The two are always close; say which you report. In our table the sample odds ratio is (6 × 123) / (148 × 6) = 0.8311.

title: 6 · Compare two unpaired groups
text:
Log-rank test
The question: Is revision-free survival different between implant A and implant C?

When to use it

The outcome is time until an event (revision), patients were followed for different lengths of time, and you’re comparing two independent groups.
It compares the whole survival curves, not the survival at one time point.
The Mantel-Haenszel test (or Mantel-Cox test) in the decision table is the same test under another name.
It’s most powerful when one group’s hazard is a steady multiple of the other’s over time (proportional hazards). If the curves cross, see page 14.
To compare three or more groups, or to adjust for other variables → Cox regression.



What the test really does
The log-rank test compares the two groups over the whole follow-up, one revision at a time.

Start at surgery and move forward in time. Each time a revision happens, look at who was still being followed just before it: the patients at risk.
If the two implants carried the same risk, that revision was equally likely to happen to any patient at risk. So each group’s expected share of it is simply its share of the patients at risk.
Add these shares up over all the revisions. Each group ends with an observed number of revisions and an expected number.
The test statistic measures how far observed is from expected, compared with how far chance alone would put it. A large gap gives a small p-value.

A patient who leaves the study early is censored: they count among the patients at risk for as long as they were followed, and not after.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
a_vs_c <- cohort |> filter(implant %in% c("A", "C"))   # two groups; page 8 compares all three

survfit2(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ implant, data = a_vs_c, conf.type = "log-log") |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable() +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Years since surgery", y = "Revision-free survival")











import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from lifelines import KaplanMeierFitter, CoxPHFitter
from lifelines.statistics import logrank_test
from lifelines.plotting import add_at_risk_counts

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")
a_vs_c = cohort[cohort["implant"].isin(["A", "C"])]   # two groups; page 8 compares all three
a = a_vs_c[a_vs_c["implant"] == "A"]
c = a_vs_c[a_vs_c["implant"] == "C"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
km_a = KaplanMeierFitter(label="A").fit(a["followup_years"], a["revised"])
km_c = KaplanMeierFitter(label="C").fit(c["followup_years"], c["revised"])
km_a.plot_survival_function(ax=ax)
km_c.plot_survival_function(ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Years since surgery")
ax.set_ylabel("Revision-free survival")
add_at_risk_counts(km_a, km_c, ax=ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()











Implant C’s curve falls faster from the start, and the gap keeps growing.


Run it

RPython



implant_logrank <- survdiff(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ implant, data = a_vs_c)
implant_logrank

Call:

implant=C 137       38     21.1     13.62      20.5

implant_logrank = logrank_test(a["followup_years"], c["followup_years"],
                               event_observed_A=a["revised"], event_observed_B=c["revised"])
print(implant_logrank.test_statistic, implant_logrank.p_value)

20.534618183417702 5.856248429692094e-06







Read the output

N: patients in each group (246 with implant A, 137 with C).
Observed / Expected: the revisions each group had, and the number it would have had if both implants carried the same risk. Implant C had 38 revisions where 21.1 were expected; implant A had 25 where 41.9 were expected.
Chisq = 20.5 on 1 degree of freedom, p < 0.001: curves this different would be very unlikely if the implants had the same revision risk. R prints the p-value as p= 6e-06, which is 0.000006 (the decimal point moves 6 places to the left).
Python prints only two numbers: the test statistic (20.53) and the p-value. N, Observed and Expected are in R’s output; the box below works out observed and expected by hand in both languages. R’s last column, (O-E)^2/V, is the test statistic again, and you can ignore (O-E)^2/E.







Note🔍 Under the hood: observed and expected revisions by hand






RPython



revision_times <- sort(unique(a_vs_c$followup_years[a_vs_c$revised == 1]))    # every time at which a revision happened
expected_a <- sum(sapply(revision_times, function(time) {
  at_risk <- a_vs_c$followup_years >= time                                    # step 1: still followed just before this time
  revisions <- sum(a_vs_c$followup_years == time & a_vs_c$revised == 1)       # revisions at this time (usually 1)
  revisions * sum(at_risk & a_vs_c$implant == "A") / sum(at_risk)             # step 2: implant A's expected share of them
}))                                                                           # step 3: add up over all the times
c(observed_a = sum(a_vs_c$revised[a_vs_c$implant == "A"]), expected_a = expected_a)

observed_a expected_a 
  25.00000   41.93934 





revision_times = sorted(a_vs_c.loc[a_vs_c["revised"] == 1, "followup_years"].unique())   # every time at which a revision happened
expected_a = 0.0
for time in revision_times:
    at_risk = a_vs_c["followup_years"] >= time                                            # step 1: still followed just before this time
    revisions = ((a_vs_c["followup_years"] == time) & (a_vs_c["revised"] == 1)).sum()     # revisions at this time (usually 1)
    expected_a += revisions * (at_risk & (a_vs_c["implant"] == "A")).sum() / at_risk.sum()   # steps 2 and 3: implant A's expected share, added up
print(a["revised"].sum(), expected_a)

25 41.93933651452793





Implant A had 25 revisions where 41.9 were expected if both implants carried the same risk. These are the Observed and Expected numbers in R’s output; lifelines doesn’t print them, so this is where a Python reader can see them.





Effect size and 95% CI
The log-rank test has no effect size of its own. The usual one is the hazard ratio from a Cox model: how many times higher the hazard of revision is, at any moment, with implant C than with implant A. Page 14 explains Cox regression in full.

RPython



implant_cox <- coxph(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ implant, data = a_vs_c)
summary(implant_cox)$conf.int    # exp(coef) is the hazard ratio, C vs A

The hazard of revision was about three times higher with implant C (hazard ratio 3.04, 95% CI 1.83 to 5.04).

Read the survival column and its two CI columns (R), or the three numbers on each line (Python), times 100: 89.9% (84.7% to 93.3%) with implant A and 71.1% (61.5% to 78.8%) with implant C.


How to report it

Methods: Revision-free survival was estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method and compared between implants with the log-rank test. Hazard ratios were estimated with Cox proportional hazards regression.
Results: Revision-free survival at 5 years was 71.1% (95% CI 61.5% to 78.8%) with implant C and 89.9% (95% CI 84.7% to 93.3%) with implant A (log-rank p < 0.001; hazard ratio 3.04, 95% CI 1.83 to 5.04).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: overlapping CIs aren’t a test



Comparing the two curves’ CIs at one time point (“the 5-year CIs overlap, so there’s no difference”) isn’t a valid test, and neither is comparing the crude percentages revised. Use the log-rank test on the whole curves. And as on page 4, deaths here are treated as censored; page 13 covers competing risks.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: one formula or two groups



R’s survdiff() takes a formula with a grouping variable. lifelines’ logrank_test() takes each group’s follow-up times and events separately (multivariate_logrank_test() takes a grouping column). They compute the same test. Both Cox models handle tied revision times with Efron’s method, so the hazard ratios agree. The R code sets conf.type = "log-log" because that is the CI method lifelines uses (page 4).

title: 4 · Describe one group
text: Before you compare anything, describe it. This page covers the first row of the decision table: one number (or one curve) that sums up a group of patients, with a 95% confidence interval that says how precisely you know it. Which summary you use depends on the column, the type of data you have. Page 3 explains how to choose.

title: 4 · Describe one group
text:
Mean and standard deviation
The question: How old are our patients, and how much do their ages vary?

When to use it

The variable is a measurement (age, BMI, operative time), not a category.
Its distribution is roughly symmetric, without extreme outliers. Check with a histogram (page 3).
If it’s skewed, has a ceiling or floor, or is ordinal → use the median and IQR instead.



What the calculation really does
The mean and the SD are two short pieces of arithmetic. The confidence interval adds a third.

Mean: add up all the ages and divide by the number of cases.
Distances: subtract the mean from each age. Some distances are positive and some negative, and together they always add up to 0, so they can’t simply be averaged.
Variance: square each distance, which makes them all positive. Add the squares up and divide by n − 1, one less than the number of cases.
Standard deviation (SD): take the square root of the variance. That brings the result back to years: the typical distance of a patient’s age from the mean.
Confidence interval (CI): divide the SD by √n to get the standard error of the mean, then go about 2 standard errors either side of the mean.

Once the numbers are in, a box under “Read the output” does each step by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(cohort, aes(age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(cohort$age), linetype = "dashed") +   # the mean
  labs(x = "Age at surgery, years", y = "Patients")











import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.hist(cohort["age"], bins=range(40, 90, 2))
ax.axvline(cohort["age"].mean(), linestyle="--")       # the mean
ax.set_xlabel("Age at surgery, years")
ax.set_ylabel("Patients")
plt.show()











A single, roughly symmetric hump: the mean sits in the middle of it, so it’s a fair summary.


Run it

RPython



age_summary <- cohort |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(age), sd = sd(age))
age_summary

Read the output

n = 600: the number of cases with an age recorded.
Mean = 65.5 years: the average age.
SD = 9.4 years: the standard deviation, the typical distance of a patient’s age from the mean. In a bell-shaped distribution about 95% of patients lie within 2 SDs of the mean, here 65.5 ± 2 × 9.4, roughly 47 to 84 years.
95% CI 64.8 to 66.3: the confidence interval for the mean. It tells you how precisely 600 patients pin down the average age of patients like ours. It says nothing about how spread out individual patients are; that’s the SD’s job.

distance <- ages - mean(ages)                          # step 2: each case's distance from the mean
head(distance, 5)

[1] -9.52 16.48 -6.52  0.48  1.48

age_variance <- sum(distance^2) / (600 - 1)            # step 3: the variance, the squared distances added up ÷ (n − 1)
c(variance = age_variance, sd = sqrt(age_variance))    # step 4: the SD is its square root

 variance        sd 
89.024641  9.435287 

age_se <- sqrt(age_variance) / sqrt(600)               # step 5: the standard error, SD ÷ √n
t_multiplier <- qt(0.975, df = 600 - 1)                # the exact multiplier that "about 2" stands for
c(standard_error = age_se, t = t_multiplier)

standard_error              t 
      0.385194       1.963932 

mean(ages) + c(-1, 1) * t_multiplier * age_se          # the 95% CI

[1] 64.76351 66.27649





ages = cohort["age"]
print(ages.head(5).to_list())                          # the first 5 ages

[56, 82, 59, 66, 67]

print(ages.sum() / 600)                                # step 1: the mean, the sum of the ages ÷ 600 cases

65.52

distance = ages - ages.mean()                          # step 2: each case's distance from the mean
print(distance.head(5).round(2).to_list())

[-9.52, 16.48, -6.52, 0.48, 1.48]

age_variance = (distance ** 2).sum() / (600 - 1)       # step 3: the variance, the squared distances added up ÷ (n − 1)
print(age_variance, age_variance ** 0.5)               # step 4: the SD is its square root

89.02464106844742 9.435287015689953

age_se = age_variance ** 0.5 / 600 ** 0.5              # step 5: the standard error, SD ÷ √n
t_multiplier = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=600 - 1)          # the exact multiplier that "about 2" stands for
print(age_se, t_multiplier)

0.38519397941913075 1.9639322489452784

print(ages.mean() - t_multiplier * age_se, ages.mean() + t_multiplier * age_se)   # the 95% CI

64.7635051217192 66.27649487828079





The first case was 56 years old, which is 56 − 65.52 = −9.52 years from the mean. The variance comes to 89.02, and its square root is the SD the software printed, 9.44 years. The standard error is 0.385 years and the exact multiplier is 1.964, so the CI is 65.52 ± 1.964 × 0.385: from 64.76 to 66.28, as in the output.
The multiplier is called t. It is close to 1.96 for large samples and a little bigger for small ones. Quadruple the sample size and the standard error halves; the SD stays about the same.





How to report it

Methods: Continuous variables are reported as mean (standard deviation, SD) when approximately normally distributed.
Results: The mean age at surgery was 65.5 years (SD 9.4; 95% CI for the mean 64.8 to 66.3).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: SD or SEM?



The standard error of the mean (SEM) is the SD divided by √n: 9.44 / √600 ≈ 0.39 years here, much smaller than the SD of 9.4 years. That is why some papers report “mean ± SEM”: it looks tidier. But it describes the precision of the mean, not your patients. Use the SD to describe patients and a 95% CI to show the precision of an estimate. Never report a bare “±” without saying which one it is.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: dividing by n or n − 1



R’s sd() and pandas’ .std() divide by n − 1 (the “sample” SD), which is what you want. NumPy’s np.std() divides by n unless you write np.std(x, ddof=1). With 600 patients the difference is tiny; with 10 it isn’t.

title: 4 · Describe one group
text:
Median and interquartile range
The question: What’s a typical Oxford Hip Score 1 year after hip replacement, and how much do scores vary?

When to use it

The variable is skewed, has a ceiling or floor, has outliers, or is ordinal (an ordered scale such as satisfaction from 1 to 5).
The median is the middle value: half the patients are above it and half below. The interquartile range (IQR) runs from the 25th to the 75th percentile (the first and third quartiles), so it holds the middle half of the patients.
If the variable is a roughly symmetric measurement → the mean and SD are fine and more familiar.



What the calculation really does
The median and the quartiles come from sorting, not from adding.

Sort the scores from lowest to highest.
Median: take the score in the middle of the sorted list. With an even number of scores there are two middle scores, and the median is halfway between them.
Quartiles: do the same a quarter and three quarters of the way along the list. The interquartile range runs from the first of these scores to the second.
Only the order matters, so extreme scores don’t move the median: the lowest score could drop to 0 and the middle of the list would stay where it is.

Once the numbers are in, a box under “Read the output” finds the same scores by their position in the list.


Look at the data first
The Oxford Hip Score (OHS) adds up 12 questions scored 0 to 4, so it runs from 0 to 48, and 48 is the best. The practice records it for every hip replacement, before surgery and at each follow-up visit.

RPython



library(tidyverse)

proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ohs_1yr <- proms |>
  filter(visit == "1yr", !is.na(ohs)) |>   # ohs is blank for knee replacements and missed visits
  pull(ohs)

length(ohs_1yr)                            # how many scores

[1] 194

sum(ohs_1yr == 48)                         # how many of them are the maximum, 48

[1] 39

ggplot(tibble(score = ohs_1yr), aes(score)) +
  geom_bar() +                             # one bar per whole score
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 48)) +       # the whole scale
  labs(x = "Oxford Hip Score at 1 year (48 = best)", y = "Patients")











import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")
ohs_1yr = proms.loc[proms["visit"] == "1yr", "ohs"].dropna()   # ohs is blank for knee replacements and missed visits

print(len(ohs_1yr))                          # how many scores

194

print((ohs_1yr == 48).sum())                 # how many of them are the maximum, 48

39

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.hist(ohs_1yr, bins=np.arange(-0.5, 49))   # one bar per whole score, over the whole scale
ax.set_xlabel("Oxford Hip Score at 1 year (48 = best)")
ax.set_ylabel("Patients")
plt.show()











Scores pile up against the maximum of 48 (a ceiling): 39 of the 194 scores were 48 (the two numbers printed above the plot, in reverse order). Below the pile there’s a long tail of patients who did less well. A mean would be dragged down by that tail; the median isn’t.


Run it

RPython



length(ohs_1yr)                                # how many patients

[1] 194

quantile(ohs_1yr, probs = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75)) # first quartile, median, third quartile

25% 50% 75% 
 39  42  46 

DescTools::MedianCI(ohs_1yr, method = "exact") # the median with its 95% CI

median lwr.ci upr.ci 
    42     41     43 
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.9629381

sum(ohs_1yr == 42)                             # how many scored exactly the median, 42

[1] 13

sum(ohs_1yr <= 39)                             # how many scored the first quartile, 39, or less

[1] 62

mean(ohs_1yr <= 39)                            # the same as a proportion

[1] 0.3195876





print(len(ohs_1yr))                                      # how many patients

194

print(np.quantile(ohs_1yr, [0.25, 0.50, 0.75]))          # first quartile, median, third quartile

[39. 42. 46.]

# scipy has no "median CI" function, but quantile_test() reports one.
# Its q argument is the value it would test against; it doesn't change the CI.
median_ci = stats.quantile_test(ohs_1yr, q=ohs_1yr.median(), p=0.5).confidence_interval()
print(median_ci)

ConfidenceInterval(low=np.float64(41.0), high=np.float64(43.0))

print((ohs_1yr == 42).sum())                             # how many scored exactly the median, 42

13

print((ohs_1yr <= 39).sum())                             # how many scored the first quartile, 39, or less

62

print((ohs_1yr <= 39).mean())                            # the same as a proportion

0.31958762886597936







Read the output

n = 194: hip replacements with an Oxford Hip Score at 1 year.
Median = 42: the middle score. With whole-number scores many patients share it (13 scored exactly 42: the first of the three numbers at the end of the output), so “half above, half below” is only roughly true.
IQR 39 to 46: the middle half of the patients scored between these two values. At least a quarter scored 39 or less: with ties, 62 of the 194 did, a proportion of 0.32 or 32% (the last two numbers of the output).
95% CI for the median 41 to 43: how precisely 194 patients pin down the median. Under the interval, R prints conf.level and 0.9629: the confidence this interval really has, a little more than the 95% asked for (the box below shows why). Python doesn’t print it.







Note🔍 Under the hood: the median, the quartiles and the CI by hand






RPython



sorted_scores <- sort(ohs_1yr)                              # step 1: sort the 194 scores
sorted_scores[c(97, 98)]                                    # step 2: the two middle scores, the 97th and the 98th

[1] 42 42

1 + (194 - 1) * c(0.25, 0.75)                               # step 3: the positions a quarter and three quarters of the way along the list

[1]  49.25 145.75

sorted_scores[c(49, 50)]                                    # the 49th and the 50th score: the first quartile lies between them

[1] 39 39

sorted_scores[c(145, 146)]                                  # the 145th and the 146th score: the third quartile lies between them

[1] 46 46

ci_position <- qbinom(0.025, size = 194, prob = 0.5)        # the CI: the binomial distribution gives a position below the middle
c(ci_position, 194 - ci_position + 1)                       # that position, and the same position counted from the top

[1]  83 112

sorted_scores[c(ci_position, 194 - ci_position + 1)]        # the scores at those two positions are the CI

[1] 41 43

1 - 2 * pbinom(ci_position - 1, size = 194, prob = 0.5)     # the confidence these two positions really give

[1] 0.9629381





sorted_scores = np.sort(ohs_1yr)                            # step 1: sort the 194 scores
print(sorted_scores[[97 - 1, 98 - 1]])                      # step 2: the two middle scores, the 97th and the 98th (Python counts from 0, so subtract 1)

[42. 42.]

print(1 + (194 - 1) * np.array([0.25, 0.75]))               # step 3: the positions a quarter and three quarters of the way along the list

[ 49.25 145.75]

print(sorted_scores[[49 - 1, 50 - 1]])                      # the 49th and the 50th score: the first quartile lies between them

[39. 39.]

print(sorted_scores[[145 - 1, 146 - 1]])                    # the 145th and the 146th score: the third quartile lies between them

[46. 46.]

ci_position = int(stats.binom.ppf(0.025, 194, 0.5))         # the CI: the binomial distribution gives a position below the middle
print(ci_position, 194 - ci_position + 1)                   # that position, and the same position counted from the top

83 112

print(sorted_scores[[ci_position - 1, 194 - ci_position]])  # the scores at those two positions are the CI

[41. 43.]

print(1 - 2 * stats.binom.cdf(ci_position - 1, 194, 0.5))   # the confidence these two positions really give

0.9629380859521739





Both middle scores are 42, so the median is 42. The quartiles sit at positions 49.25 and 145.75. The 49th and 50th scores are both 39, and the 145th and 146th are both 46, so the quartiles are 39 and 46.
The CI for a median uses no formula with an SD in it. It counts instead. Each patient is as likely to score above the true median as below it, like a coin toss. The binomial distribution, which describes coin tosses, says that out of 194 patients, fewer than 83 landing on one side would happen less than 2.5% of the time. So the 83rd score from the bottom is rarely above the true median, and the 83rd from the top (the 112th from the bottom) is rarely below it. Those two scores are 41 and 43, the CI in the output. Because positions are whole numbers, the confidence comes out a little over 95%: 0.9629, the number R reports. This “exact” method needs no assumption about the shape of the data.





How to report it

Methods: Continuous variables that were skewed or bounded are reported as median (interquartile range, IQR).
Results: The median Oxford Hip Score at 1 year was 42 points (IQR 39 to 46; 95% CI for the median 41 to 43).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: report the IQR as two numbers



Write “IQR 39 to 46”, not “IQR 7” (the width). Readers want to know where the middle half of patients sits, not just how wide it is. And don’t report a median with an SD: they belong to different summaries.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: quartiles



R’s quantile() and NumPy’s np.quantile() use the same default method (R calls it “type 7”), so they agree. Other software doesn’t always: gtsummary, SPSS and SAS can give slightly different quartiles on the same data (page 2 shows an example). Say which software you used.

title: 4 · Describe one group
text:
Proportion
The question: What proportion of hip fracture patients died within 30 days?

When to use it

The outcome is yes/no (binomial): death within 30 days, complication, discharge home.
Report the count, the percentage, and a 95% CI for the percentage.
If patients were followed for different lengths of time and the event can happen at any time (revision, death) → use a Kaplan-Meier curve instead. Here every patient was followed for at least 30 days or until death, so the 30-day proportion is complete (“Look at the data first” checks this).



What the calculation really does
A proportion is one count divided by another. The work is in its confidence interval.

Count the patients with the event, and the patients whose outcome is known.
Divide the first count by the second. That is the proportion; multiply it by 100 for a percentage.
The simple recipe for the CI is the proportion ± 1.96 standard errors, with the standard error worked out from the sample’s own proportion. This is the Wald interval, and it works badly when the event is rare or the group is small.
The Wilson interval turns the question around. It collects every true proportion from which our observed proportion would lie no more than 1.96 standard errors away, and it works the standard error out from each of those candidates in turn. The result is not centered on the observed proportion: it is pulled a little toward 50%, and it can never go below 0% or above 100%.

Once the numbers are in, a box under “Read the output” calculates both intervals by hand.


Look at the data first
The hip fracture data hold one row per patient aged 65 or over who was treated for a hip fracture. For a yes/no variable, “looking” means counting, including the missing values.

RPython



library(tidyverse)

hip_fracture <- read_csv("data/hip_fracture.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

count(hip_fracture, death_30d)   # 1 = died within 30 days, 0 = alive at 30 days

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  death_30d     n
      <dbl> <int>
1         0  1126
2         1    74

count(hip_fracture, died, followup_days <= 30)   # died: 1 = died during follow-up. Did the follow-up end by day 30?

# A tibble: 3 × 3
   died `followup_days <= 30`     n
  <dbl> <lgl>                 <int>
1     0 FALSE                   847
2     1 FALSE                   279
3     1 TRUE                     74





import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

hip_fracture = pd.read_csv("data/hip_fracture.csv")

print(hip_fracture["death_30d"].value_counts(dropna=False))   # 1 = died within 30 days, 0 = alive at 30 days

death_30d
0    1126
1      74
Name: count, dtype: int64

print(pd.crosstab(hip_fracture["died"], hip_fracture["followup_days"] <= 30))   # died: 1 = died during follow-up. Did the follow-up end by day 30?

followup_days  False  True 
died                       
0                847      0
1                279     74





No missing values, and only the two codes the codebook allows (0 and 1). The second table checks the follow-up. It ended by day 30 only for the 74 patients who died in that time. All 847 patients who were still alive at the end of their follow-up (died = 0) were followed for longer, so nobody’s 30-day outcome is unknown.


Run it

RPython



deaths   <- sum(hip_fracture$death_30d == 1)
patients <- nrow(hip_fracture)

deaths / patients                                           # the proportion

[1] 0.06166667

# Wilson 95% CI: prop.test() without the continuity correction
prop.test(deaths, patients, correct = FALSE)$conf.int

[1] 0.04940522 0.07672555
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95





deaths = int((hip_fracture["death_30d"] == 1).sum())
patients = len(hip_fracture)

print(deaths / patients)                                    # the proportion

0.06166666666666667

# Wilson 95% CI
print(stats.binomtest(deaths, patients).proportion_ci(method="wilson"))

ConfidenceInterval(low=np.float64(0.04940522288254482), high=np.float64(0.07672555431251947))







Read the output

74 of 1,200 = 0.062: the first count shows 74 deaths and 1,126 survivors, 1,200 patients in all. 74 / 1,200 = 0.0617, so 6.2% of patients died within 30 days of admission.
95% CI 0.049 to 0.077: the true 30-day mortality for patients like ours is plausibly anywhere from 4.9% to 7.7%.







Note🔍 Under the hood: the Wald and Wilson intervals by hand






RPython



p_hat <- deaths / patients                                     # the observed proportion
z <- qnorm(0.975)                                              # the multiplier for 95%, 1.96
wald_se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / patients)                # the standard error, worked out from our own proportion
p_hat + c(-1, 1) * z * wald_se                                 # the Wald interval: the proportion ± 1.96 standard errors

[1] 0.04805657 0.07527677

wilson_center <- (p_hat + z^2 / (2 * patients)) / (1 + z^2 / patients)   # Wilson: the center, pulled toward 0.5, and the half-width
wilson_half <- z * sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / patients + z^2 / (4 * patients^2)) / (1 + z^2 / patients)
c(center = wilson_center, half_width = wilson_half)

    center half_width 
0.06306539 0.01366017 

wilson_center + c(-1, 1) * wilson_half                         # the Wilson interval

[1] 0.04940522 0.07672555

lower_limit <- wilson_center - wilson_half
c(p_hat - lower_limit, z * sqrt(lower_limit * (1 - lower_limit) / patients))   # at the lower limit: the distance to our proportion, and 1.96 standard errors worked out from the limit

[1] 0.01226144 0.01226144





p_hat = deaths / patients                                      # the observed proportion
z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975)                                      # the multiplier for 95%, 1.96
wald_se = (p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / patients) ** 0.5              # the standard error, worked out from our own proportion
print(p_hat - z * wald_se, p_hat + z * wald_se)                # the Wald interval: the proportion ± 1.96 standard errors

0.04805656789247553 0.0752767654408578

wilson_center = (p_hat + z ** 2 / (2 * patients)) / (1 + z ** 2 / patients)   # Wilson: the center, pulled toward 0.5, and the half-width
wilson_half = z * (p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / patients + z ** 2 / (4 * patients ** 2)) ** 0.5 / (1 + z ** 2 / patients)
print(wilson_center, wilson_half)

0.06306538859753215 0.013660165714987323

print(wilson_center - wilson_half, wilson_center + wilson_half)   # the Wilson interval

0.04940522288254483 0.07672555431251947

lower_limit = wilson_center - wilson_half
print(p_hat - lower_limit, z * (lower_limit * (1 - lower_limit) / patients) ** 0.5)   # at the lower limit: the distance to our proportion, and 1.96 standard errors worked out from the limit

0.01226144378412184 0.012261443784121851





The Wald interval would run from 0.048 to 0.075. The Wilson interval runs from 0.049 to 0.077, as in the output. It sits a little higher because its center is 0.0631, not our proportion of 0.0617. The last line shows what defines it: the lower limit, 0.0494, lies 0.0123 below our proportion, and 1.96 standard errors worked out from 0.0494 are also 0.0123. With 74 deaths among 1,200 patients the two intervals are close. With fewer patients or a rarer event they move apart.





How to report it

Methods: Categorical variables are reported as number (percentage). 95% confidence intervals for proportions were calculated with the Wilson score method.
Results: Within 30 days of admission, 74 of 1,200 patients died (6.2%; 95% CI 4.9% to 7.7%).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: percent of what?




Say what the denominator is. Here it’s 1,200 patients: the hip fracture data have one row per patient. In the joint replacement cohort, rows are procedures, and the 80 patients who had both sides operated on (page 2 counts them) count twice, so a percentage there is a percentage of procedures. If some outcomes were missing, the denominator is the patients with a known outcome; say how many were missing.
Don’t use the simple “± 1.96 standard errors” CI (the Wald interval) for proportions. For rare events it can dip below 0%. The Wilson interval doesn’t.









Tip🔀 R vs Python: which CI for a proportion?



R’s prop.test() gives the Wilson interval, but adds a continuity correction unless you set correct = FALSE. scipy’s proportion_ci() calls the uncorrected version "wilson" and the corrected one "wilsoncc". R’s binom.test() and scipy’s method="exact" give the more conservative Clopper-Pearson interval (page 5 uses it). All are acceptable; say which you used.

title: 4 · Describe one group
text:
Kaplan-Meier survival curve
The question: What proportion of implants are still unrevised 5 years after surgery?

When to use it

The outcome is time until an event (revision, death), and patients were followed for different lengths of time.
Some patients are censored: their follow-up ended (the study closed, they moved away, they died) before any revision. We know they went at least that long without one.
A plain percentage (81 of our 600 cases were revised, 13.5%; the next step counts them) ignores follow-up time: a patient operated on last year hasn’t had time to need a revision. The Kaplan-Meier method uses each patient’s follow-up for as long as it lasts.

Page 13 covers survival analysis in depth. This section shows the basic curve.


What the calculation really does
The Kaplan-Meier method builds the curve one revision at a time.

Put the cases in order of follow-up time. At any moment, the cases still being followed and not yet revised are at risk.
Each time a revision happens, work out the fraction of the cases at risk that got past that moment without one: 1 − revisions ÷ cases at risk.
Multiply these fractions together, from the day of surgery up to the time you are interested in. The product is the estimated proportion still unrevised at that time. Plotted against time, it is the curve.
A censored case counts among those at risk until its follow-up ends, and then leaves the count. It never makes the curve step down. But every later revision is divided by fewer cases at risk, so each later step is a little bigger.

Once the curve is drawn, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds the 5-year estimate by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# followup_years: time from surgery to revision or censoring; revised: 1 = revised, 0 = censored
cohort |> select(case_id, followup_years, revised) |> head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  case_id followup_years revised
  <chr>            <dbl>   <dbl>
1 C0001             6.23       0
2 C0002             3.27       0
3 C0003            11.0        0
4 C0004            10.9        0
5 C0005             5.79       1

cohort |> summarise(patients = n(), revisions = sum(revised),
                    median_followup = median(followup_years))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  patients revisions median_followup
     <int>     <dbl>           <dbl>
1      600        81            4.36





import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from lifelines import KaplanMeierFitter
from lifelines.plotting import add_at_risk_counts

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")

# followup_years: time from surgery to revision or censoring; revised: 1 = revised, 0 = censored
print(cohort[["case_id", "followup_years", "revised"]].head(5))

  case_id  followup_years  revised
0   C0001            6.23        0
1   C0002            3.27        0
2   C0003           10.96        0
3   C0004           10.94        0
4   C0005            5.79        1

600 81 4.365





Each row needs exactly two things: how long the patient was followed and whether the follow-up ended with the event (1) or was censored (0). The first case was followed for 6.2 years without a revision; the fifth was revised at 5.8 years. The second output counts 600 cases and 81 revisions, the 81 / 600 = 0.135 above, with a median follow-up of 4.365 years (R shows it as 4.36). Python prints the three numbers without labels.


Run it

               conf.type = "log-log")              # the CI method lifelines uses

km |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable() +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Years since surgery", y = "Revision-free survival")

km.plot_survival_function(ax=ax, legend=False)
ax.set_xlabel("Years since surgery")
ax.set_ylabel("Revision-free survival")

263







Read the output

The curve starts at 100% and steps down at each revision. Censored patients don’t make it step; they just leave the group “at risk”.
The shaded band is the 95% CI. It widens to the right as fewer patients remain under follow-up.
The numbers at risk under the plot show how many patients were still being followed at each time. Trust the right-hand end of the curve less: by 10 years only 21 of the 600 cases remain (the last number in the first row under the plot).
At 5 years: survival 0.863 (95% CI 0.828 to 0.892), with 263 patients still at risk (n.risk in R, the last number Python prints).
The rest of what is printed: in R’s line, n.event 66 is the number of revisions up to 5 years (81 over the whole follow-up) and std.err is the standard error of the estimate. Python’s first line, “600 total observations, 519 right-censored observations”, restates the data: 600 cases − 81 revisions = 519 censored.







Note🔍 Under the hood: the 5-year estimate by hand






RPython



km_steps <- cohort |>
  filter(revised == 1, followup_years <= 5) |>                # the revisions in the first 5 years
  count(followup_years, name = "revisions") |>                # one row per moment at which a revision happened
  mutate(at_risk = map_int(followup_years, \(t) sum(cohort$followup_years >= t)),   # step 1: the cases still at risk at that moment
         got_past = 1 - revisions / at_risk)                  # step 2: the fraction that got past it

early = cohort[(cohort["revised"] == 1) & (cohort["followup_years"] <= 5)]   # the revisions in the first 5 years
km_steps = early.groupby("followup_years").size().rename("revisions").reset_index()   # one row per moment at which a revision happened
km_steps["at_risk"] = [(cohort["followup_years"] >= t).sum() for t in km_steps["followup_years"]]   # step 1: the cases still at risk at that moment
km_steps["got_past"] = 1 - km_steps["revisions"] / km_steps["at_risk"]       # step 2: the fraction that got past it

The first revisions came 0.03 years after surgery: 2 among the 599 cases still at risk, so a fraction of 0.997 got past that moment. The first 5 years hold 59 such moments, with 66 revisions between them. The 59 fractions multiplied together give 0.863, the estimate at 5 years.





How to report it

Methods: Implant survivorship was estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method, with revision for any reason as the end point. Patients were censored at death or at their last follow-up.
Results: Revision-free survival at 5 years was 86.3% (95% CI 82.8% to 89.2%; 263 patients at risk).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: death isn’t just “lost to follow-up”



Treating deaths as censored, as here, assumes the patients who died would have gone on to be revised at the same rate as everyone else. They can’t be: a patient who has died can never be revised. When many patients die during follow-up, 1 minus the Kaplan-Meier estimate overstates the risk of revision. Page 13 shows the competing-risks method that fixes this.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: the confidence band



R’s survfit() uses a “log” CI by default; lifelines uses “log-log”. The estimates are identical but the CIs differ slightly. We set conf.type = "log-log" in R so the two match. Log-log keeps the CI between 0% and 100%; say which you used.
The tables under the two plots differ by one case at 4 years and at 8 years (332 and 84 in R, 331 and 83 in Python). R counts a case whose follow-up ends exactly at that time as still at risk; lifelines doesn’t. For the same reason lifelines’ own count at 5 years would be 258, not 263: the follow-up of 5 cases ends at exactly 5 years. The Python code above counts the way R does. lifelines also adds a row for the cases censored so far.

Software guesses variable types, and the guesses are often wrong:

ASA class looks like a number, so tableone averages it unless you list it under categorical: “mean (SD) 2.4 (0.7)” in the Python output above. It’s a category.

title: 2 · Demographics (Table 1)
text:
Mean (SD) or median (IQR)?

Roughly symmetric continuous variables (age, BMI): mean (SD).
Skewed or bounded variables (length of stay, most PROMs): median (IQR). One patient with a 30-day stay drags the mean far more than the median.
Categories: n (%).

How do you know whether a variable is skewed? Look at it: Distributions & choosing a test shows how. Length of stay is strongly right-skewed, which is why it gets a median.






Tip🔀 R vs Python: quartiles



gtsummary and tableone use different formulas for quartiles (in R’s terms, quantile() types 2 and 7). With whole-number data like length of stay the results can differ. In the table above the two agree (0 to 1 day). In the THA column of the next table they don’t: the upper quartile is 2 days in R (1 (0–2)) and 1.8 in Python (1.0 [0.0,1.8]). Neither is wrong. Say in your Methods which software you used.

text:
p-values or standardized mean differences?
Look at sex in the table above: 66% of THA patients are women against 50% of TKA patients, p < 0.001. Is that a real difference between hip and knee patients?
In this practice dataset we know the answer, because we wrote the program that made it: sex was drawn completely independently of procedure. The difference is pure chance. (In real arthroplasty cohorts, TKA patients are usually more often female.) That’s the first problem with p-values in Table 1: across a long table, chance differences turn up.
The second problem is that a p-value mixes up how big a difference is with how many patients you have. With 6,000 patients a trivial difference gets p < 0.001. With 30, a large one doesn’t.
The standardized mean difference (SMD) measures only the size of the imbalance, in standard-deviation units, whatever the sample size. A common rule of thumb: |SMD| below 0.1 is negligible.

smd::smd(cohort$age, cohort$procedure)   # the function gtsummary calls; its table rounds this to 0.10

  term  estimate
1  TKA 0.1047628





print(round(abs(balance.smd_table.loc["age"].iloc[0]), 4))   # the age row of the table above, without its sign

0.1046











Tip🔀 R vs Python: SMDs differ slightly




Sign. For the variables entered as numbers (age, BMI, length of stay), gtsummary subtracts TKA from THA and tableone subtracts THA from TKA, so the signs are opposite. For categories (sex, ASA class, smoking) the SMD has no direction and is positive in both. Report the absolute value, or say which group was subtracted from which.
Fourth decimal. For continuous variables, R’s smd package divides the variances by n, while tableone divides by n − 1 (the usual textbook formula). Age comes out as 0.1048 in R and 0.1046 in Python (the two numbers printed just above the box). Categorical SMDs match exactly.



Which should you report?

Matched or weighted cohorts (propensity-score studies, such as a matched study of patients over 80): SMDs only. The matching made the groups alike on purpose, so a test of “did they differ?” makes no sense.
Other observational comparisons: many journals still expect p-values. Give SMDs alongside, and discuss differences by their size, not their p-value.

Exporting to Word
Journals want Table 1 in Word. Save it into your scratch/ folder (git ignores it), open it, and paste it into the manuscript.

  as_flex_table() |>
  flextable::save_as_docx(path = "scratch/table1.docx")




from docx import Document

table = by_procedure.tableone.reset_index()
headers = [" ".join(str(part) for part in col if part).strip() for col in table.columns]

doc = Document()
grid = doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=len(headers))
for cell, header in zip(grid.rows[0].cells, headers):
    cell.text = header
for _, row in table.iterrows():

doc.save("scratch/table1-python.docx")

Here is a tiny example: five pretend patients’ ages, their mean, and their standard deviation (SD).

ages <- c(64, 71, 58, 69, 75)   # five pretend patients' ages

67.4

Tip🔀 R vs Python: the standard deviation trap



Python has two common ways to compute an SD, and they disagree. pandas (ages.std()) divides by n − 1, like R’s sd(). numpy (np.std(ages)) divides by n unless you write np.std(ages, ddof=1). Medical papers report the n − 1 version. Whenever the two languages’ defaults differ, this site sets them explicitly and explains why in a box like this one.

text:
How results are reported
Every “How to report it” paragraph on this site follows the same rules, which match what reviewers at journals such as JBJS, The Bone & Joint Journal and CORR expect.



What
Report it as
Example




Continuous, roughly symmetric
mean (SD)
age 67.4 (6.6) years


Continuous, skewed
median (IQR: the interquartile range, from the 25th to the 75th percentile)
length of stay 1 (0 to 2) days


Categories
n (%)
312 (52%) female


p-values
three decimals; never “p = 0.000” or “p = 1.000”
p = 0.017; p < 0.001; p > 0.999


Effect estimates
with a 95% confidence interval
difference 1.6 kg/m² (95% CI 0.7 to 2.5)



The examples in the table are illustrations, not results from our data. Demographics (Table 1) shows the full Table 1 layout.
Results sentences give the numbers and stop there: each group’s value, the estimate with its 95% CI, and the p-value. Leave out words that interpret them, such as “similar”, “higher than”, “more often”, “improved”, “significant”, “no clear evidence”, or labels like “good” or “moderate”. Saying what the numbers mean is the Discussion’s job. An illustration:

KOOS JR at 1 year was a median of 87 points (IQR 76 to 94) in men and 85 (IQR 73 to 94) in women (Hodges-Lehmann difference 1 point, 95% CI −2 to 4; p = 0.432).

The Hodges-Lehmann difference in this illustration is the median of all the differences between one man’s score and one woman’s score. It is not the difference between the two medians, so it needn’t equal 87 − 85 = 2 (page 6 explains it).
Around each Results sentence, this site’s text does interpret the numbers, because that’s how you learn to read an output. The Results sentence itself is the part to copy into a manuscript.

title: Working with real HFR data
text: Everything on this site uses invented data. Your real project won’t. This page covers the rules that keep patients and HFR safe. Read it before you open any real dataset.

title: Working with real HFR data
text:
The Swiss rules
Two sets of rules apply to every HFR research project that uses patient data:

The Human Research Act (HRA; in German HFG, in French LRH) and its ordinances. Research with health data needs approval from the cantonal ethics committee before anyone touches the data. For HFR that is the CER-VD, and every project gets a BASEC number when it is submitted (BASEC is the Swiss ethics committees’ online submission portal). Clinical trials, such as randomized trials, also fall under the Clinical Trials Ordinance (ClinO; in German KlinV, in French OClin), and trials of medical devices, such as implants, under its counterpart for devices (ClinO-MD; in German KlinV-Mep, in French OClin-Dim).
Data protection law. Health data are sensitive personal data. HFR is a cantonal hospital, so Fribourg’s cantonal data protection law applies to it, alongside the Human Research Act’s own rules on research data.

Your project lead has the approval and the protocol. Read them before you start: they say which data you may use and how.

Coded, not anonymous
HFR studies work with coded data. Each patient gets a study code (for example C0001), and a separate code key links the codes back to the patients. The code key is kept apart from the study data, by the person the ethics application names for it, who isn’t involved in the project, and never in a repository.
“Coded” and “anonymous” mean different things in Swiss law. Data are anonymous only when they can no longer be linked back to a person, so data with a code key are never anonymous. Use the word “coded” in everything you write, including emails, protocols and Methods sections.


General consent
HFR asks patients for a general consent to the further use of their data for research. In a retrospective study, which uses data already collected during care, only patients with a signed general consent are included, unless the ethics committee approved something else for your project. Patients who refused are never included and are not contacted to ask again. A prospective study asks each patient for consent to that study.

title: Working with real HFR data
text:
What identifies a patient
Direct identifiers never leave the clinical systems:

names, initials, date of birth, address, phone numbers, email addresses
the AHV/AVS number (756.…), HFR patient numbers and case numbers
implant serial and lot numbers
photographs of patients, and images with names burned in

Quasi-identifiers identify patients in combination. In a small cohort, age + sex + surgery date + hospital can point to one person. Coarsen them before data leave the secure environment:

age in bands, with “90 or older” for the very old
the surgery month or year, or “days from surgery”, instead of the date
“a Swiss regional hospital” instead of the hospital’s name, where the protocol allows it

title: Working with real HFR data
text:
HFR traps

Surgery dates are dates. Use “days from surgery” or the surgery year instead.
Very old patients. In a small cohort an age of 97 can identify someone. Group them as “90 or older”.
Study IDs built from patient details. A study ID made from initials, a patient number or a birth date (like JS-0412) is still an identifier. Use arbitrary codes such as C0001.
Patient numbers hide in file names. Watch for names like 12345678_xray.png or extraction_AHV.xlsx.
Implant stickers. Lot and serial numbers are device identifiers.
Radiographs. DICOM files carry the patient’s name, patient number and dates in their headers, and some images have them burned into the pixels.
Free-text “notes” columns. They collect names, phone numbers and dates.
Screenshots of the patient record. They’re patient data too.

title: Working with real HFR data
text:
Where HFR data lives

Keep study data in the project’s REDCap database (REDCap is a secure web application for collecting and storing study data): HFR Ortho encourages every project to keep its data there. Don’t copy them anywhere else.
Analysis code lives in a private repository in HFR Ortho’s GitHub organization. The repository reads the data at run time from git-ignored folders (data/raw/, db/, exports/) that are listed in .gitignore before the first commit.
The code key stays with the person the ethics application names for it, who isn’t involved in the project, never in a repository.
What leaves the secure environment is aggregate: tables, figures and model results. Your protocol may require hiding small counts.

title: Working with real HFR data
section: How HFR projects handle data in code
text:
How HFR projects handle data in code
These rules come from HFR Ortho project repositories. Tidy data practices each one.

Read everything as text at first. Dates arrive in several formats, numbers contain stray text, and lists sit inside single cells. Convert types as a deliberate, recorded step, never silently while reading.
Match columns by name, not position. Two tabs of the same sheet can have different columns.
Check what you changed. After every cleaning step, compare row counts and summaries before and after.

title: Working with real HFR data
text:
AI tools
Never paste real patient data into an AI chatbot or any website. That includes ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot and online “data cleaners”. The only exception is a tool HFR has approved for patient data; ask your project lead. The synthetic data on this site is fine to paste anywhere.

title: Working with real HFR data
text:
Before every commit
Run these two commands in the project’s terminal and read the output:
git status
git diff --staged
git status lists the files git has noticed. git diff --staged shows exactly what the next commit will contain (“staged” means marked for the next commit). No data file, export or screenshot may appear in either. If one is listed under “Changes to be committed”, take it out with git restore --staged <file>. If one is listed under “Untracked files”, git is not ignoring it: stop, and ask your project lead to add it to .gitignore before you commit anything.

title: Working with real HFR data
text:
If something goes wrong
If patient data reaches a commit, a push or an issue:

Stop. Don’t try to fix it with another commit. Git keeps the history.
Tell your project lead right away. The data has to be purged from history, and your project lead decides whether the incident has to be reported, and to whom.

Reporting quickly is always the right call, and nobody will be upset that you did.

title: Glossary
text:
Terms with a dotted underline on any page link here. Hover over one to read its definition without leaving the page.

At risk

Still being followed, and not yet having had the event, at a given moment.

Ceiling (or floor) effect

Many patients score the best (or worst) value a scale allows, so the scale cannot show how much better (or worse) they really are.

Censored

Followed for a while without having the event, then no longer observed: the study ended, the patient moved away, or the patient died. All we know is that the event had not happened by then.

Confidence interval (CI)

A range of values for the true effect that fit the data. A 95% CI comes from a method that captures the true value in 95 of 100 repeated studies.

Degrees of freedom (df)

Roughly, the number of independent pieces of information left for estimating the noise: the sample size minus the number of quantities already estimated. Software uses it to pick the reference distribution for a test statistic.

Effect size

A number that says how large a difference or an association is. The p-value doesn’t say that.

Expected count

The count a table cell would hold if the outcome had nothing to do with the group: row total × column total ÷ grand total.

Hazard ratio (HR)

One group’s hazard divided by the other’s. The hazard is the moment-to-moment risk of the event among those still at risk, so a hazard ratio of 2 means the event is twice as likely at any moment.

Interquartile range (IQR)

The range that holds the middle half of the values, from the 25th percentile to the 75th.

Mean

The average: add up the values and divide by how many there are.

Median

The middle value when the values are sorted: half lie below it and half above.

Null hypothesis

The assumption a test starts from: that there is no difference or no association. The p-value is calculated as if it were true.

Odds ratio

The odds of the outcome in one group divided by the odds in the other. The odds are the number with the outcome divided by the number without it.

p-value

The probability of a result at least as extreme as yours if there were truly no difference. A small p-value means the data would be surprising if there were no difference. It is not the probability that there is no difference.

Paired

Two measurements that belong together: the same patient before and after surgery, or the left and right hip of one person.

Percentile

The value below which a given percentage of the values lie. A quarter of the values lie below the 25th percentile.

Rank

A value’s position when all the values are sorted from lowest to highest. Tied values share the average of their positions.

Scientific notation

How software prints very small or very large numbers. 2.7e-08 means 2.7 with the decimal point moved 8 places to the left: 0.000000027.

Skewed

Lopsided: most values sit at one end and a long tail stretches out to the other.

Standard deviation (SD)

The typical distance of a value from the mean. A small SD means the values sit close together.

Standard error

How much an estimate, such as a mean or a difference between two means, would vary from one sample to the next. It shrinks as the sample grows. It is not the SD, which describes how spread out the patients are.

Test statistic

A single number, such as t, U or χ², that a test calculates from the data to measure how far they are from “no difference”.

Variance

The standard deviation squared. Tests such as ANOVA compare variances because they can be added up.

Wald confidence interval

The simplest kind of CI: the estimate plus and minus about 2 standard errors (1.96 for a 95% CI).

title: Install & set up
text: This takes 30–45 minutes the first time, and you only do it once per computer. Follow the steps in order. Steps 1 to 3 end with a quick check, and step 8 checks everything at the end.

title: Install & set up
text:
1. Install R

Go to https://cloud.r-project.org.
Click Download R for macOS or Download R for Windows.

Mac: pick the installer for your chip. Apple menu → About This Mac: “Apple M…” means Apple silicon (arm64), and “Intel” means Intel (x86_64).
Windows: click base, then the download link at the top of the page.

Open the downloaded file and accept the defaults.

Check: you will see R in Positron’s language picker in step 6. On a Mac you can also open Terminal and type R --version.

title: Install & set up
text:
2. Install uv and Python
Mac: open Terminal and run:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
Windows: open PowerShell and run:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
Close the window, open a new one, and install Python:
uv python install 3.13
Check: uv --version prints a version number.

title: Install & set up
text:
3. Install Git

Mac: in Terminal, run xcode-select --install and click Install. This installs Apple’s command-line tools, which include Git.
Windows: download Git from https://git-scm.com/downloads and accept the defaults.

Check: git --version prints a version number.

title: Install & set up
text:
4. Install Positron
Download Positron from https://positron.posit.co and install it like any other app. Positron runs R and Python side by side. Prefer RStudio or VS Code? See Other editors.

title: Install & set up
text:
5. Get this repository
In Terminal (Mac) or PowerShell (Windows), make a projects folder and download (“clone”) the repository into it:
mkdir -p ~/projects
cd ~/projects
git clone https://github.com/hfr-ortho/stats-formation.git
Use a folder that is not synced to the cloud. Documents and Desktop are often synced by iCloud (Mac) or OneDrive (Windows). Syncing slows down, and can break, the R and Python environments that steps 6 and 7 create.
Then, in Positron: File → Open Folder… and choose stats-formation.

title: Install & set up
text:
6. Install the R packages
In Positron, start an R console: use the language picker at the top right of the Console pane and choose R. Because R starts inside the repository folder, it switches on this project’s package list. Then run:
renv::restore()
Answer Y if asked. This installs every R package the tutorials use, at the exact versions we tested. It takes a few minutes.

title: Install & set up
text:
7. Install the Python packages
Open Positron’s terminal (Terminal → New Terminal). It opens in the repository folder. Run:
uv sync
This creates a private Python environment in the .venv folder with every package the tutorials use. Then tell Positron to use it: in the Console pane’s language picker, choose the Python whose path includes .venv.

title: Install & set up
text:
8. Check that everything works
In Positron’s terminal, run both checks:
Rscript scripts/check_setup.R
uv run python scripts/check_setup.py
Each check ends with All good - you are ready. If a line says PROBLEM, it tells you what to do. Fix it and run the check again.
On Windows, if Rscript is “not recognized”, run the R check from Positron’s R console instead:
source("scripts/check_setup.R")

title: Install & set up
text:
Reading the data without cloning
You can skip steps 5 to 8 and read the practice data straight from GitHub, for example to use it in a project of your own. You still need R (step 1) or uv and Python (step 2), and the packages below.

RPython


install.packages(c("readr", "readxl"))   # once

cohort <- readr::read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hfr-ortho/stats-formation/main/data/cohort.csv")


Start Python with the packages it needs. In a terminal:
uv run --with pandas --with openpyxl python
Then:
import pandas as pd

cohort = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hfr-ortho/stats-formation/main/data/cohort.csv")



Every CSV works the same way: replace "data/" with "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hfr-ortho/stats-formation/main/data/". To run a whole example from a tutorial page, clone the repository instead (steps 5 to 7): the pages use many more packages than these, and cloning installs them all at the versions we tested.
Excel files are different. R’s read_excel() can’t read a web address, so download the file first. Python’s pd.read_excel() can read the address directly.

RPython


url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hfr-ortho/stats-formation/main/data/messy_abstraction_workbook.xlsx"
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
download.file(url, path, mode = "wb")   # "wb" keeps the file intact on Windows
site_a <- readxl::read_excel(path, sheet = "Site A")


url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hfr-ortho/stats-formation/main/data/messy_abstraction_workbook.xlsx"
site_a = pd.read_excel(url, sheet_name="Site A")

text:
Troubleshooting







You see
Do this




You have not agreed to the Xcode license (Mac, during renv::restore())
In Terminal, run sudo xcodebuild -license accept and type your Mac password. Then run renv::restore() again.


there is no package called 'renv'
In the R console, run install.packages("renv"). Restart R (Session → Restart R) and run renv::restore() again.

Close the terminal window, open a new one, and try again.


git: command not found
Repeat step 3.


Python can’t find pandas in Positron
Choose the .venv Python in the Console language picker (step 7), then restart the console.


Anything else
Copy the whole error message and send it to your project lead.

title: Install & set up
text:
Other editors

RStudio (https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) is great for R. It can run Python too, but Positron is simpler when you use both.
VS Code (https://code.visualstudio.com) works too: install the R and Python extensions.

Everything else on this page stays the same.

title: 1 · Tidy data
text: Most of the time in a research project goes into getting the data into shape, not into the statistics. Mistakes made here are the dangerous kind: the code runs, the tables look fine, and the numbers are wrong. This page shows how to collect data so it arrives clean, how to clean it when it doesn’t, and how to prove your cleaning didn’t change anything it shouldn’t have.

title: 1 · Tidy data
text:
What tidy data means
Data are tidy when:

every variable is a column,
every observation is a row, and
every kind of observational unit gets its own table.







Note💡 In plain language



One fact per cell, one patient-thing per row, and never two kinds of rows mixed in one table. A spreadsheet that’s easy for a person to read is often hard for a computer to analyze, and the other way round. Statistics software wants the second kind.


Here’s a typical untidy PROM sheet: one row per patient, with a column for each visit. The visit is a variable, but it’s hiding in the column names.

RPython



library(tidyverse)

wide <- tibble(
  case_id = c("C0001", "C0002", "C0003"),
  preop   = c(41.2, 55.0, 38.7),
  `6wk`   = c(60.1, NA,   58.3),
  `1yr`   = c(88.0, 92.4, 79.5)
)
wide

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  case_id preop `6wk` `1yr`
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 C0001    41.2  60.1  88  
2 C0002    55    NA    92.4
3 C0003    38.7  58.3  79.5

# Tidy: one row per case per visit
long <- wide |>
  pivot_longer(-case_id, names_to = "visit", values_to = "prom_score")
long

# A tibble: 9 × 3
  case_id visit prom_score
  <chr>   <chr>      <dbl>
1 C0001   preop       41.2
2 C0001   6wk         60.1
3 C0001   1yr         88  
4 C0002   preop       55  
5 C0002   6wk         NA  
6 C0002   1yr         92.4
7 C0003   preop       38.7
8 C0003   6wk         58.3
9 C0003   1yr         79.5





import pandas as pd

wide = pd.DataFrame({
    "case_id": ["C0001", "C0002", "C0003"],
    "preop":   [41.2, 55.0, 38.7],
    "6wk":     [60.1, None, 58.3],
    "1yr":     [88.0, 92.4, 79.5],
})
print(wide)

  case_id  preop   6wk   1yr
0   C0001   41.2  60.1  88.0
1   C0002   55.0   NaN  92.4
2   C0003   38.7  58.3  79.5

# Tidy: one row per case per visit
long = wide.melt(id_vars="case_id", var_name="visit", value_name="prom_score")
print(long)

  case_id  visit  prom_score
0   C0001  preop        41.2
1   C0002  preop        55.0
2   C0003  preop        38.7
3   C0001    6wk        60.1
4   C0002    6wk         NaN
5   C0003    6wk        58.3
6   C0001    1yr        88.0
7   C0002    1yr        92.4
8   C0003    1yr        79.5





In the long version, “Is the 6-week score missing?” is just a row with a blank, and “average score at each visit” is one line of code. In the wide version, every new visit means a new column and rewritten code.
Untidy patterns we see most often in abstraction sheets, and the tidy fix for each:








You see
Problem
Tidy fix




DM, HTN, OSA in one cell
Several values in one cell
One yes/no column per condition


R TKA
Two variables in one cell
Separate side and procedure columns


32.1 kg/m2
Units typed into a number
A number column; units go in the data dictionary


Red-filled cells mean “revised”
Color as data (invisible to software)
A revised column


Date, Score, Date, Score
Repeated columns per visit
Long format: one row per visit


N/A, unk, -, 999, blank
Five ways to say “missing”
One: an empty cell


A title row, a totals row
Not data
Delete them; keep notes elsewhere

title: 1 · Tidy data
text:
Collecting tidy data
The cheapest cleaning is the cleaning you never have to do. Before anyone abstracts a single chart, write the data dictionary: every variable’s name, meaning, type, units and allowed values. Then build the collection sheet from the dictionary.
This site includes a template you can copy: templates/data-collection-template.xlsx. It has four sheets:

README — the rules below, for whoever does the abstraction.
data — one header row, and dropdowns or range checks on every column except the study ID, so typos can’t get in.
dictionary — what each column means.
missing_codes — exactly what to enter when a value isn’t in the chart.

The rules the template enforces:

One row per procedure, one column per variable, one value per cell.
A study ID (the study code), never the patient number or name. The code key, which links study codes to patient numbers, is kept in a separate, secured file by the person the ethics application names for it, who isn’t involved in the project.
Categories from dropdowns only (no F vs female).
Numbers only in number columns; units live in the dictionary.
Real dates, not text.
Missing means: dropdown “Not recorded”, or an empty number/date cell.
No colors, bold, comments, merged cells, title rows or totals rows.

You can read the dictionary sheet like any other data:

RPython



library(readxl)

dictionary <- read_excel("templates/data-collection-template.xlsx", sheet = "dictionary")
dictionary

title: 1 · Tidy data
text:
Tidying a messy workbook
Real abstraction sheets rarely follow those rules. data/messy_abstraction_workbook.xlsx copies the problems we see in real abstraction sheets. Open it in Excel and look before you run any code:

two tabs, Site A and Site B, whose columns don’t line up (Site B has an extra MUA column in the middle)
two banner rows and a row of merged group headers above the real header
a TOTAL row at the bottom of each tab
two Date and two Score columns (pre-op and 1-year PROMs)
mixed date formats, units in number cells, Roman-numeral ASA classes, five spellings of “missing”
revisions marked only by a red fill on the Study ID cell
duplicated rows

We’ll fix it one step at a time. Every step is small enough to check. Run the steps in order: each one starts from the result of the step before.

Step 1: read both tabs, as text
Read everything as text first. If you let the software guess types, it silently turns 32.1 kg/m2 into a missing value, and you never find out. We’ll convert types deliberately in step 5.

RPython



path <- "data/messy_abstraction_workbook.xlsx"

read_site <- function(sheet) {
  # skip = 3 jumps over the two banner rows and the group-header row
  raw <- read_excel(path, sheet = sheet, skip = 3, col_types = "text",
                    .name_repair = "minimal")
  names(raw) <- str_trim(names(raw))   # "Study ID " has a trailing space on Site B

  # The two Date/Score pairs: the group header says pre-op first, then 1 year
  names(raw)[names(raw) == "Date"]  <- c("prom_preop_date", "prom_1yr_date")
  names(raw)[names(raw) == "Score"] <- c("prom_preop", "prom_1yr")

  raw |>
    janitor::clean_names() |> # "Pt Name" -> pt_name, "Study ID" -> study_id
    mutate(site = sheet)      # remember which tab each row came from
}

raw <- bind_rows(read_site("Site A"), read_site("Site B"))   # matches columns by name
nrow(raw)

[1] 126

names(raw)

 [1] "pt_name"         "mrn"             "study_id"        "dos"            
 [5] "age"             "sex"             "bmi"             "asa"            
 [9] "comorbidities"   "procedure"       "los"             "prom_preop_date"
[13] "prom_preop"      "prom_1yr_date"   "prom_1yr"        "notes"          
[17] "site"            "mua"            

count(raw, site)                            # rows read from each tab

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  site       n
  <chr>  <int>
1 Site A    63
2 Site B    63

sum(raw$pt_name == "TOTAL", na.rm = TRUE)   # totals rows

[1] 2

sum(duplicated(raw))                        # rows that exactly repeat an earlier row

[1] 4

head(raw$dos)                               # the first six surgery dates, exactly as read

[1] "42026"      "08.02.15"   "14.05.15"   "42236"      "23.8.2015" 
[6] "16.10.2015"





import re

path = "data/messy_abstraction_workbook.xlsx"

def read_site(sheet):
    # header=3 uses the 4th row as column names (after banners and group headers)
    raw = pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=sheet, header=3, dtype=str)
    names = [str(c).strip() for c in raw.columns]   # "Study ID " has a trailing space on Site B

    # pandas renames repeated headers to "Date.1" and "Score.1"
    pairs = {"Date": "prom_preop_date", "Score": "prom_preop",
             "Date.1": "prom_1yr_date", "Score.1": "prom_1yr"}
    names = [pairs.get(n, n) for n in names]

    # "Pt Name" -> pt_name, "Study ID" -> study_id
    raw.columns = [re.sub(r"[^0-9a-z]+", "_", n.lower()).strip("_") for n in names]
    return raw.assign(site=sheet)   # remember which tab each row came from

raw = pd.concat([read_site("Site A"), read_site("Site B")], ignore_index=True)  # matches by name
print(len(raw))

126

print(list(raw.columns))

['pt_name', 'mrn', 'study_id', 'dos', 'age', 'sex', 'bmi', 'asa', 'comorbidities', 'procedure', 'los', 'prom_preop_date', 'prom_preop', 'prom_1yr_date', 'prom_1yr', 'notes', 'site', 'mua']

print(raw["site"].value_counts())           # rows read from each tab

site
Site A    63
Site B    63
Name: count, dtype: int64

print((raw["pt_name"] == "TOTAL").sum())    # totals rows

2

print(raw.duplicated().sum())               # rows that exactly repeat an earlier row

4

print(raw["dos"].head(6).tolist())          # the first six surgery dates, exactly as read

['2015-01-22 00:00:00', '08.02.15', '14.05.15', '2015-08-20 00:00:00', '23.8.2015', '16.10.2015']





126 rows: 63 from each tab. Each tab has 1 totals row and 2 rows that repeat an earlier row (2 totals rows and 4 duplicates in all), and these are not patients. That leaves 63 − 1 − 2 = 60 patients per tab. Because we stacked the tabs by column name, Site B’s extra MUA column didn’t shift anything. Site A rows simply have mua missing. Copying cells by position would have put LOS values under the wrong heading.
In R we call janitor::clean_names() with the package name in front instead of loading janitor with library(). Loading janitor masks R’s own chisq.test() and fisher.test() with janitor’s versions. They give the same answers for ordinary tables, but the masking message is confusing, and it becomes harder to tell which function you’re actually calling.






Tip🔀 R vs Python: the same Excel file, read differently




Repeated headers. R (with .name_repair = "minimal") keeps both Date columns as Date. pandas renames the second to Date.1.
Real Excel dates. Read as text, R gives the Excel serial number and pandas a date-time text. Compare the first date in the two outputs: 42026 in R (22 Jan 2015), 2015-01-22 00:00:00 in pandas. Step 5 handles both.





Step 2: drop rows and columns that aren’t data

RPython



step2 <- raw |>

In this sheet 999 means “missing” in number columns. In another sheet it could be a real value. Write every missing code into the data dictionary before collection starts.




Step 4: recover the color-coded revisions
The sheet marks revised cases only with a red fill on the Study ID cell. Most software reading a spreadsheet can’t see colors at all, which is exactly why color must never carry data. Here we have to dig it out.

Step 5: give every column its real type
Now convert each text column into what it really is. One small function handles the mixed date formats. Each recode lists the values it expects and turns anything else into a missing value, so a surprise like U for sex shows up instead of silently becoming “Male”.

RPython



# Dates arrive as Excel serial numbers ("42010"), ISO dates ("2015-04-21"),
# or Swiss day-first text ("13.01.15", "13.1.2015"). Handle the serial
# numbers, then the ISO dates, then read the rest day-first.
parse_messy_date <- function(x, day_first = TRUE) {
  serial <- !is.na(x) & str_detect(x, "^\\d{5}$")
  iso    <- !is.na(x) & str_detect(x, "^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$")
  rest   <- !is.na(x) & !serial & !iso
  out <- as.Date(rep(NA, length(x)))
  out[serial] <- janitor::excel_numeric_to_date(as.numeric(x[serial]))
  out[iso]    <- ymd(x[iso])
  out[rest]   <- if (day_first) dmy(x[rest], quiet = TRUE) else mdy(x[rest], quiet = TRUE)
  out
}

tidy <- step3 |>

    age          = parse_number(age),            # "67 yo"      -> 67
    sex          = case_when(str_detect(sex, regex("^f", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Female",

    revised      = as.integer(case_id %in% revised_ids),

    prom_preop      = parse_number(prom_preop),

import numpy as np

def number(text):
    # The first number in each cell: "67 yo" -> 67, "BMI 31.2" -> 31.2
    return pd.to_numeric(text.str.extract(r"(\d+\.?\d*)")[0])

asa_roman = {"I": "1", "II": "2", "III": "3", "IV": "4"}
procedure_text = step3["procedure"]   # keep the raw text until we've split it

def parse_messy_date(col, dayfirst=True):
    """Every cell arrives as text: ISO dates ("2015-04-21", and real Excel dates as
    "2015-01-06 00:00:00") or Swiss day-first dates ("13.01.15", "13.1.2015").
    dayfirst=True would also flip ISO dates, so they're read on their own."""
    iso = col.str.match(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", na=False)
    swiss = col.notna() & ~iso
    dates = pd.concat([pd.to_datetime(col[iso], format="ISO8601"),
                       pd.to_datetime(col[swiss], format="mixed", dayfirst=dayfirst)])
    return dates.reindex(col.index)   # back in row order; empty cells stay missing (NaT)

tidy = pd.DataFrame({
    "case_id":      step3["study_id"].str.strip(),
    "site":         step3["site"],
    "surgery_date": parse_messy_date(step3["dos"]),
    "age":          number(step3["age"]),
    "sex":          step3["sex"].str[0].str.lower().map({"f": "Female", "m": "Male"}),
    "bmi":          number(step3["bmi"]),
    "asa":          pd.to_numeric(step3["asa"].str.replace("ASA ", "").replace(asa_roman)),
    "diabetes":     step3["comorbidities"].str.contains(r"\bDM\b", case=False).astype(int),
    "hypertension": step3["comorbidities"].str.contains(r"\bHTN\b", case=False).astype(int),
    "sleep_apnea":  step3["comorbidities"].str.contains(r"\bOSA\b", case=False).astype(int),
    "procedure":    np.select([procedure_text.str.contains(r"TKA|knee", case=False),
                               procedure_text.str.contains(r"THA|hip", case=False)],
                              ["TKA", "THA"], default=None),          # anything else -> missing
    "side":         np.select([procedure_text.str.contains(r"\b(?:L|Left)\b"),
                               procedure_text.str.contains(r"\b(?:R|Right)\b")],
                              ["L", "R"], default=None),
    "los_days":     number(step3["los"]),
    "revised":      step3["study_id"].str.strip().isin(revised_ids).astype(int),
    "prom_preop_date": parse_messy_date(step3["prom_preop_date"]),
    "prom_preop":      number(step3["prom_preop"]),
    "prom_1yr_date":   parse_messy_date(step3["prom_1yr_date"]),
    "prom_1yr":        number(step3["prom_1yr"]),
}).sort_values(["site", "case_id"]).reset_index(drop=True)

Tip🔀 R vs Python: dates



R needs a separate step for Excel serial numbers (janitor::excel_numeric_to_date()). pandas already turned those cells into date-time text (2015-01-22 00:00:00), which its parse_messy_date() reads with the other ISO dates. Both read "14.05.15" day-first: Swiss style, which is what HFR sheets use. Both read ISO dates on their own, because pandas’ dayfirst=True would also flip them (2015-11-02 would become 11 February). pandas also stores a whole-number column that has missing values as decimals, so ASA class 2 prints as 2.0. The value is the same.

Reshaping a survey export
data/messy_survey_export.csv is what survey platforms produce: one row per patient, one column per question per visit (KOOS_Q3_6wk), and a second header row of question labels. To analyze it we need one row per patient, visit and item.

                 col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

items <- wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    -c(ResponseId, case_id, instrument),
    names_to = c("inst", "item", "visit"),
    names_pattern = "(KOOS|HOOS)_Q(\\d)_(.*)",       # "KOOS_Q3_6wk" -> KOOS, 3, 6wk
    values_to = "response"

  filter(substr(instrument, 1, 4) == inst) |>         # keep each patient's own instrument

         visit_order = match(visit, c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"))) |>
  arrange(case_id, visit_order, item) |>
  select(case_id, instrument, visit, item, response)
