What a failing check looks like
Suppose we had parsed the surgery dates month-first (US style, as many online examples do) by mistake. Nothing crashes. Two checks catch it: a missing count (check 2, applied to the dates) and a new logic check that every pre-op PROM falls within a month before surgery.

RPython



wrong <- parse_messy_date(step3$dos, day_first = FALSE)   # the mistake
preop <- parse_messy_date(step3$prom_preop_date)

outside_window <- function(surgery) {
  days_before <- as.numeric(surgery - preop)
  sum(days_before < 0 | days_before > 31, na.rm = TRUE)
}
c(missing_correct     = sum(is.na(tidy$surgery_date)),
  missing_month_first = sum(is.na(wrong)),

  window_month_first  = outside_window(wrong))

def outside_window(surgery):
    days_before = (surgery - preop).dt.days
    return int(((days_before < 0) | (days_before > 31)).sum())

print(pd.Series({
    "missing_correct": tidy["surgery_date"].isna().sum(),
    "missing_month_first": wrong.isna().sum(),
    "window_correct": outside_window(parse_messy_date(step3["dos"])),
    "window_month_first": outside_window(wrong),
}))

window_correct          0
window_month_first     12
dtype: int64





With the correct parse, nothing is missing and every pre-op PROM falls in its window. The month-first versions go wrong in different ways:

R can’t read dates like "14.05.15" month-first (there’s no 14th month), so 30 surgery dates go missing. Others, like "08.02.15", parse “successfully” as 2 August instead of 8 February, and the window check flags 12 of them.
pandas never returns a missing date here: when month-first is impossible it quietly switches to day-first, so "14.05.15" comes out right by luck while "08.02.15" becomes 2 August. Only the window check notices: it flags 12 dates.







Warning⚠️ Watch out: one check is never enough



Never parse a column that mixes formats with one setting: read each format on its own, as parse_messy_date() does. And notice that the missing count caught this bug in R but not in Python, while the logic check caught it in both. Run all the checks every time; they catch different mistakes.




Finally: compare with the answer key
Because this is a teaching dataset, there is a known right answer: data/answer-keys/abstraction_workbook_tidy.csv. Our result matches it exactly.

RPython



answer <- read_csv("data/answer-keys/abstraction_workbook_tidy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
all.equal(as.data.frame(tidy), as.data.frame(answer), check.attributes = FALSE)

[1] TRUE





answer = pd.read_csv("data/answer-keys/abstraction_workbook_tidy.csv",
                     parse_dates=["surgery_date", "prom_preop_date", "prom_1yr_date"])
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(tidy, answer, check_dtype=False)   # silent means identical
print("identical")

identical

title: 3 · Distributions & choosing a test
text: The decision table asks two questions: what’s your goal (the row), and what type of data do you have (the column). This page is about the second question, especially the hardest part of it: is a measurement “Gaussian” (normally distributed) enough for the left-hand column?

title: 3 · Distributions & choosing a test
section: Why the shape of your data matters
text:
Why the shape of your data matters
The tests in the first column (t tests, ANOVA, Pearson correlation) compare means, and they assume the data within each group follow a roughly bell-shaped, normal distribution. The tests in the second column (Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis, Spearman) work on ranks. They don’t assume a normal distribution.






Note💡 In plain language



A mean is a fair summary of a bell-shaped pile of numbers. It’s a poor summary of a lopsided one: a few very long hospital stays drag the mean far away from what’s typical. Tests built on means inherit that problem. Rank-based tests only ask “which values are bigger?”, so a few extreme values can’t dominate.

title: 3 · Distributions & choosing a test
section: Look first: histograms and QQ plots
text:
Look first: histograms and QQ plots
Always plot before you test. Here are three variables from the practice data: age, length of stay, and the 1-year PROM score.

RPython



library(tidyverse)

cohort   <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
proms    <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
one_year <- proms |> filter(visit == "1yr", !is.na(prom_score))

shapes <- bind_rows(
  tibble(variable = "Age, years",           value = cohort$age),
  tibble(variable = "Length of stay, days", value = cohort$los_days),
  tibble(variable = "1-year PROM score",    value = one_year$prom_score)
)

ggplot(shapes, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free")











import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")
proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")
one_year = proms[(proms["visit"] == "1yr") & proms["prom_score"].notna()]

shapes = {
    "Age, years": cohort["age"],
    "Length of stay, days": cohort["los_days"],
    "1-year PROM score": one_year["prom_score"],
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3))
for ax, (name, values) in zip(axes, shapes.items()):
    ax.hist(values, bins=30)
    ax.set_title(name)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()












Age is a fairly symmetric bell.
Length of stay piles up at 0 and 1 days and has a long tail to the right: right-skewed.
1-year PROM piles up against the top of the scale (100), with a tail to the left: a ceiling effect.

A QQ plot makes the comparison with a normal distribution easier to see. If the data are normal, the points fall on the straight line.

RPython



ggplot(shapes, aes(sample = value)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free")











fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3))
for ax, (name, values) in zip(axes, shapes.items()):
    stats.probplot(values, plot=ax)
    ax.set_title(name)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()











How to read them:

Points on the line: close to normal (age).
Points curving up at the right end: right skew (length of stay). The flat steps are the many ties at 0, 1 and 2 days.
Points flattening at the top: a ceiling (the PROM). Many patients share the maximum score.

A number for lopsidedness is the skewness: 0 for a symmetric shape, positive for a tail to the right, negative for a tail to the left.

RPython



skewness <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3

c(age      = skewness(cohort$age),
  los      = skewness(cohort$los_days),
  prom_1yr = skewness(one_year$prom_score))

        age         los    prom_1yr 
-0.05351075  1.60890277 -0.72708937 





def skewness(x):
    return ((x - x.mean()) ** 3).mean() / x.std() ** 3

print(pd.Series({
    "age": skewness(cohort["age"]),
    "los": skewness(cohort["los_days"]),
    "prom_1yr": skewness(one_year["prom_score"]),
}))

age        -0.053511
los         1.608903
prom_1yr   -0.727089
dtype: float64





Age: −0.05, practically symmetric. Length of stay: 1.61, a long tail to the right. 1-year PROM score: −0.73, a tail to the left. The numbers say what the histograms showed.






Tip🔀 R vs Python: skewness functions



Packages define skewness in slightly different ways (scipy.stats.skew() and the R package e1071 each use their own formula), so the third decimal can differ between them. We wrote the formula out by hand in both languages so the numbers match exactly.

title: 3 · Distributions & choosing a test
section: Formal tests: Shapiro-Wilk, and why not to trust it alone
text:
Formal tests: Shapiro-Wilk, and why not to trust it alone
The Shapiro-Wilk test asks: “Could these numbers plausibly come from a normal distribution?” A small p-value means “probably not”. It’s tempting to let it decide: p < 0.05 → rank test, otherwise → t test. That rule fails in both directions.
It’s too sensitive with large samples. Our 600 ages look like a textbook bell curve, yet:

RPython



shapiro.test(cohort$age)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  cohort$age
W = 0.99131, p-value = 0.001361





print(stats.shapiro(cohort["age"]))

ShapiroResult(statistic=np.float64(0.991313509056761), pvalue=np.float64(0.001361050169338618))





p = 0.001: “not normal”. With 600 values the test can detect departures far too small to matter. A t test on these ages would be perfectly fine. The other number, W (statistic in Python), is the test statistic: 1 would be a perfect fit to the normal curve. You don’t report it; read the p-value (p-value in R, pvalue in Python).
It’s too weak with small samples. Take just the first 10 patients’ 1-year PROM scores, from a variable we know is skewed with a ceiling:

RPython



first_ten <- head(one_year$prom_score, 10)
first_ten

 [1] 89.3 97.1 82.6 91.6 92.9 96.1 97.5 95.2 84.3 81.2

shapiro.test(first_ten)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  first_ten
W = 0.89073, p-value = 0.1728





first_ten = one_year["prom_score"].head(10)
print(first_ten.tolist())

[89.3, 97.1, 82.6, 91.6, 92.9, 96.1, 97.5, 95.2, 84.3, 81.2]

print(stats.shapiro(first_ten))

ShapiroResult(statistic=np.float64(0.8907320100006012), pvalue=np.float64(0.17282366095024826))





p = 0.173: “no evidence against normality”. Ten values simply can’t reveal the shape, which is exactly when the shape matters most.






Warning⚠️ Watch out: don’t let one p-value choose your test



Decide from the plots, from what you know about the measurement (a bounded score, a count of days), and from the sample size. Use Shapiro-Wilk as supporting evidence, not as the judge. Then say how you decided in your Methods.

title: 3 · Distributions & choosing a test
section: Check within groups, not the pooled data
text:
Check within groups, not the pooled data
The normality assumption is about the data within each group (or, for regression models, the residuals: what’s left after the model’s prediction). Pooling groups with different centers can make perfectly normal data look non-normal.
Here’s an extreme, made-up example: two groups of 200 values, each exactly normal, with means of 40 and 60 and an SD of 5, so 4 standard deviations apart.

RPython



group_a <- qnorm(ppoints(200), mean = 40, sd = 5)   # 200 perfectly normal values
group_b <- qnorm(ppoints(200), mean = 60, sd = 5)

shapiro.test(group_a)$p.value                       # one group alone

[1] 1

shapiro.test(c(group_a, group_b))$p.value           # both groups pooled

[1] 9.267769e-11

ggplot(tibble(value = c(group_a, group_b)), aes(value)) +   # the pooled values: two humps
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)











points = (np.arange(1, 201) - 0.5) / 200            # the same probabilities as R's ppoints(200)
group_a = stats.norm.ppf(points, loc=40, scale=5)   # 200 perfectly normal values
group_b = stats.norm.ppf(points, loc=60, scale=5)

print(stats.shapiro(group_a).pvalue)                              # one group alone

0.999999999999995

print(stats.shapiro(np.concatenate([group_a, group_b])).pvalue)   # both groups pooled

9.26776946181564e-11

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.hist(np.concatenate([group_a, group_b]), bins=30)              # the pooled values: two humps
plt.show()











Each group alone passes easily (p ≈ 1). Pooled, p < 0.001: the histogram of the pooled values has two humps, one around 40 and one around 60, which is not what a normal distribution looks like.
The pooled p-value prints as 9.267769e-11. That is scientific notation: 9.27 × 10⁻¹¹, or 0.0000000000927. For one group alone, R rounds the p-value to 1 and Python prints 0.999999999999995.
In real data the groups are usually much closer together. BMI differs by only about a third of a standard deviation between THA and TKA patients (the SMD of 0.33 in Table 1), so pooling barely matters. What you see instead is Shapiro-Wilk’s verdict bouncing around 0.05 depending on how you slice the same data:

RPython



shapiro.test(cohort$bmi)$p.value                         # pooled

[1] 0.04425462

cohort |>
  group_by(procedure) |>
  summarise(shapiro_p = shapiro.test(bmi)$p.value)       # each group on its own

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  procedure shapiro_p
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 THA          0.0513
2 TKA          0.124 

fit <- lm(bmi ~ procedure, data = cohort)                # residual = BMI minus its group's mean
shapiro.test(residuals(fit))$p.value

[1] 0.306292

ggplot(tibble(residual = residuals(fit)), aes(sample = residual)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line()











print(stats.shapiro(cohort["bmi"]).pvalue)               # pooled

0.04425461560416669

for procedure, group in cohort.groupby("procedure"):     # each group on its own
    print(procedure, stats.shapiro(group["bmi"]).pvalue)

THA 0.05134144815391971
TKA 0.12354544393057915

# residual = BMI minus its group's mean
residuals = cohort["bmi"] - cohort.groupby("procedure")["bmi"].transform("mean")
print(stats.shapiro(residuals).pvalue)

0.30629201181168864

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))
qq = stats.probplot(residuals, plot=ax)                  # naming the result keeps its numbers out of the output
plt.show()











Pooled p = 0.044, THA alone 0.051, TKA alone 0.124, residuals 0.306: four slices of the same data, on both sides of 0.05, while the QQ plot is a near-perfect straight line. That’s the lesson of the previous section again: decide from the plots and what you know about the measurement, not from one p-value.

title: 3 · Distributions & choosing a test
text:
How much does normality matter?
Less than you might think, once groups are reasonably large. Tests on means rely on the average being roughly normal, not on every individual value. Thanks to the central limit theorem, averages of about 30 or more values are close to normal even when the values themselves are skewed.
A practical guide:

About 30 or more per group, moderate skew, no wild outliers: t tests and ANOVA are fine. With very skewed data, the rank test is still often the better summary.
Strong skew or extreme outliers: use the rank column.
Small groups (under about 15 per group): plots can’t show the shape, and no test has much power. Choose from what you know about the measurement: the rank column for skewed or ordinal measures, the Gaussian column for measurements known to be roughly normal. Expect wide confidence intervals either way.
Ordinal scales, or a ceiling or floor: use the rank column whatever the sample size (below).







Note🔍 Under the hood: the central limit theorem





If you take many random samples of size n from almost any distribution and compute each sample’s mean, those means form a distribution that gets closer to normal as n grows. Its spread shrinks in proportion to 1/√n. t tests are built on the distribution of the mean, which is why they tolerate non-normal raw data when n is large. “About 30” is a rule of thumb, not a law: the more skewed the data, the larger n needs to be.

title: 3 · Distributions & choosing a test
text:
Skew, ceilings and transformations
A common fix for right skew is to analyze the logarithm of the values. For length of stay we have to use log(days + 1), because log(0) doesn’t exist.

RPython



c(skew_raw      = skewness(cohort$los_days),
  skew_log      = skewness(log1p(cohort$los_days)),   # log1p(x) = log(1 + x)
  share_zero    = mean(cohort$los_days == 0),
  ceiling_1yr   = mean(one_year$prom_score == 100))

   skew_raw    skew_log  share_zero ceiling_1yr 
  1.6089028   0.5940202   0.4850000   0.1696035 





import numpy as np

print(pd.Series({
    "skew_raw": skewness(cohort["los_days"]),
    "skew_log": skewness(np.log1p(cohort["los_days"])),   # log1p(x) = log(1 + x)
    "share_zero": (cohort["los_days"] == 0).mean(),
    "ceiling_1yr": (one_year["prom_score"] == 100).mean(),
}))

skew_raw       1.608903
skew_log       0.594020
share_zero     0.485000
ceiling_1yr    0.169604
dtype: float64





The log helps (skewness falls from about 1.6 to 0.6), but nearly half the stays are 0 days (share_zero: 0.485, or 48.5%) and no transformation can spread out a pile of identical values. Results on a log scale are also harder to explain (“a 0.3 difference in log(days + 1)”). Here the rank-based tests are simpler and more honest.
The same goes for the ceiling: 17% of the patients with a 1-year score reach the maximum (ceiling_1yr: 0.17), and no transformation can tell those patients apart. Compare groups with rank-based tests, or report the proportion reaching the ceiling (or a clinically important improvement) as a yes/no outcome.

title: 3 · Distributions & choosing a test
section: Ordinal data always go in the rank column
text:
Ordinal data always go in the rank column
Ordinal data have an order but no fixed spacing: satisfaction from 1 (“very dissatisfied”) to 5 (“very satisfied”), ASA class, pain “none / mild / moderate / severe”. The step from 4 to 5 isn’t necessarily the same size as the step from 1 to 2, so averages are hard to interpret.

RPython



count(cohort, satisfaction_1yr)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  satisfaction_1yr     n
             <dbl> <int>
1                1    15
2                2    23
3                3    52
4                4   162
5                5   250
6               NA    98





print(cohort["satisfaction_1yr"].value_counts(dropna=False).sort_index())

satisfaction_1yr
1.0     15
2.0     23
3.0     52
4.0    162
5.0    250
NaN     98
Name: count, dtype: int64





250 patients chose 5 (“very satisfied”) and 15 chose 1. The last row (NA in R, NaN in Python) is the 98 patients with no answer; say how many are missing when you report the scale. Python prints the scores as 1.0 to 5.0 because the column has blanks.
Report ordinal data as counts and percentages, or as a median (IQR), and compare groups with rank-based tests. Never compute a t test on Likert scores, however many patients you have.

title: 3 · Distributions & choosing a test
section: Paired or unpaired? Matched or unmatched?
text:
Paired or unpaired? Matched or unmatched?
The decision table’s rows also ask whether your groups are independent or paired/matched.

Unpaired (independent): different patients in each group. THA vs TKA; Site A vs Site B; men vs women.
Paired: the same patients measured twice, or natural pairs. Pre-op vs 1-year PROM in the same patients; left vs right knee in bilateral patients; two raters measuring the same X-rays.
Matched: each patient in one group has been chosen to resemble a patient in the other group (by age, sex, BMI…). Treat matched sets like pairs.

Bilateral patients need care. In our cohort, 80 patients appear twice, once for each side (page 2 counts them). Their two procedures share the same person’s age, sex and health, so they are not independent. When both fall in the same comparison group, tests that treat every row as a separate patient are a little overconfident (p-values too small, CIs too narrow). Either analyse one procedure per patient (for example, the first), or use methods built for clustered data, such as mixed models. Say which you did.
Pairing matters because measurements on the same patient are related. A paired analysis uses each patient as their own control, which removes the patient-to-patient variation and usually gives a more precise answer. Analyzing paired data as if unpaired is one of the most common mistakes in the literature.

title: 3 · Distributions & choosing a test
section: From your question to a test
text:
From your question to a test





flowchart TD
  A[What is your goal?] --> B[Describe one group]
  A --> M[Compare one group to a hypothetical value]
  A --> C[Compare groups or measurements]
  A --> D[Association or prediction]
  C --> E{Same patients or matched?}
  E -->|No| F[Unpaired rows]
  E -->|Yes| G[Paired / matched rows]
  B --> H{What type of outcome?}
  M --> H
  F --> H
  G --> H
  D --> H
  H -->|Measurement, roughly normal within groups| I[Gaussian column]
  H -->|Strongly skewed, bounded, or ordinal| J[Rank column]
  H -->|Yes / no| K[Binomial column]
  H -->|Time until an event| L[Survival column]






Then find your row and column in the decision table. Some worked examples from typical orthopaedic research questions:



Question
Row
Column
Test




Is the EFAS score at 3 months different with a boot than with a cast?
Two unpaired groups
Gaussian
Unpaired t test


Is pain 6 weeks after the injury different with a boot than with a cast?
Two unpaired groups
Rank (ordinal)
Mann-Whitney test


Did KOOS JR improve from pre-op to 1 year?
Two paired groups
Rank (ceiling)
Wilcoxon signed-rank test


Does graft failure within 2 years differ between hamstring and BPTB grafts?
Two unpaired groups
Binomial
Fisher’s exact test


Does satisfaction differ between surgeons S1, S2 and S3?
Three or more unmatched groups
Rank (ordinal)
Kruskal-Wallis test


Does implant design affect revision-free survival?
Three or more unmatched groups
Survival
Cox regression

title: 3 · Distributions & choosing a test
section: p-values, effect sizes and confidence intervals
text:
p-values, effect sizes and confidence intervals
Every test on this site reports three things. They answer different questions, and a good Results section gives all three.

The effect size answers how big? For example, the difference between two means.
The 95% confidence interval (CI) answers how sure are we about that size? It’s the range of effect sizes compatible with the data.
The p-value answers how surprising would data like these be if there were really no difference at all? It doesn’t measure the size or importance of an effect.

Here’s all three for BMI in TKA vs THA, using the unpaired (Welch’s) t test from page 6:

RPython



bmi_test <- t.test(bmi ~ procedure, data = cohort)   # Welch's t test (R's default)
bmi_test


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  bmi by procedure
t = -4.0705, df = 580.09, p-value = 5.341e-05
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group THA and group TKA is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -2.647347 -0.924101
sample estimates:
mean in group THA mean in group TKA 
         29.46185          31.24758 

difference <- unname(bmi_test$estimate[2] - bmi_test$estimate[1])   # TKA minus THA
ci <- -rev(bmi_test$conf.int)                                        # flip to TKA minus THA
tibble(difference = difference, ci_low = ci[1], ci_high = ci[2], p = bmi_test$p.value)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  difference ci_low ci_high         p
       <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>
1       1.79  0.924    2.65 0.0000534





tka = cohort.loc[cohort["procedure"] == "TKA", "bmi"]
tha = cohort.loc[cohort["procedure"] == "THA", "bmi"]

bmi_test = stats.ttest_ind(tka, tha, equal_var=False)   # Welch's t test
ci = bmi_test.confidence_interval()

print(pd.Series({"difference": tka.mean() - tha.mean(),
                 "ci_low": ci.low, "ci_high": ci.high, "p": bmi_test.pvalue}))

difference    1.785724
ci_low        0.924101
ci_high       2.647347
p             0.000053
dtype: float64





Reading the output: the difference is 1.786, so 1.8 to one decimal. The CI runs from 0.924 to 2.647, so 0.9 to 2.6 (R’s small table shows 2.65 because it prints three significant figures). R prints p as 5.341e-05, which is 0.00005 and is written as p < 0.001. R’s first printout also shows t and df, the test statistic and its degrees of freedom; page 6 explains them, and here we need only the difference, its CI and p.

TKA patients had a higher BMI than THA patients (mean difference 1.8 kg/m², 95% CI 0.9 to 2.6; p < 0.001).

Is a difference of 1.8 kg/m² clinically important? The p-value can’t tell you. Ask whether a difference anywhere in the CI (0.9 to 2.6 kg/m²) would change risk or management, for example complication rates. That’s clinical judgment, not statistics. Statistically significant means only that data like these would be unusual if there were really no difference. It doesn’t mean the difference is large or important.






Warning⚠️ Watch out: two classic misreadings




“p = 0.20, so there’s no difference.” No. It means the data couldn’t rule out zero. Look at the CI: if it runs from “harmful” to “very helpful”, the study was too small to say.
“p < 0.001, so the effect is large.” No. With enough patients, tiny differences get tiny p-values. Look at the effect size and CI.









Tip🔀 R vs Python: which group comes first



R’s t.test(bmi ~ procedure) subtracts in alphabetical order of the groups (THA minus TKA). scipy’s ttest_ind(tka, tha) subtracts the second argument from the first. Same answer, opposite sign. Always say which group was subtracted from which, as we did above.


For PROMs, judge differences against the minimal clinically important difference (MCID): the smallest change patients notice as meaningful. Published MCIDs vary with the study and the method used to derive them, so cite the one you use. Be careful how you use it: an MCID is a within-patient threshold for one person’s change. A difference between two groups’ averages that is smaller than the MCID doesn’t prove no patient benefited, and a larger one doesn’t mean every patient did. Comparing the proportion of patients in each group who reached the MCID is often the clearer analysis.

Much closer to normal: skewness about 0.1 and the QQ points follow the line. Before surgery, scores sit in the middle of the scale, far from the ceiling. After a successful operation many patients hit the maximum, which creates the ceiling.



2. A fellow wants to compare operative time between surgeons S1 and S2, about 40 cases each. The histogram is fairly symmetric, with a few long cases. Which column of the decision table would you use, and how would you justify it in the Methods?






TipSolution





The Gaussian column (an unpaired t test, Welch’s version) is reasonable. With about 40 cases per group and a roughly symmetric shape, the t test is robust. Check the QQ plot within each surgeon, and check that the few long cases aren’t extreme outliers. Methods: “Operative time was approximately normally distributed within each group on visual inspection of histograms and QQ plots, and was compared with Welch’s t test.” If the long cases were extreme, a Mann-Whitney test would be the safer choice; say so.



3. A study reports: “1-year KOOS JR was 2.1 points higher with the new implant (95% CI −1.5 to 5.7; p = 0.25).” Suppose the MCID for KOOS JR is 14 points. Write one sentence interpreting this result.






TipSolution





“The study found no clear difference in 1-year KOOS JR between implants: the estimate (2.1 points) and the whole 95% CI (−1.5 to 5.7) are far smaller than the 14-point MCID, so a large average benefit of the new implant is unlikely.”
This is stronger than “not significant”: the CI rules out a large average difference. Strictly, the MCID is a within-patient threshold, so the clearest follow-up analysis compares the proportion of patients in each group who improved by at least 14 points.

title: 5 · Compare one group to a hypothetical value
text: Sometimes there is only one group of patients, and the comparison is with a number that comes from outside your data: a target set by the hospital, a value published by a registry, a benchmark in a quality report. Is our group different from that number?

title: 5 · Compare one group to a hypothetical value
text:
One-sample t test
The question: The operating room books 90 minutes for every primary joint replacement. Is our average operative time different from 90 minutes?

When to use it

The outcome is a measurement (minutes, kg/m², points).
It’s roughly normal, or the sample is large (about 30 or more) and not badly skewed (page 3).
Each patient is counted once and patients are independent of each other.
If the data are skewed, bounded or ordinal → the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.



What the test really does
The one-sample t test asks whether the sample mean is far from the hypothetical value, compared with how much a mean like this would wobble from one sample to the next.

Take the difference between the sample mean and the hypothetical value.
Estimate the noise in the mean, its standard error: the standard deviation divided by √n.
Divide: t = difference ÷ standard error. A t of 0 means the mean is exactly the hypothetical value. A t beyond about ±2 means the difference is large compared with the noise.
Turn t into a p-value: the chance of a t at least this far from 0 if the true mean really were the hypothetical value.

Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds t by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(cohort, aes(op_time_min)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 90, linetype = "dashed") +   # the booked time
  labs(x = "Operative time, minutes", y = "Patients")

A roughly symmetric hump, centered a little to the left of the dashed line at 90 minutes.

Effect size and 95% CI
The effect size is simply the difference from the hypothetical value: subtract 90 from the mean and from both ends of its CI.

Operations took 5.5 minutes less than the booked 90 on average (95% CI 4.2 to 6.8 minutes less). Whether that matters is a scheduling question, not a statistical one: over a day of four joints, it adds up to 4 × 5.5 = 22 minutes.


How to report it

Methods: Mean operative time was compared with the 90 minutes booked per case using a one-sample t test.
Results: Mean operative time was 84.5 minutes (SD 16.4); the booked time was 90 minutes (difference −5.5 minutes, 95% CI −6.8 to −4.2; p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: a published mean has its own uncertainty



A one-sample test treats the hypothetical value as exact. A registry mean is itself an estimate with a CI. If you’re comparing your patients with a published series and its CI is wide, say so, and don’t over-read a small difference.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: what the CI is a CI for



Both R’s t.test(x, mu = 90) and scipy’s ttest_1samp(x, popmean=90) report the CI for the mean (83.2 to 85.8), not for the difference from 90. Subtract the hypothetical value yourself, as above.

title: 5 · Compare one group to a hypothetical value
text:
Wilcoxon signed-rank test
The question: Suppose our practice’s target is a 1-year KOOS JR of 80 points after knee replacement. Is our typical patient’s score different from 80?

When to use it

The outcome is skewed or has a ceiling or floor, so a mean isn’t a fair summary (page 3).
It ranks how far each patient is above or below the hypothetical value. It doesn’t assume a normal distribution, but it does need distances that can be compared, so the outcome must be a measurement.
For an ordinal scale (satisfaction from 1 to 5), count the patients above and below the value and compare the two counts with a binomial test. This is called the sign test.
Strictly, it tests the pseudomedian (the Hodges-Lehmann estimate below), which equals the median only for a symmetric distribution. With a ceiling the two differ a little; report both.
If the data are roughly normal → the one-sample t test is more familiar and slightly more powerful.



What the test really does
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test compares the scores with the hypothetical value by rank, so a few extreme scores can’t dominate.

For each patient, take the distance between their score and the hypothetical value, and note whether the score is above or below it.
Set aside any patient who scores exactly the hypothetical value.
Line the distances up by size, ignoring the direction, and give each its position: its rank. The smallest distance gets rank 1; tied distances share the average of their ranks.
Add up the ranks of the patients above the value, and separately the ranks of those below. Either sum can serve as the test statistic.
If the typical patient scored exactly the hypothetical value, the two sums would be about equal. The more one-sided they are, the smaller the p-value.

Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” adds up the ranks by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
koos_1yr <- proms |>
  filter(instrument == "KOOS JR", visit == "1yr", !is.na(prom_score)) |>
  pull(prom_score)

length(koos_1yr)       # how many patients

[1] 260

sum(koos_1yr > 80)     # how many scored above the target

[1] 170

sum(koos_1yr < 80)     # how many scored below it

[1] 90

ggplot(tibble(score = koos_1yr), aes(score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 80, linetype = "dashed") +   # the target
  labs(x = "KOOS JR at 1 year (100 = best)", y = "Patients")











import numpy as np

import pingouin as pg

The ranks of the 170 scores above 80 add up to 22698.5, R’s V (printed as 22698), and those of the 90 scores below to 11231.5, Python’s W_val. Together they make 33930, which is 260 × 261 ÷ 2. Nobody scored exactly 80, so step 2 sets nobody aside.





Effect size and 95% CI
Two effect sizes are useful here:

The Hodges-Lehmann estimate (the pseudomedian): a center of the scores, in points. It’s the median of all the averages of pairs of scores, so it’s less affected by the ceiling than a mean.
The rank-biserial correlation (r): from −1 (every patient below 80) through 0 (balanced) to +1 (every patient above 80). As a rough guide, 0.1 is small, 0.3 moderate and 0.5 large. It is the rank sum above 80 minus the rank sum below, as a share of their total: (22,698.5 − 11,231.5) ÷ 33,930 = 0.34.

- Deviation from a difference of 80.

[74.7   85.75  93.925]

# Hodges-Lehmann estimate: the median of the averages of every pair of scores
def hodges_lehmann(x):
    x = np.asarray(x)
    i, j = np.triu_indices(len(x))          # every pair, including each score with itself
    return np.median((x[i] + x[j]) / 2)

print(hodges_lehmann(koos_1yr))

84.35

# scipy has no CI for it, so use a bootstrap: recompute it on 9999 resampled datasets
boot = stats.bootstrap((koos_1yr.to_numpy(),), hodges_lehmann, vectorized=False,
                       rng=np.random.default_rng(2026))
print(boot.confidence_interval)

ConfidenceInterval(low=np.float64(82.69999999999999), high=np.float64(86.05))

print(koos_test["RBC"])                               # rank-biserial r

Wilcoxon    0.337961
Name: RBC, dtype: float64





The typical 1-year score was about 4 points above the target (Hodges-Lehmann estimate 84.4), and the rank-biserial r of 0.34 is a moderate effect: 170 patients scored above 80 and 90 below, and those above tended to be further from it. The median is 85.75 (IQR 74.7 to 93.9, the first line of output), a little above the Hodges-Lehmann estimate, as expected with a ceiling. R’s effectsize also prints a 95% CI for r, 0.21 to 0.46 (its footnote only restates the target of 80); pingouin gives r without a CI.


How to report it

Methods: Because 1-year KOOS JR scores showed a ceiling effect, they were compared with the 80-point target using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with the Hodges-Lehmann estimate and its 95% CI as the effect size.
Results: The median 1-year KOOS JR was 85.8 points (IQR 74.7 to 93.9); the target was 80 points (Hodges-Lehmann estimate 84.4, 95% CI 82.7 to 86.1; rank-biserial r = 0.34; p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: two different “Wilcoxon” tests



The Wilcoxon signed-rank test (this one) compares one group with a value, or two paired measurements (page 7). The Wilcoxon rank-sum test compares two independent groups; it’s the same as the Mann-Whitney test. Always write the full name.
Also: patients who score exactly 80 carry no information about the direction and are dropped from the test.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: Wilcoxon defaults




The statistic. R reports V, the sum of the ranks of patients above 80 (22698.5, printed as 22698). scipy (and pingouin) report the smaller of the two sums (11231.5). The two sums always add up to n(n + 1)/2, here 260 × 261 / 2 = 33,930, so they carry the same information and give the same p-value.
Exact or approximate. For small samples without ties, both programs compute an exact p-value; otherwise they use a normal approximation. R adds a continuity correction to the approximation by default; scipy doesn’t. We set exact = FALSE, correct = FALSE in R and method="approx", correction=False in Python so they match.
The Hodges-Lehmann CI. R computes it by inverting the test. scipy has no function for it, so the Python code uses a bootstrap, a different method, so the two CIs differ slightly (82.75 to 86.10 in R, 82.70 to 86.05 from the bootstrap).

title: 5 · Compare one group to a hypothetical value
text:
Chi-square goodness-of-fit test
The question: Suppose a national registry reports that its patients are 10% ASA class 1, 55% class 2, 33% class 3 and 2% class 4. Is our mix of ASA classes the same?

When to use it

The outcome is categorical with two or more categories, and you have hypothetical proportions for every category.
Each patient falls in exactly one category, and is counted once.
The expected count in every category (total × hypothetical proportion) should be at least 5. Otherwise combine small categories, or with only two categories use the binomial test.



What the test really does
The goodness-of-fit test compares the counts you observed with the counts the hypothetical proportions would predict.

Work out the expected count for each category: the total number of patients × that category’s hypothetical proportion.
For each category, take (observed − expected)² ÷ expected, then add up the results. The sum is the test statistic, χ²: 0 when the observed counts match the expected ones exactly, and larger the further apart they are.
Turn χ² into a p-value with the chi-square distribution. This step is an approximation, and a poor one when expected counts are small. That is where the “at least 5” rule comes from.

Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds χ² by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
registry <- c(0.10, 0.55, 0.33, 0.02)                 # the hypothetical proportions, ASA 1 to 4

asa_counts <- table(cohort$asa)
tibble(asa = names(asa_counts), observed = as.vector(asa_counts),
       expected = sum(asa_counts) * registry)

# A tibble: 4 × 3

1 1           36       60
2 2          300      330
3 3          246      198
4 4           18       12

ASA 3 makes the biggest difference: 41.0% of our patients (95% CI 37.1% to 45.0%) against 33% in the registry. The CI doesn’t include 33%.


How to report it

Methods: The distribution of ASA classes was compared with the registry’s using a chi-square goodness-of-fit test.
Results: ASA class 3 accounted for 41.0% of our patients (95% CI 37.1% to 45.0%) and 33% of the registry’s, and ASA class 1 for 6.0% and 10% (χ² = 27.0, df = 3, p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: counts, not percentages



The test needs the counts of patients in each category. Feeding it percentages (“6, 50, 41, 3”) gives a wrong p-value, because the test’s precision depends on how many patients there are.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: proportions or counts



R’s chisq.test(counts, p = ...) takes the hypothetical proportions (they must add up to 1). scipy’s chisquare(counts, f_exp=...) takes the expected counts (they must add up to the observed total). Same test, different inputs.

title: 5 · Compare one group to a hypothetical value
text:
Binomial test
The question: Suppose the target is that 90% of hip fracture patients are operated on within 48 hours of admission. Is our proportion different?

When to use it

The outcome is yes/no, and you’re comparing one group’s proportion with a hypothetical proportion.
Each patient is counted once.
The binomial test is exact: it works for any sample size, including small numbers of events. (The chi-square goodness-of-fit test with two categories is its large-sample approximation.)



What the test really does
The binomial test works out exact probabilities, with no approximation.

Suppose the hypothetical proportion were true. The binomial distribution then gives the exact probability of every possible result: 0 patients with the outcome, 1 patient, 2 patients, and so on up to all of them.
Find the probability of the result you observed.
Add up the probabilities of all the results that are no more likely than yours, on either side of the expected number. That sum is the p-value.

Because it uses exact probabilities, the test works for any sample size. Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” adds up the probabilities by hand.


Look at the data first

95% CI 0.841 to 0.881: our true proportion is plausibly anywhere from 84.1% to 88.1%. This is the exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval.







Note🔍 Under the hood: the exact p-value by hand

If 90% were the true proportion, 1,080 of the 1,200 patients would be expected. Seeing exactly 1,034 would be very unlikely, and so would every result further from 1,080 on either side. Their probabilities add up to 0.0000268, the p-value both programs printed (2.682e-05).





Effect size and 95% CI
The effect size is the difference from the target: 86.2% − 90% = −3.8 percentage points. Its 95% CI is the CI for our proportion minus 90%: −5.9 to −1.9 percentage points. It excludes 0, which matches the p-value below 0.05. In patients: at 90%, 1,080 of the 1,200 would have been operated on within 48 hours, 46 more than were.


How to report it

Methods: The proportion of patients operated on within 48 hours of admission was compared with the target of 90% using an exact binomial test. 95% CIs for proportions are exact (Clopper-Pearson).
Results: Within 48 hours of admission, 1,034 of 1,200 patients (86.2%; 95% CI 84.1% to 88.1%) were operated on; the target was 90% (binomial test p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: decide one- or two-sided before you look



A target invites a one-sided question: are we below 90%? A one-sided test roughly halves the p-value, so choosing one after seeing which side of the target you landed on makes the p-value too small. Use a one-sided test only when the protocol named it before the data came in, and a result on the other side would genuinely change nothing. Otherwise report the two-sided test, as here.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: exact CIs



R’s binom.test() and scipy’s binomtest() agree on the p-value. R prints the exact (Clopper-Pearson) CI automatically; in scipy, ask for it with proportion_ci(method="exact"). It’s a little wider than the Wilson interval that page 4 uses, which for these 1,034 of 1,200 patients runs from 84.1% to 88.0% (the last line of output under “Run it”). Either is fine; say which you used.

title: 7 · Compare two paired groups
text: Paired data come in twos that belong together: the same patient before and after surgery, two X-ray views of the same hip, two raters measuring the same X-ray, or two patients matched to each other on age, sex and BMI. Paired tests compare each patient with themselves (or with their match), which removes the patient-to-patient variation that unpaired tests have to wade through. If your two groups are different patients, use page 6 instead.

title: 7 · Compare two paired groups
text:
Paired t test
The question: Do the frog-leg and Dunn 45° views give different alpha angles in the same hips?

When to use it

Each patient (or matched pair) gives two measurements of the same thing: here, the alpha angle of the same hip on two X-ray views.
The differences between the two measurements are roughly normal, or there are about 30 or more pairs. The assumption is about the differences, not about each measurement on its own.
Pairs are independent of each other.
If the differences are skewed, or the measurements are bounded or ordinal → the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.



What the test really does
The paired t test turns two columns into one. Each hip has two readings, and the test looks only at the difference between them.

For each hip, subtract one reading from the other. From here on, the two original columns are not used again.
Take the mean of these differences.
Estimate the noise in that mean, its standard error: the SD of the differences divided by √n, where n is the number of hips.
Divide: t = mean difference ÷ standard error, and turn t into a p-value.

Because each hip is compared with itself, the large differences between hips drop out. That is why a paired test can detect a small difference that an unpaired test would miss.
Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds t by hand.


Look at the data first
The alpha angle measures how far the front of the femoral head-neck junction bulges (cam morphology): the larger the angle, the bigger the bump. The hip-preservation data hold one row per hip (one hip per patient), from young adults assessed for hip-preservation surgery, with the alpha angle measured on two views: the frog-leg lateral and the Dunn 45°.
Paired data need to be wide: one row per patient, with the two measurements side by side. These data already are; page 1 shows how to reshape data that aren’t.

library(tidyverse)

Cohen’s dz divides the mean difference by the standard deviation of the differences: how consistently the two views differ across hips. The usual guide (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large) applies.

dz = 0.87 is a large effect: 62 of the 80 hips (78%) read higher on the Dunn view. It matters in clinic, because cam morphology is often defined by an alpha angle above a threshold. With a threshold of 55°, 56 hips count as cam-positive on the Dunn view and 48 on the frog-leg view. Say which view you measured. The last lines of the code count them: 62 hips, a share of 0.775, and 56 and 48 hips above 55°.


How to report it

Methods: The alpha angle on the Dunn 45° and frog-leg views of the same hip was compared with a paired t test.
Results: In 80 hips, the mean alpha angle was 61.8° (SD 11.2) on the Dunn 45° view and 58.2° (SD 10.8) on the frog-leg view (mean difference 3.7°, 95% CI 2.7 to 4.6; dz = 0.87, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.12; p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: don’t analyze paired data as unpaired



Running an unpaired t test on the two columns ignores which readings belong to the same hip. Here it gives p = 0.037 instead of p < 0.001: the 3.7° difference between the views is small next to the 11° spread between hips, and only the paired test takes that spread out. It’s wrong even when it happens to give the same answer, because its standard error assumes 160 independent hips when there are only 80. (The unpaired p-value, 0.0365, is the last line under “Run it”; each view’s SD, about 11°, is in the first table.)








Tip🔀 R vs Python: paired effect sizes



pingouin’s compute_effsize(x, y, paired=True) does not return dz: it returns dav (the mean difference divided by the square root of the average of the two variances), 0.33 here. Both are legitimate, but they answer different questions and aren’t interchangeable: dav compares the difference with how much hips differ from each other, dz with how consistently the two views differ within a hip. We compute dz directly so the two languages match; say which one you report. Here dav is 3.67 / √((11.2² + 10.8²) / 2) = 3.67 / 11.0 = 0.33. The Python code gives dz without a CI; the CI in the Results sentence is the one R’s effectsize prints.

title: 7 · Compare two paired groups
text:
Wilcoxon signed-rank test
The question: Did KOOS JR improve from before surgery to 1 year after knee replacement?

When to use it

Two paired measurements, and the outcome is skewed or has a ceiling or floor. The 1-year KOOS JR has a ceiling (page 3).
For an ordinal scale (satisfaction from 1 to 5), count the patients who went up and down and compare the two counts with a binomial test (the sign test, page 5).
It ranks the sizes of the changes and compares the ranks of improvements with the ranks of declines.
Changes of exactly zero carry no information about direction and are dropped.
If the changes are roughly normal → the paired t test.



What the test really does
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test also works on each patient’s change, but it uses the order of the changes instead of their size.

For each patient, take the change (here, 1 year minus pre-op).
Set aside any patient whose change is exactly 0.
Line the changes up by size, ignoring whether they are improvements or declines, and give each one its position: its rank. The smallest change gets rank 1.
Add up the ranks of the improvements, and separately the ranks of the declines. Either sum can serve as the test statistic: R reports the first (V), Python the smaller of the two (W).
If there were no real change, improvements and declines would share the ranks about evenly. The more one-sided the two sums, the smaller the p-value.

Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” adds up the ranks by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

koos <- proms |>
  filter(instrument == "KOOS JR", visit %in% c("preop", "1yr")) |>
  select(case_id, visit, prom_score) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit, values_from = prom_score, names_prefix = "koos_") |>
  filter(!is.na(koos_preop), !is.na(koos_1yr)) |>
  mutate(change = koos_1yr - koos_preop)

ggplot(koos, aes(change)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Change in KOOS JR, 1 year minus pre-op", y = "Patients")







koos |> summarise(n = n(), improved = sum(change > 0),
                  median_preop = median(koos_preop), median_1yr = median(koos_1yr))

# Hodges-Lehmann estimate: the median of the averages of every pair of changes
def hodges_lehmann(x):
    x = np.asarray(x)
    i, j = np.triu_indices(len(x))          # every pair, including each change with itself
    return np.median((x[i] + x[j]) / 2)

Results: In all 246 patients with both scores, the change was positive. Median KOOS JR was 50.0 (IQR 40.8 to 58.2) before surgery and 85.8 (IQR 75.0 to 94.0) at 1 year (Hodges-Lehmann estimate of the change 34.1 points, 95% CI 32.3 to 35.9; p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: “significant improvement” isn’t the whole story



A tiny p-value says the scores went up on average; it doesn’t say how many patients improved by a meaningful amount. For PROMs, also report the proportion of patients whose change reached the minimal clinically important difference (MCID), a within-patient threshold (page 3).








Tip🔀 R vs Python: Wilcoxon defaults




The statistic. R reports V, the sum of the ranks of the positive changes. scipy (and pingouin) report the smaller of the two sums. The p-values agree.
Exact or approximate. R uses an exact p-value for fewer than 50 pairs without ties and adds a continuity correction to the normal approximation; scipy’s defaults differ. We set exact = FALSE, correct = FALSE in R and method="approx", correction=False in Python so they match.
The Hodges-Lehmann CI. R computes it by inverting the test; the Python code uses a bootstrap, a different method. Here they agree to two decimals (32.30 to 35.90), as they do on page 6, but on other data they can differ a little.

title: 7 · Compare two paired groups
text:
McNemar’s test
The question: Are patients more likely to use a walking aid 6 weeks after surgery than before it?

When to use it

A yes/no outcome measured twice in the same patients (or once in each member of a matched pair).
It uses only the discordant pairs: the patients who changed (no → yes, or yes → no). Patients who stayed the same tell you nothing about the direction of change.
The chi-square version needs at least about 10 discordant pairs in total. With fewer, use the exact version (see the R vs Python box).



What the test really does
McNemar’s test looks only at the patients whose answer changed.

Cross-tabulate the two answers: before in the rows, after in the columns.
Set aside the patients who gave the same answer both times. They say nothing about change.
Among the patients who changed, count each direction: from no to yes, and from yes to no.
If nothing had really changed, the two directions would be equally likely, like heads and tails. The test statistic measures how far the split is from even, and the further it is, the smaller the p-value.

The first bullet under “Read the output” works it out by hand.


Look at the data first
For paired yes/no data, “looking” means a 2 × 2 table of before × after: each patient appears once.

RPython



library(tidyverse)

proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

aid <- proms |>
  filter(visit %in% c("preop", "6wk")) |>
  select(case_id, visit, walking_aid) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit, values_from = walking_aid, names_prefix = "aid_") |>
  filter(!is.na(aid_preop), !is.na(aid_6wk))

aid_table <- table(preop = aid$aid_preop, six_weeks = aid$aid_6wk)   # 1 = uses a walking aid
aid_table

     six_weeks
preop   0   1
    0 134 193
    1  70 108

colMeans(aid[, c("aid_preop", "aid_6wk")])                          # proportion using an aid

aid_preop   aid_6wk 
0.3524752 0.5960396 





import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import mcnemar

proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")

aid = (proms[proms["visit"].isin(["preop", "6wk"])]
       .pivot(index="case_id", columns="visit", values="walking_aid")
       .dropna())

aid_table = pd.crosstab(aid["preop"], aid["6wk"])   # 1 = uses a walking aid
print(aid_table)

6wk    0.0  1.0
preop          
0.0    134  193
1.0     70  108

print(aid[["preop", "6wk"]].mean())                 # proportion using an aid

visit
preop    0.352475
6wk      0.596040

Of 505 patients seen at both visits, 134 never used an aid and 108 used one at both times. The other 263 changed: 193 started using an aid and 70 stopped. The table’s four cells add up: 134 + 193 + 70 + 108 = 505, and 193 + 70 = 263 changed. “Started” is row 0, column 1 (no aid before, an aid at 6 weeks); “stopped” is row 1, column 0.


Run it

RPython



aid_test <- mcnemar.test(aid_table)   # with a continuity correction, R's default
aid_test


    McNemar's Chi-squared test with continuity correction

data:  aid_table
McNemar's chi-squared = 56.593, df = 1, p-value = 5.36e-14





aid_test = mcnemar(aid_table.to_numpy(), exact=False, correction=True)   # chi-square version, as in R
print(aid_test)

pvalue      5.3598068806119586e-14
statistic   56.59315589353612







Read the output

McNemar’s chi-squared = 56.6, df = 1: how lopsided the 193 vs 70 split is, compared with the even split you’d expect if walking-aid use hadn’t changed. By hand: (193 − 70 − 1)² / (193 + 70) = 122² / 263 = 56.6; the −1 is the continuity correction.
p < 0.001. R prints p-value = 5.36e-14.



Effect size and 95% CI
The effect size for McNemar’s test is the discordant-pair odds ratio: patients who started using an aid divided by patients who stopped, 193 / 70. Its exact CI comes from a binomial test on the discordant pairs. 193 of the 263 patients who changed started using an aid, a share of 0.734. Odds are share / (1 − share): 0.734 / 0.266 = 2.76, the same as 193 / 70. The code does the same to both ends of the share’s exact CI (0.676 to 0.786).

RPython



started <- aid_table["0", "1"]    # no aid before, aid at 6 weeks
stopped <- aid_table["1", "0"]    # aid before, no aid at 6 weeks

started / stopped                                    # discordant-pair odds ratio

[1] 2.757143

ci <- binom.test(started, started + stopped)$conf.int  # CI for the share of changers who started
ci / (1 - ci)                                        # turned into a CI for the odds ratio

[1] 2.087169 3.678298
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95





started = int(aid_table.loc[0, 1])    # no aid before, aid at 6 weeks
stopped = int(aid_table.loc[1, 0])    # aid before, no aid at 6 weeks

print(started / stopped)                                                # discordant-pair odds ratio

2.757142857142857

ci = stats.binomtest(started, started + stopped).proportion_ci(method="exact")   # share of changers who started
print(ci.low / (1 - ci.low), ci.high / (1 - ci.high))                   # turned into a CI for the odds ratio

2.0871688376583153 3.6782978561318966





Patients were 2.8 times as likely to start using an aid as to stop (95% CI 2.1 to 3.7).


How to report it

Methods: Walking-aid use before surgery and at 6 weeks was compared with McNemar’s test, with the discordant-pair odds ratio and its exact 95% CI as the effect size.
Results: Among 505 patients assessed at both visits, 35.2% used a walking aid before surgery and 59.6% at 6 weeks; 193 patients started and 70 stopped using an aid (discordant-pair odds ratio 2.76, 95% CI 2.09 to 3.68; p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: no chi-square or Fisher’s test on paired yes/no data



A common mistake is to tabulate “aid yes/no” against “pre-op / 6 weeks” and run an ordinary chi-square test. That table counts each patient twice, as if 1010 independent patients had been studied. McNemar’s test uses each patient once, through the before × after table.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: chi-square or exact?



R’s mcnemar.test() gives the chi-square version, with a continuity correction unless correct = FALSE. statsmodels’ mcnemar() gives the exact (binomial) version unless you set exact=False. With few discordant pairs (under about 10), the exact version is the right one: in R, run binom.test(started, started + stopped).

title: 7 · Compare two paired groups
text:
Stratified Cox regression
The question: Among patients matched on procedure, age, sex, BMI and ASA class, is the revision risk higher with implant C than with implant A?

When to use it

The outcome is time until an event, and the patients come in matched pairs (or sets), or the two “patients” are the two joints of one person.
A Cox model stratified by pair lets each pair have its own baseline risk, and compares implants only within pairs. The decision table calls this conditional proportional hazards regression.
Only pairs in which one patient was revised while the other was still being followed tell the model anything; with few events, expect a wide CI.
Page 14 covers Cox regression in full.



What the test really does
A stratified Cox model compares the implants within each matched pair, never across pairs.

Take one pair at a time and follow its two patients forward from surgery.
Find the one whose follow-up ends first. If that patient was revised while the partner was still being followed, the pair is informative: note which implant failed first. Otherwise the pair tells the model nothing.
Count the informative pairs in each direction: implant C revised first, or implant A revised first.
With one patient per implant in each pair, the hazard ratio is the ratio of these two counts. The fewer informative pairs there are, the wider its CI.

“Look at the data first” counts the pairs for our data.


Look at the data first
The matched file has one row per patient and a set_id shared by each matched set. Each set holds one patient with each implant (A, B and C); here we keep A and C, which makes pairs.

RPython



library(tidyverse)
library(survival)

matched <- read_csv("data/matched_sets.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

pairs <- matched |>
  filter(implant %in% c("A", "C")) |>
  mutate(revised = as.integer(event_status == 1))   # 1 = revised; deaths and censoring = 0

pairs |> select(set_id, implant, age, sex, bmi, followup_years, revised) |> head(4)

n = 104, number of events = 22: 52 pairs, 22 revisions.
exp(coef) = 3.5: the hazard ratio, implant C vs implant A, within pairs. Because every pair holds one patient with each implant, it is simply the ratio of the two counts above: 14 / 4 = 3.5.
lower .95 = 1.15, upper .95 = 10.63: its 95% CI. Wide, because only 18 revisions inform it.

Effect size and 95% CI
The hazard ratio is the effect size: within matched pairs, the hazard of revision was 3.5 times as high with implant C (95% CI 1.15 to 10.63).


How to report it

Methods: Revision risk was compared between implants in matched pairs using Cox regression stratified by pair.
Results: In 52 pairs matched on procedure, age, sex, BMI and ASA class, 17 implant C and 5 implant A procedures were revised (hazard ratio for implant C vs A 3.50, 95% CI 1.15 to 10.63; p = 0.027).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: don’t ignore the matching



An ordinary Cox model on the same 104 patients (without strata()) treats them as unrelated. That throws away the matching you worked to create. Here it gives a slightly different answer (hazard ratio 3.60); with stronger matching factors the difference can be large. Analyze matched data as matched. (The last line under “Run it” fits it: 3.597.)








Tip🔀 R vs Python: strata and convergence



R puts strata(set_id) in the model formula; lifelines takes strata=["set_id"] as a separate argument. With so few events and many strata, lifelines’ default convergence rule stops a little early (a hazard ratio of 3.4997 instead of 3.5), so we tighten it with fit_options={"precision": 1e-9}. (Run the fit without fit_options and it prints 3.4997.)

title: 9 · Compare three or more matched groups
text:
Repeated-measures ANOVA
The question: Does physical function (PROMIS-29+2) change over the first year after surgery?

When to use it

A measurement taken three or more times on the same patients (or once on each member of a matched set).
The changes between visits are roughly normal, or there are plenty of patients.
Sphericity: the spread of the changes is similar for every pair of visits. Mauchly’s test checks it; if it fails, the Greenhouse-Geisser correction adjusts the degrees of freedom. Both programs below report both.
Only patients measured at every visit are included (see the warning above).
If the outcome is skewed, bounded or ordinal → the Friedman test.

PROMIS physical function is a T-score: 50 is the average of the US general population. The four-question form in PROMIS-29+2 runs from 22.5 to 57.0, and 57.0 is the best it can record.


What the test really does
Repeated-measures ANOVA is a one-way ANOVA that first sets aside the differences between patients.

Work out the mean of each visit, and each patient’s own mean over all the visits.
Split the variation in the scores into three parts. Between the visits: how far the visit means are from the overall mean. Between the patients: how far each patient’s own mean is from the overall mean. Left over: how much each patient’s scores still bounce around once the visit means and that patient’s own level are taken into account.
Set the part between the patients aside. Some patients score high at every visit and others low, and that says nothing about change over time.
Divide each of the other two parts by its degrees of freedom, then divide the results: F = variation between the visits ÷ variation left over. If the scores didn’t change over time, F would be close to 1. The larger F, the smaller the p-value.

Setting the differences between patients aside is what makes the test sensitive: each patient serves as their own comparison, as in the paired t test. Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds F by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

  filter(all(!is.na(promis_pf))) |>     # keep procedures measured at all four visits
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr")))   # in time order

The last line is partial eta squared: 28578 ÷ (28578 + 28655) = 0.499, the pes in R’s table and np2 in Python’s.





Effect size and 95% CI
Partial eta squared (η²p) is the share of the within-patient variation that the visits account for. As a rough guide, 0.01 is small, 0.06 medium and 0.14 large. Generalized eta squared (ges = 0.417 in R) also counts the differences between patients, which makes it comparable with designs that aren’t repeated measures; report it when readers will compare studies of different designs.

RPython

---------------------------------------------------------

- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].





print(pf_anova.loc[0, "np2"])    # pingouin doesn't compute a CI for it

0.4993302359186056





η²p = 0.50: a very large effect. The visits account for about half of the variation in each patient’s scores over the year. R also prints a one-sided 95% CI, 0.47 to 1.00: η²p can’t be negative, so R reports a lower bound only and fixes the upper bound at 1.00. pingouin doesn’t compute a CI. R’s headings mention “type III” and “Type I”: these are ways of dividing up the variation when a model has several predictors, and with one predictor they give the same result.


How to report it

Methods: PROMIS-29+2 physical function T-scores across the four visits were compared with one-way repeated-measures ANOVA in patients with all four measurements. Sphericity was assessed with Mauchly’s test, with the Greenhouse-Geisser correction planned if it was violated. Partial eta squared (η²p) is reported as the effect size.
Results: Of 574 procedures with a pre-op PROMIS physical function score, 328 had all four measurements. Their mean T-score was 36.1 (SD 5.4) before surgery, 39.4 (SD 5.5) at 6 weeks, 44.9 (SD 5.5) at 3 months and 48.2 (SD 5.6) at 1 year (F(3, 981) = 326.1, p < 0.001; η²p = 0.50, one-sided 95% CI 0.47 to 1.00; Mauchly’s test of sphericity p = 0.903).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: a significant F doesn’t say which visits differ



The ANOVA says the visit means aren’t all the same. To say when, compare the visits with paired tests and a correction for multiple comparisons (page 15). And remember who’s missing: the patients behind the 246 procedures without complete data may have recovered differently.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: which tools check sphericity




R: base aov(... + Error(case_id / visit)) gives the same F test but ignores sphericity; rstatix::anova_test() adds Mauchly’s test and the corrections. rstatix rounds its numbers to 3 decimals.
Python: pingouin’s rm_anova(correction=True) reports Mauchly’s test and the Greenhouse-Geisser correction. statsmodels’ AnovaRM gives the F test only.
Effect sizes: pingouin returns either partial (effsize="np2") or generalized (effsize="ng2") eta squared; rstatix returns both if asked.

title: 9 · Compare three or more matched groups
text:
Friedman test
The question: With a removable boot, does the EFAS score keep changing between 6 weeks, 3 months and 12 months?

When to use it

An outcome measured three or more times on the same patients, when it’s skewed, ordinal or has a ceiling or floor. The EFAS score adds up six questions, and by 12 months scores crowd toward its maximum of 24.
It ranks each patient’s own scores (1st, 2nd, 3rd) and asks whether some visits tend to rank higher than others.
Only patients measured at every visit are included.
If the outcome is a roughly normal measurement → repeated-measures ANOVA.



What the test really does
The Friedman test compares the visits inside each patient, using only the order of that patient’s own scores.

Take one patient at a time and give their scores a rank across the visits: 1 for the lowest, 2 for the next and 3 for the highest. Tied scores share the average of their ranks.
Work out the mean rank of each visit across all the patients.
If the scores didn’t change between visits, each visit would be equally likely to get any rank, and every visit’s mean rank would be close to 2, the middle of 1, 2 and 3.
The test statistic measures how far the visits’ mean ranks are from that middle value. The further they are, the smaller the p-value.

Because each patient is ranked separately, it doesn’t matter that some patients score high at every visit and others low. Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds the statistic by hand.

The boot arm of the trial from page 6 has 60 randomized patients, and some missed visits.

Effect size and 95% CI
Kendall’s W measures how consistently patients’ scores rank the visits in the same order: 0 means no agreement at all, 1 means every patient’s scores rank the three visits identically. As a rough guide, 0.1 is small, 0.3 moderate and 0.5 large. W is the Friedman statistic divided by the largest value it could take, n × (k − 1) for n patients and k visits: 84.94 ÷ (50 × 2) = 0.85.

W = 0.85: a large effect. 45 of the 50 patients scored higher at 3 months than at 6 weeks, and 42 scored higher at 12 months than at 3 months. R also prints a one-sided 95% CI, 0.78 to 1.00: W can’t be negative, so R reports a lower bound only. The CI comes from a bootstrap, which is why the code sets a seed; pingouin doesn’t compute one.


How to report it

Methods: Because EFAS scores crowd toward the ceiling of the scale, scores at 6 weeks, 3 months and 12 months in the boot arm were compared with the Friedman test in patients with all three measurements, with Kendall’s W as the effect size.
Results: Among 50 of the 60 patients randomized to a boot, those with all three measurements, the median EFAS score was 12.5 (IQR 11 to 14) at 6 weeks, 17 (IQR 16 to 20) at 3 months and 20 (IQR 19 to 22) at 12 months (Friedman χ² = 84.9, df = 2, p < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.85, one-sided 95% CI 0.78 to 1.00).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: the Friedman test ignores how big the changes are



It only uses each patient’s ranking of the visits. A patient who gained 1 point and one who gained 10 count the same. Report the medians (or the changes) so readers can see the size of the improvement, and judge it against the MCID (page 3).








Tip🔀 R vs Python: data formats



R’s friedman.test() takes a formula, outcome ~ visit | patient, on long data. pingouin’s friedman() also takes long data; scipy’s friedmanchisquare() instead wants one column per visit in wide data. All three correct for tied scores within a patient, so they agree.

title: 9 · Compare three or more matched groups
text:
Cochran’s Q test
The question: Does walking-aid use change over the first year after surgery?

When to use it

A yes/no outcome measured three or more times on the same patients (or once on each member of a matched set).
It extends McNemar’s test to more than two visits, and, like McNemar’s, it only learns from patients whose answer changed.
Only patients measured at every visit are included.



What the test really does
Cochran’s Q compares how many patients answer yes at each visit, within the same patients.

Count the yes answers at each visit.
Count each patient’s yes answers across the visits. A patient who answers yes at every visit, or no at every visit, says nothing about change and drops out of the calculation.
If nothing changed over time, each of a patient’s yes answers would be equally likely to fall on any visit, so the visit totals would come out about equal.
The test statistic, Q, measures how unequal the visit totals are, compared with how unequal chance alone would make them. The larger Q, the smaller the p-value.

With only two visits, Q is the statistic of McNemar’s test without its continuity correction. Once the test has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds Q by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

aid <- proms |>
  select(case_id, visit, walking_aid) |>
  group_by(case_id) |>
  filter(all(!is.na(walking_aid))) |>    # keep procedures measured at all four visits
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr")))

aid |>
  group_by(visit) |>
  summarise(procedures = n(), using_aid = sum(walking_aid), percent = 100 * mean(walking_aid))

def cochran_q(yes):                                                                    # step 4: Q from a table of 0s and 1s
    k = yes.shape[1]

Cochran’s Q has no standard single effect size. Describe the proportion at each visit, with its 95% CI (the Wilson interval from page 4), and the changes between visits in percentage points.

Use rose from 114 to 194 of the 328 procedures between pre-op and 6 weeks (the using column in R; Python prints these counts under “Look at the data first”): 80 more, or 80 ÷ 328 = 24.4 percentage points. By 1 year it had fallen to 34, which is 80 fewer than before surgery, again 24.4 points. Subtracting the rounded percentages instead, 59.1 − 34.8, gives 24.3: work from the counts.


How to report it

Methods: Walking-aid use at the four visits was compared with Cochran’s Q test in patients assessed at all four. Proportions are reported with Wilson 95% CIs.
Results: Among 328 procedures assessed at all four visits, walking-aid use was 34.8% (95% CI 29.8% to 40.1%) before surgery, 59.1% (95% CI 53.8% to 64.3%) at 6 weeks, 24.4% (95% CI 20.1% to 29.3%) at 3 months and 10.4% (95% CI 7.5% to 14.1%) at 1 year (Cochran’s Q = 186.8, df = 3, p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: Q doesn’t tell you the direction



Use went up and then down. Cochran’s Q only says it wasn’t the same at every visit. To say which changes are real, compare pairs of visits with McNemar’s test and a correction for multiple comparisons (page 15).








Tip🔀 R vs Python: where to find Cochran’s Q



Base R doesn’t have Cochran’s Q; DescTools::CochranQTest() (or rstatix::cochran_qtest()) does. In Python, pingouin’s cochran() takes long data; statsmodels’ cochrans_q() takes a wide array with one column per visit. All give the same Q.

title: 9 · Compare three or more matched groups
text:
Stratified Cox regression
The question: In sets of three patients matched on procedure, age, sex, BMI and ASA class, does the risk of revision differ between implants A, B and C?

When to use it

The outcome is time until an event, and the patients come in matched sets of three or more.
A Cox model stratified by matched set compares the implants only within sets, as on page 7, which used just the A and C patients from the same sets.
With few events, expect wide CIs. Page 14 covers Cox regression in full.



What the test really does
A stratified Cox model works like the Cox model on page 8, with one change: every comparison stays inside a matched set.

Take one matched set at a time and follow its three patients forward from surgery.
Each time one of them is revised, look at which members of the set were still being followed just before: the patients at risk in that set.
If the implants carried the same risk, the revision would be equally likely to happen to any of those members. The model tries out values for each implant’s hazard ratio and keeps the values under which the revisions that really happened, taken together, were most likely.
A revision tells the model nothing if no other member of the set was still being followed, and neither does a set with no revision at all.

The patients in a set are alike in the factors they were matched on, so those factors can’t explain a difference between the implants. Once the model has run, a box under “Read the output” works out the observed and expected revisions inside the sets by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)
library(survival)

matched <- read_csv("data/matched_sets.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(revised = as.integer(event_status == 1))   # 1 = revised; deaths and censoring = 0

matched |> select(set_id, implant, age, sex, bmi, followup_years, revised) |> head(6)

Python prints it on the line under its table: the statistic, its degrees of freedom and the p-value (0.00118). Don’t confuse it with R’s “Score (logrank) test” two lines below, which happens to print 13.5.







Note🔍 Under the hood: observed and expected revisions inside the sets, by hand






RPython



revisions <- matched |> filter(revised == 1)                 # the 24 revisions
expected <- c(A = 0, B = 0, C = 0)
alone <- 0
for (i in seq_len(nrow(revisions))) {
  at_risk <- matched |>                                      # members of the same set still followed just before this revision
    filter(set_id == revisions$set_id[i], followup_years >= revisions$followup_years[i])
  if (nrow(at_risk) == 1) alone <- alone + 1                 # nobody else left in the set: this revision tells the model nothing
  expected <- expected + as.vector(table(factor(at_risk$implant, levels = c("A", "B", "C")))) / nrow(at_risk)   # each member at risk gets an equal share of the revision
}
rbind(observed = table(revisions$implant), expected = expected)

                A        B         C
observed 5.000000 2.000000 17.000000
expected 7.833333 6.833333  9.333333

alone

[1] 2





revisions = matched[matched["revised"] == 1]                  # the 24 revisions
expected = pd.Series({"A": 0.0, "B": 0.0, "C": 0.0})
alone = 0
for revision in revisions.itertuples():
    at_risk = matched[(matched["set_id"] == revision.set_id)                 # members of the same set still followed just before this revision
                      & (matched["followup_years"] >= revision.followup_years)]
    alone += len(at_risk) == 1                                # nobody else left in the set: this revision tells the model nothing
    for group in expected.index:
        expected[group] += (at_risk["implant"] == group).sum() / len(at_risk)   # each member at risk gets an equal share of the revision
print(pd.DataFrame({"observed": revisions["implant"].value_counts().sort_index(), "expected": expected}).T)

                 A         B          C
observed  5.000000  2.000000  17.000000
expected  7.833333  6.833333   9.333333

print(alone)

2





If the implants carried the same risk, the 24 revisions would have been shared out inside the sets as 7.8 (A), 6.8 (B) and 9.3 (C). Implant C had 17, almost twice its share; implant A had 5 and implant B 2. 2 of the 24 revisions happened when no other member of the set was still being followed (alone); each adds 1 to both observed and expected for its implant and so tells the model nothing. R’s “Score (logrank) test” line tests these gaps between observed and expected.





Effect size and 95% CI
The hazard ratios with their 95% CIs: within matched sets, implant C carried about four times the hazard of revision of implant A (3.91, 95% CI 1.28 to 11.95). The estimate for implant B (0.43, 95% CI 0.08 to 2.25) is too imprecise to interpret.


How to report it

Methods: Revision risk was compared between implants in matched sets using Cox regression stratified by set, with implant A as the reference.
Results: In 52 sets of three patients matched on procedure, age, sex, BMI and ASA class, the hazard ratio for revision compared with implant A was 3.91 (95% CI 1.28 to 11.95) for implant C and 0.43 (95% CI 0.08 to 2.25) for implant B (likelihood ratio test for implant type, χ² = 13.5, df = 2, p = 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: only 24 events



A Cox model needs events, not just patients. With 24 revisions across three implants, the CIs are wide and the model can’t support adjustment for anything else. Page 14 covers how many events a model needs.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: strata and convergence



As on page 7, R puts strata(set_id) in the formula while lifelines takes strata=["set_id"]. Here lifelines’ default convergence matches R exactly; with page 7’s pairs it stopped a little early and needed fit_options={"precision": 1e-9}. If the two programs disagree in the fourth decimal, tighten it.

Which visits differ?
Each test above answers “is there any difference among the visits (or implants)?”. When the answer is yes, the next question is which pairs differ. Comparing every pair with an ordinary paired test inflates the chance of a false positive: four visits make six pairs.
