title: 11 · Predict a value from another variable
text: A correlation (page 10) says how strongly two things go together. Regression says how much the outcome changes for each unit of the predictor, and lets you predict the outcome for a new patient. Which regression depends on the outcome: a measurement on a straight line or a curve, a measurement that isn’t normal, a yes/no outcome, or time until an event. With several predictors at once, see page 12.
crumbs: 11 · Predict a value from another variable

title: 11 · Predict a value from another variable
text:
Simple linear regression
The question: How much longer does the operation take for each extra point of BMI?

When to use it

The outcome is a measurement, and you want to know how much it changes per unit of one predictor, or to predict it.
The relationship is roughly a straight line, and each patient’s outcome is independent of the others’.
The residuals (each patient’s distance from the line) are roughly normal, with a similar spread all along the line. Check them after fitting.
If the relationship curves → nonlinear regression. If the outcome is skewed or has a ceiling → nonparametric regression. If it’s yes/no → logistic regression.



What the test really does
Linear regression draws the straight line that fits the points best, and then asks how sure we can be of its slope.

For any line you could draw, measure each patient’s vertical distance from it: the residual.
Square the residuals and add them up. The least-squares line is the one line for which this sum is as small as possible. Software finds it with a formula, not by trial and error.
The slope of that line says how much the outcome changes, on average, for each extra unit of the predictor. The line always passes through the point where both variables are at their mean.
The test asks whether the slope is further from 0 than chance would explain: t = slope ÷ its standard error, turned into a p-value. The standard error is smaller with more patients, with less scatter around the line, and with a wider spread of the predictor.

Once the model has run, a box under “Read the output” rebuilds the line by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(cohort, aes(bmi, op_time_min)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +   # the least-squares line
  labs(x = "BMI, kg/m²", y = "Operative time, minutes")







range(cohort$bmi)   # lowest and highest BMI in the data

Before trusting the line, plot the residuals against the fitted values: they should form a band of even width around 0, with no curve.

Effect size and 95% CI
The slope with its 95% CI is the effect size: 1.37 minutes per kg/m² (95% CI 1.15 to 1.58). Scale it to a difference that matters clinically: 5 kg/m² of BMI goes with 5 × 1.368 = 6.8 more minutes (95% CI 5 × 1.151 = 5.8 to 5 × 1.585 = 7.9). The slope and both ends of its CI are multiplied by 5, using the unrounded numbers in the output. R² = 0.20 says how much of the variation the line explains.


How to report it

Methods: Operative time was modeled on BMI with simple linear regression.
Results: The slope of operative time on BMI was 1.37 minutes per kg/m² (95% CI 1.15 to 1.58; p < 0.001; R² = 0.20), or 6.8 minutes (95% CI 5.8 to 7.9) per 5 kg/m².







Warning⚠️ Watch out: the line is an average, and only inside your data



The line predicts the average operative time at each BMI. Individual patients scatter around it by about 15 minutes either way (the residual standard error), so it’s a poor tool for scheduling one patient’s case. And BMI here runs from 18.0 to 44.5 (printed under “Look at the data first”): don’t use the line to predict outside that range.

title: 11 · Predict a value from another variable
text:
Nonlinear regression
The question: How quickly does KOOS JR recover after knee replacement, and where does it level off?

When to use it

The outcome follows a curve whose shape you know in advance, and the curve’s numbers mean something: here a starting score, a plateau and a recovery rate.
You supply the formula and rough starting guesses, and the program finds the values that fit best (nonlinear least squares).
If you don’t know the shape → splines or LOWESS. If it’s a straight line → linear regression.

The recovery curve used here:
\[\text{score} = \text{plateau} - (\text{plateau} - \text{start}) \times e^{-\text{days}/\tau}\]

start: the score on the day of surgery.
plateau: the level the score settles at.
τ (tau): the time constant. After τ days patients have made 63% of their eventual gain (1 − e−1 = 0.63), and half of it after τ × ln 2 ≈ 0.69 τ days.



What the test really does
Nonlinear regression fits a curve the way linear regression fits a line: by making the squared distances between the points and the curve as small as possible.

Start from your rough guesses for the curve’s numbers (here plateau, start and τ) and draw that curve.
Measure each score’s vertical distance from the curve, square the distances and add them up.
Change the numbers a little in the direction that makes the sum smaller, and repeat. For a curve there is no formula that gives the answer in one step, which is why the program needs starting guesses.
Stop when no small change makes the sum any smaller: the fit has converged. The numbers at that point are the estimates.

Once the model has run, a box under “Read the output” shows the sum for the starting guesses and for the fitted curve.


Look at the data first

koos <- proms |>
  filter(instrument == "KOOS JR", !is.na(prom_score)) |>
  mutate(days = pmax(visit_days, 0))   # pre-op visits have negative days (before surgery); count them as day 0

tau = 80.9: the time constant in days.
Std. Error: each estimate’s uncertainty. The t values and p-values test whether each number is zero, which nobody doubts here; ignore them.
Residual standard error 12.33 on 1143 degrees of freedom (R only): individual scores scatter about 12 points around the curve.







Note🔍 Under the hood: the sum the program makes as small as it can






RPython



squared_distance <- function(plateau, start, tau) {    # step 2: the sum of squared distances between the scores and a curve
  sum((koos$prom_score - (plateau - (plateau - start) * exp(-koos$days / tau)))^2)
}
fit <- coef(recovery)
squared_distance(85, 50, 100)                                              # step 1: the curve drawn from the starting guesses

[1] 176095.1

squared_distance(fit[["plateau"]], fit[["start"]], fit[["tau"]])           # step 4: the curve the program settled on

[1] 173841.5

squared_distance(fit[["plateau"]], fit[["start"]], 60)                     # the same curve with tau moved to 60 days: worse again

[1] 181008.6

sqrt(squared_distance(fit[["plateau"]], fit[["start"]], fit[["tau"]]) / (1146 - 3))   # residual standard error: 1146 scores, 3 estimated numbers

[1] 12.33257





def squared_distance(plateau, start, tau):             # step 2: the sum of squared distances between the scores and a curve
    return ((koos["prom_score"] - recovery_curve(koos["days"], plateau, start, tau)) ** 2).sum()

print(squared_distance(85, 50, 100))                               # step 1: the curve drawn from the starting guesses

176095.08873316215

print(squared_distance(*estimates))                                # step 4: the curve the program settled on

173841.4891850255

print(squared_distance(estimates[0], estimates[1], 60))            # the same curve with tau moved to 60 days: worse again

181008.5562390127

print(np.sqrt(squared_distance(*estimates) / (1146 - 3)))          # residual standard error: 1146 scores, 3 estimated numbers

12.332570352544508





The starting guesses give a sum of 176095. The fitted curve brings it down to 173841, and no other values of the three numbers give a smaller sum: moving τ from 80.9 to 60 days, for example, raises it to 181009. Dividing the smallest sum by 1146 − 3 and taking the square root gives the residual standard error, 12.33 points.





Effect size and 95% CI
The curve’s numbers, with their 95% CIs, are the effect sizes. Half of the eventual gain comes after τ × ln 2 days.

RPython



confint(recovery)                       # profile CIs; see the R vs Python box

            2.5%    97.5%
plateau 82.60453 85.86557
start   48.50027 51.15240
tau     70.98023 92.53621

log(2) * coef(recovery)[["tau"]]        # days to half of the eventual gain

[1] 56.0507

log(2) * confint(recovery)["tau", ]

    2.5%    97.5% 
49.19974 64.14121 





t_crit = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=len(koos) - 3)   # 3 parameters
print(pd.DataFrame({"low": estimates - t_crit * standard_errors, "high": estimates + t_crit * standard_errors},
                   index=["plateau", "start", "tau"]))

               low       high
plateau  82.561762  85.850467
start    48.495962  51.159541
tau      69.941098  91.787025

print(np.log(2) * estimates[2])                  # days to half of the eventual gain

56.05069619705848

print(np.log(2) * (estimates[2] - t_crit * standard_errors[2]), np.log(2) * (estimates[2] + t_crit * standard_errors[2]))   # its 95% CI

48.479474903009695 63.62191749110726





KOOS JR rose from about 49.8 points (95% CI 48.5 to 51.2) on the day of surgery toward a plateau of 84.2 (95% CI 82.6 to 85.9). Half of the gain came by about 56 days, 8 weeks (95% CI 49 to 64 days). Python’s CI for the half-gain time, computed differently, is 48 to 64 days: see the R vs Python box.


How to report it

Methods: KOOS JR was modeled against days since surgery with an exponential recovery curve fitted by nonlinear least squares, counting the pre-op score as the score on the day of surgery.
Results: In 330 knees (1146 scores), the fitted curve gave an estimated KOOS JR of 49.8 points (95% CI 48.5 to 51.2) at surgery and a plateau of 84.2 points (95% CI 82.6 to 85.9); half of the change was reached at about 56 days (95% CI 49 to 64).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: each knee appears up to four times



Each knee has up to four scores (pre-op, 6 weeks, 3 months and 1 year). Nonlinear least squares treats the 1146 scores as 1146 independent patients, but they come from 330 knees, and scores from the same knee are related. So these CIs can’t be trusted: depending on the number, they may be too narrow or too wide. A mixed model (page 16) accounts for this. And if the fit fails to converge, try starting guesses closer to what the plot shows.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: two kinds of CI




R’s nls() and scipy’s curve_fit() use different fitting algorithms but find the same estimates and standard errors.
R’s confint() profiles the fit: it moves each number away from its estimate until the fit gets significantly worse. scipy gives only the standard errors, so the Python code uses estimate ± t × standard error. The two CIs differ slightly; here τ’s CI runs from 71.0 to 92.5 days in R and 69.9 to 91.8 in Python, so the CI for the half-gain time is 49 to 64 days in R and 48 to 64 in Python. Either is fine; say which you used.

text:
Nonparametric regression
The question: How does KOOS JR at 1 year depend on KOOS JR before surgery, when many patients reach the ceiling of 100?

When to use it

The outcome is a measurement that isn’t normal: it has a ceiling, a skew or outliers, so the residuals of a straight line won’t be normal.
LOWESS (locally weighted smoothing) draws the shape without a formula: it fits many small lines, each to the points near it, and joins them into a smooth curve. It gives a picture, not a p-value.
The Theil-Sen slope is the median of the slopes between every pair of patients. A few extreme patients barely move it, and its CI comes from ranks, not from normal residuals.
If the residuals are roughly normal → linear regression.



What the test really does
This section uses two tools, and neither assumes normal residuals.

LOWESS takes one patient at a time and fits a straight line to the patients whose pre-op score is nearest (here the nearest two-thirds), giving the closest ones the most weight. It keeps only that line’s height at the patient’s own pre-op score.
Joining these heights gives a smooth curve that follows the data wherever they go. LOWESS gives a picture, with no slope and no p-value.
The Theil-Sen slope takes every pair of patients and works out the slope of the line through the two of them. The 246 knees here make 30135 pairs.
It then takes the median of all these slopes. A few unusual patients change only a few of the pairwise slopes, so they barely move the median.

The R code under “Run it” does steps 3 and 4 by hand.


Look at the data first

RPython



library(tidyverse)

proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

koos_wide <- proms |>
  filter(instrument == "KOOS JR", visit %in% c("preop", "1yr")) |>
  select(case_id, visit, prom_score) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit, values_from = prom_score) |>   # one row per knee
  rename(one_year = `1yr`) |>
  filter(!is.na(preop), !is.na(one_year))

smooth <- lowess(koos_wide$preop, koos_wide$one_year)   # LOWESS curve, R's defaults

ggplot(koos_wide, aes(preop, one_year)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = tibble(preop = smooth$x, one_year = smooth$y), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "KOOS JR before surgery", y = "KOOS JR at 1 year")







nrow(koos_wide)

[1] 246

sum(koos_wide$one_year == 100)   # at the ceiling

[1] 37

smooth$y[c(1, length(smooth$y))]   # the curve's height at the lowest and highest pre-op score

[1] 70.09071 98.55335





import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.nonparametric.smoothers_lowess import lowess

proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")

koos_wide = (proms[(proms["instrument"] == "KOOS JR") & proms["visit"].isin(["preop", "1yr"])]
             .pivot(index="case_id", columns="visit", values="prom_score")   # one row per knee
             .dropna(subset=["preop", "1yr"]))

smooth = lowess(koos_wide["1yr"], koos_wide["preop"], frac=2/3, it=3,
                delta=0.01 * np.ptp(koos_wide["preop"]))   # R's lowess() defaults

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.scatter(koos_wide["preop"], koos_wide["1yr"], alpha=0.4)
ax.plot(smooth[:, 0], smooth[:, 1], linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel("KOOS JR before surgery")
ax.set_ylabel("KOOS JR at 1 year")
plt.show()







print(len(koos_wide), (koos_wide["1yr"] == 100).sum())   # knees, at the ceiling

246 37

print(smooth[[0, -1], 1])   # the curve's height at the lowest and highest pre-op score

[70.09071294 98.55334783]





246 knees have both scores, and 37 of them (37 ÷ 246 = 15.0%) score the maximum of 100 at 1 year. The LOWESS curve rises steadily from about 70 to about 99 across the range of pre-op scores (the last line of output: 70.1 and 98.6).


Run it

RPython



x <- koos_wide$preop
y <- koos_wide$one_year
n <- length(x)

pairs <- combn(n, 2)                                  # every pair of knees
dx <- x[pairs[2, ]] - x[pairs[1, ]]
dy <- y[pairs[2, ]] - y[pairs[1, ]]
slopes <- sort(dy[dx != 0] / dx[dx != 0])             # pairs with the same pre-op score have no slope
ts_slope <- median(slopes)
ts_intercept <- median(y - ts_slope * x)

# Sen's 95% CI: step in from both ends of the sorted slopes by an amount set by the
# variance of Kendall's S, corrected for tied scores (the same method as scipy)
tie_term <- function(v) { counts <- table(v); sum(counts * (counts - 1) * (2 * counts + 5)) }
var_s <- (n * (n - 1) * (2 * n + 5) - tie_term(x) - tie_term(y)) / 18
step <- qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(var_s)
m <- length(slopes)
ts_ci <- c(slopes[max(round((m - step) / 2), 1)], slopes[min(round((m + step) / 2) + 1, m)])

c(intercept = ts_intercept, slope = ts_slope, low = ts_ci[1], high = ts_ci[2])

 intercept      slope        low       high 
65.3917949  0.3948718  0.2741117  0.5186441 





koos_slope = stats.theilslopes(koos_wide["1yr"], koos_wide["preop"], method="joint")   # see the R vs Python box
print(koos_slope)

TheilslopesResult(slope=np.float64(0.394871794871795), intercept=np.float64(65.39179487179487), low_slope=np.float64(0.2741116751269039), high_slope=np.float64(0.5186440677966101))







Read the output

slope = 0.39: each extra point before surgery goes with 0.39 more points at 1 year (the median of all the pairwise slopes).
intercept = 65.4: the predicted 1-year score for a pre-op score of 0; it anchors the line.
low, high (R) or low_slope, high_slope (Python): the 95% CI for the slope, 0.27 to 0.52.



Effect size and 95% CI
The Theil-Sen slope with its CI is the effect size: 0.39 points at 1 year per pre-op point (95% CI 0.27 to 0.52). An ordinary least-squares line gives 0.43 (the code below fits it); the two would differ more if a few unusual patients pulled the least-squares line.

RPython



coef(lm(one_year ~ preop, data = koos_wide))   # the least-squares line, for comparison: its slope is the number under preop

(Intercept)       preop 
 62.7022110   0.4280834 





print(stats.linregress(koos_wide["preop"], koos_wide["1yr"]).slope)   # the least-squares slope, for comparison

0.42808344542661636







How to report it

Methods: Because 1-year KOOS JR clustered at the ceiling, its relationship with pre-op KOOS JR was described with a LOWESS smoother and summarized with the Theil-Sen slope.
Results: Among 246 knees, 37 (15.0%) scored 100 at 1 year. The Theil-Sen slope of the 1-year KOOS JR on the pre-op KOOS JR was 0.39 points per point (95% CI 0.27 to 0.52).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: robust isn’t ceiling-proof



Theil-Sen resists outliers, but nothing can see above a ceiling: the 37 knees at 100 might have scored higher on a longer scale, so the true slope at the top of the range is unknown. And a LOWESS curve is least reliable at its two ends, where it rests on few patients.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: Theil-Sen in R, and LOWESS settings




Theil-Sen in R: some R packages get the CI wrong when scores are tied, as PROM scores always are (deming 1.4-1 misapplies its tie correction; mblm’s CI is far too narrow). So the R code computes the slope and Sen’s CI directly, the same way scipy does, and the two agree exactly.
Intercept: scipy’s default (method="separate") computes it as median(y) − slope × median(x). The R code computes median(y − slope × x), which scipy calls method="joint". The slope is the same either way.
LOWESS: R’s lowess() and statsmodels’ lowess() run the same algorithm, but statsmodels’ defaults differ (it sets delta to 0), so the Python code spells out R’s settings. ggplot2’s geom_smooth() uses a different smoother, loess(), which draws a similar but not identical curve.

text:
Simple logistic regression
The question: Does the risk of death within 30 days rise with the time to surgery?

When to use it

The outcome is yes/no (died or not), and you want the odds ratio per unit of one predictor.
It assumes the log odds change in a straight line with the predictor: each extra day of delay multiplies the odds by the same amount.
You need enough patients with the outcome: a common rule of thumb is at least 10 per predictor.
If the outcome is time until an event → Cox regression.



What the test really does
Logistic regression draws a straight line too, but on a scale where a yes/no outcome can follow one: the log odds.

A risk can’t follow a straight line for long, because it has to stay between 0% and 100%. So the model works with the odds (the risk divided by 1 minus the risk) and then with their logarithm, the log odds, which can take any value.
The model assumes the log odds change in a straight line with the predictor: log odds = intercept + coefficient × predictor.
It tries out values for the intercept and the coefficient, and keeps the pair under which the outcomes that really happened (who died and who survived), taken together, were most likely. This is called maximum likelihood.
Adding the coefficient to the log odds is the same as multiplying the odds by e raised to the coefficient. That number is the odds ratio per unit of the predictor.

Once the model has run, a box under “Read the output” turns the two coefficients into predicted risks by hand.


Look at the data first
The model uses time to surgery as a number, in units of 24 hours, so the odds ratio is per day of delay. The bands are only for the picture.

RPython



library(tidyverse)

hip_fracture <- read_csv("data/hip_fracture.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(hours_24 = hours_to_surgery / 24)   # time in days, so the odds ratio is per 24 hours

by_delay <- hip_fracture |>
  mutate(delay_band = cut(hours_to_surgery, breaks = c(-Inf, 24, 48, 72, Inf),
                          labels = c("up to 24 h", "24 to 48 h", "48 to 72 h", "over 72 h"))) |>
  group_by(delay_band) |>
  summarise(n = n(), deaths = sum(death_30d), percent = 100 * mean(death_30d))
by_delay

1 up to 24 h   574     29    5.05
2 24 to 48 h   460     29    6.30

4 over 72 h     44      8   18.2 

c(deaths = sum(hip_fracture$death_30d), patients = nrow(hip_fracture), percent = 100 * mean(hip_fracture$death_30d))   # all patients

     deaths    patients     percent 
  74.000000 1200.000000    6.166667 

ggplot(by_delay, aes(delay_band, percent)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Time from admission to surgery", y = "Deaths within 30 days, %")











import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

hip_fracture = pd.read_csv("data/hip_fracture.csv")

bands = pd.cut(hip_fracture["hours_to_surgery"], bins=[-np.inf, 24, 48, 72, np.inf],
               labels=["up to 24 h", "24 to 48 h", "48 to 72 h", "over 72 h"])

Run it

Read the output

hours_24 = 0.41: the change in the log odds of death within 30 days per 24 hours of delay. Log odds are hard to read, so turn the coefficient into an odds ratio (next step).
Std. Error 0.11, z = 3.78, p < 0.001: the test of whether time to surgery matters at all.
Intercept = −3.29: the log odds at surgery on admission (0 hours), which only anchors the line.
Null and residual deviance (R): the misfit of the model without and with time to surgery. Their difference, 555.67 − 543.20 = 12.47 on 1 degree of freedom, is the likelihood ratio test of the model. Python prints its p-value as LLR p-value (0.0004). With one predictor it says the same as the z test above.

RPython

odds = np.exp(log_odds)                                                # undo the logarithm

For surgery on the day of admission the model predicts a risk of 3.6%; after 1 day 5.3%, after 2 days 7.8% and after 4 days 16.0%. The log odds rise by the same 0.41 with each day, so the odds are multiplied by the same 1.50 each time. The risk itself doesn’t rise by a fixed amount, which is why the result is reported as an odds ratio.





Effect size and 95% CI
The odds ratio is e raised to the coefficient.

RPython



exp(cbind(odds_ratio = coef(delay_model), confint(delay_model)))   # profile CIs; see the R vs Python box

            odds_ratio     2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept) 0.03731891 0.0246604 0.05528913
hours_24    1.50372521 1.2097970 1.85443149

odds_ratios.columns = ["odds_ratio", "low", "high"]
print(odds_ratios)

           odds_ratio       low      high
Intercept    0.037319  0.024959  0.055798
hours_24     1.503725  1.217208  1.857686





Each 24 hours of delay multiplied the odds of death within 30 days by 1.50 (95% CI 1.21 to 1.85).


How to report it

Methods: The association between time from admission to surgery and death within 30 days was estimated with logistic regression, with time in 24-hour units.
Results: Within 30 days, 74 of 1,200 patients died (6.2%). The odds ratio for death per 24 hours of delay to surgery was 1.50 (95% CI 1.21 to 1.85; p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: a straight line on the log-odds scale is an assumption



The model says each 24 hours multiplies the odds by the same 1.50. That’s an assumption, and the bands above can’t test it by eye. The last band is open-ended: its patients waited 97 hours on average, so a straight line already predicts its higher rate (17.2% from the model, 18.2% observed; the code below computes all three numbers). To test the shape, let the effect bend and compare the two fits, as exercise 3 on page 12 does with splines. An odds ratio isn’t a risk ratio: the two are close only when the outcome is rare, as it is here (6.2%). And it isn’t proof of cause: patients too unwell to operate on may wait longer, and they’d die more often whenever they were operated on.

RPython



over_72 <- hip_fracture$hours_to_surgery > 72       # the open-ended last band
mean(hip_fracture$hours_to_surgery[over_72])        # its mean wait, in hours

[1] 97.26818

100 * mean(fitted(delay_model)[over_72])            # the death rate the model predicts for these patients, %

[1] 17.19794

100 * mean(hip_fracture$death_30d[over_72])         # the death rate observed, %

[1] 18.18182





over_72 = hip_fracture["hours_to_surgery"] > 72     # the open-ended last band
print(hip_fracture.loc[over_72, "hours_to_surgery"].mean())      # its mean wait, in hours

97.26818181818182

print(100 * delay_model.predict(hip_fracture[over_72]).mean())   # the death rate the model predicts for these patients, %

17.19793824332725

print(100 * hip_fracture.loc[over_72, "death_30d"].mean())       # the death rate observed, %

18.181818181818183













Tip🔀 R vs Python: profile and Wald CIs



R’s confint() on a glm() profiles the likelihood, which is more accurate in small samples. statsmodels’ conf_int() uses the simpler Wald method (estimate ± 1.96 standard errors), which gives 1.22 to 1.86 here; R’s confint.default() does the same. Say which you used.

title: 11 · Predict a value from another variable
text:
Cox regression
The question: Does the hazard of ACL graft failure rise with posterior tibial slope?

When to use it

The outcome is time until an event (graft failure), and the predictor is a measurement (tibial slope).
Cox regression gives a hazard ratio per unit of the predictor. Choose a unit that means something: here, per degree.
It assumes the hazard ratio stays the same over time (proportional hazards) and that the log hazard changes in a straight line with slope. Page 14 shows how to check both and covers Cox regression in full.
Deaths are censored in any Cox model of another event. That hardly matters in young ACL patients, who rarely die during follow-up. In older patients it does: the hazard ratio then describes the rate among patients still alive, and a patient’s actual chance of the event needs the cumulative incidence or a Fine-Gray model.



What the test really does
The Cox model works as on page 8, with a measurement in place of groups.

Start at surgery and move forward in time. Each time a graft fails, look at who was still being followed just before it: the patients at risk.
The model assumes each extra degree of slope multiplies the hazard by the same factor, the hazard ratio. A patient whose slope is 2° steeper has the hazard multiplied by that factor twice.
It tries out values for the hazard ratio and keeps the one under which the failures that really happened, taken together, were most likely: at each failure, was it one of the steeper slopes among the patients at risk?
The test asks whether that hazard ratio is further from 1 than chance would explain, and gives a p-value.

A patient who leaves the study early is censored: they count among the patients at risk for as long as they were followed, and not after.


Look at the data first
Splitting slope in two is only for the picture; the model uses slope as a number.

RPython



library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)

acl <- read_csv("data/acl_cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(slope_group = if_else(tibial_slope_deg >= 12, "12° or more", "under 12°"))   # for the plot only

survfit2(Surv(followup_years, graft_failure) ~ slope_group, data = acl, conf.type = "log-log") |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_risktable() +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Years since reconstruction", y = "Graft survival")











import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from lifelines import KaplanMeierFitter, CoxPHFitter
from lifelines.plotting import add_at_risk_counts

acl = pd.read_csv("data/acl_cohort.csv")
acl["slope_group"] = acl["tibial_slope_deg"].map(lambda slope: "12° or more" if slope >= 12 else "under 12°")   # for the plot only

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
curves = []
for group_name, group in acl.groupby("slope_group"):
    km = KaplanMeierFitter(label=group_name).fit(group["followup_years"], group["graft_failure"])
    km.plot_survival_function(ax=ax, ci_show=False)
    curves.append(km)
ax.set_xlabel("Years since reconstruction")
ax.set_ylabel("Graft survival")
add_at_risk_counts(*curves, ax=ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()











11 of the 73 reconstructions with a slope of 12° or more failed, and 20 of the 277 with a smaller slope. The table under the plot gives these counts: the numbers at risk at year 0 (73 and 277) and the events by the end of follow-up (11 and 20).


Run it

summary(slope_cox)

Read the output

exp(coef) = 1.27: the hazard ratio per degree of tibial slope: the hazard of graft failure is 1.27 times higher for a slope 1° steeper.
lower .95 / upper .95 = 1.09 to 1.48: the 95% CI, which excludes 1 (no difference). R prints 1.095 and 1.485, which are 1.0946 and 1.4847 already rounded (Python shows more digits), so don’t round them a second time.
Pr(>|z|) = 0.002: the p-value for slope.
Likelihood ratio test = 10.1 on 1 df, p = 0.002: the overall test; with one predictor it says the same as the p-value for slope. R prints it as 10.08 on 1 df, p=0.002; Python prints the statistic, its degrees of freedom and the p-value on the line under its table. R’s first line, n= 350, number of events= 31, gives the reconstructions and the failures; Python prints them last.
Concordance = 0.67 (R only): how often the model ranks two patients’ graft failure times correctly. 0.5 is a coin toss, so slope alone is better than a coin toss, but far from a prediction for one patient. R prints 0.665 (0.6654 before rounding).



Effect size and 95% CI
The hazard ratio per degree, 1.27 (95% CI 1.09 to 1.48), is the effect size. Hazard ratios multiply: a slope 5° steeper carries 3.37 times the hazard (95% CI 1.57 to 7.21), computed from the unrounded hazard ratio raised to the power 5: 1.27485 = 3.37. The code below does the same for the CI.

RPython



exp(5 * coef(slope_cox))      # the hazard ratio for 5° more slope: the per-degree ratio to the power 5

tibial_slope_deg 
        3.366859 

exp(5 * confint(slope_cox))   # its 95% CI

                    2.5 %   97.5 %
tibial_slope_deg 1.571142 7.214967





print(slope_cox.summary[["exp(coef)", "exp(coef) lower 95%", "exp(coef) upper 95%"]] ** 5)   # the hazard ratio for 5° more slope, with its 95% CI: each number to the power 5

                  exp(coef)  exp(coef) lower 95%  exp(coef) upper 95%
covariate                                                            
tibial_slope_deg   3.366855              1.57114             7.214958







How to report it

Methods: The association between posterior tibial slope and ACL graft failure was estimated with Cox proportional hazards regression, with slope in degrees.
Results: The hazard ratio for graft failure per degree of posterior tibial slope was 1.27 (95% CI 1.09 to 1.48; p = 0.002), with 31 failures in 350 reconstructions.







Warning⚠️ Watch out: a hazard ratio isn’t a treatment effect



Slope wasn’t assigned: patients with a steep slope may differ in other ways. A hazard ratio of 1.27 per degree doesn’t show that an osteotomy reducing the slope by 1° would lower the hazard by that much. Only a study of the osteotomy itself can show that. At about 10 failures per term, the 31 failures here allow about three terms (page 14).








Tip🔀 R vs Python: lifelines stops early



lifelines stops iterating slightly early by default, so the Python code tightens it with fit_options={"precision": 1e-9}. Here that changes nothing visible; on page 12 it does.

title: 13 · Kaplan-Meier & the log-rank test
text:
“How long do the implants last?” is the central question of arthroplasty research, and it needs its own methods. Patients join the study over several years and are followed for different lengths of time, and most of them are never revised. Survival analysis uses every patient’s follow-up for as long as it lasts.
Pages 4, 6 and 8 each showed one survival method in a few steps. This page covers the whole method: - what censoring is - how to set up the data - how to read and report a Kaplan-Meier curve - how long the patients were followed - how to compare groups - what to do when patients die before they can be revised
Page 14 covers Cox regression.

title: 13 · Kaplan-Meier & the log-rank test
text:
What censoring means
Picture six patients, each followed from surgery until either a revision or the end of their follow-up:



Patient
Years followed
Revised?




A
1
yes


B
2
no: the study closed


C
3
yes


D
4
no: moved away


E
5
yes


F
6
no: the study closed



Patients B, D and F are censored. We know they went at least that long without a revision, but not what happened afterwards. Censoring isn’t missing data: it’s partial information, and survival methods use all of it.
Two simple summaries both get this wrong: - “3 of 6 (50%) were revised” ignores time. Patient B was followed for only 2 years, so B’s implant never had the chance to fail at 4 or 5 years. - Dropping the censored patients (“3 of 3 were revised”) throws away the years B, D and F spent without a revision.
The Kaplan-Meier method gets it right. It moves through time and recalculates at each revision, using only the patients still being followed (at risk) at that moment:

RPython



library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)

toy <- tibble(
  patient = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"),
  years   = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
  revised = c(1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0)        # 1 = revised, 0 = censored
)

toy_km <- survfit(Surv(years, revised) ~ 1, data = toy)
summary(toy_km)

Call: survfit(formula = Surv(years, revised) ~ 1, data = toy)

 time n.risk n.event survival std.err lower 95% CI upper 95% CI
    1      6       1    0.833   0.152       0.5827            1
    3      4       1    0.625   0.213       0.3200            1
    5      2       1    0.312   0.245       0.0671            1





import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from lifelines import KaplanMeierFitter

toy = pd.DataFrame({
    "patient": ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"],
    "years":   [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
    "revised": [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0],     # 1 = revised, 0 = censored
})

toy_km = KaplanMeierFitter().fit(toy["years"], event_observed=toy["revised"])
print(toy_km.event_table[["at_risk", "observed", "censored"]])   # observed = revisions

          at_risk  observed  censored
event_at                             
0.0             6         0         0
1.0             6         1         0
2.0             5         0         1
3.0             4         1         0
4.0             3         0         1
5.0             2         1         0
6.0             1         0         1

print(toy_km.survival_function_)

          KM_estimate
timeline             
0.0          1.000000
1.0          0.833333
2.0          0.833333
3.0          0.625000
4.0          0.625000
5.0          0.312500
6.0          0.312500





R’s table has a row only for the times when a revision happens. Python’s has a row for every time, with the patients at risk just before it.
Reading the output, one revision at a time: - Year 1: 6 patients at risk, 1 revised. Survival = 5/6 = 0.833. - Year 2: B is censored. Nothing happens to the curve, but the at-risk group shrinks from 5 to 4 before the next revision. - Year 3: 4 at risk, 1 revised. Survival = 0.833 × 3/4 = 0.625. - Year 5: 2 at risk (D was censored at year 4), 1 revised. Survival = 0.625 × 1/2 = 0.3125.
So the estimated chance of a revision by 5 years is 1 − 0.3125 = 69%, not 50%. Each censored patient counts fully while they’re followed and then leaves the at-risk group. The CIs R prints are very wide (the upper limit is 1 in every row) because there are only six patients.






Note🔍 Under the hood: the product-limit formula





At each time \(t_i\) when at least one revision happens, with \(n_i\) patients at risk and \(d_i\) revisions, the chance of getting past \(t_i\) unrevised is \(1 - d_i/n_i\). Kaplan-Meier survival at time \(t\) multiplies these together for every revision time up to \(t\):
\[\hat S(t) = \prod_{t_i \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\right)\]
This is why the method is also called the product-limit estimator. Censored patients appear only in the \(n_i\) of the revision times before they leave.









Warning⚠️ Watch out: censoring must be unrelated to the outcome



Kaplan-Meier assumes a censored patient has the same future risk as the patients still being followed. That’s reasonable when follow-up ends because the study closed. It isn’t when patients stop coming back because their hip hurts, or stay away because it’s perfect. If many patients are lost to follow-up, say how many and why.

title: 13 · Kaplan-Meier & the log-rank test
text:
Time zero and the event
Every survival analysis needs two definitions, fixed before you look at the results:

Time zero, when the clock starts. For implant survival it’s the date of surgery: every patient starts at the same clinical moment. Starting at the first clinic visit instead would ignore revisions that happened before that visit.
The event, what stops the clock. Here it’s revision for any reason: any reoperation that removes or exchanges a component. Other studies use aseptic revision, or any reoperation. Choose one in advance and define it in the Methods.

Real data rarely arrive as “years followed” and “revised: yes/no”. You build those columns from dates. The practice cohort already has them: followup_years and event_status, where 0 means censored, 1 means revised and 2 means died without a revision. Here’s how to make them from a table of dates, for four made-up patients:

RPython



dates <- tibble(
  patient       = c("P1", "P2", "P3", "P4"),
  surgery_date  = as.Date(c("2016-03-14", "2018-11-05", "2020-06-30", "2017-01-09")),
  revision_date = as.Date(c("2019-07-02", NA, NA, "2017-04-18")),
  death_date    = as.Date(c("2023-02-11", "2022-01-20", NA, NA)),
  last_seen     = as.Date(c("2022-10-03", "2021-12-02", "2025-11-17", "2024-08-15"))
)

follow_up <- dates |>
  mutate(
    # the first event wins: a revision, else a death, else censored at the last visit
    event_status = case_when(!is.na(revision_date) ~ 1,
                             !is.na(death_date)    ~ 2,
                             .default = 0),
    end_date = case_when(event_status == 1 ~ revision_date,
                         event_status == 2 ~ death_date,
                         .default = last_seen),
    followup_years = as.numeric(end_date - surgery_date) / 365.25
  )

follow_up |> select(patient, event_status, end_date, followup_years)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  patient event_status end_date   followup_years
  <chr>          <dbl> <date>              <dbl>
1 P1                 1 2019-07-02          3.30 
2 P2                 2 2022-01-20          3.21 
3 P3                 0 2025-11-17          5.38 
4 P4                 1 2017-04-18          0.271





dates = pd.DataFrame({
    "patient":       ["P1", "P2", "P3", "P4"],
    "surgery_date":  ["2016-03-14", "2018-11-05", "2020-06-30", "2017-01-09"],
    "revision_date": ["2019-07-02", None, None, "2017-04-18"],
    "death_date":    ["2023-02-11", "2022-01-20", None, None],
    "last_seen":     ["2022-10-03", "2021-12-02", "2025-11-17", "2024-08-15"],
})
for column in ["surgery_date", "revision_date", "death_date", "last_seen"]:
    dates[column] = pd.to_datetime(dates[column])

# the first event wins: a revision, else a death, else censored at the last visit
dates["event_status"] = np.select([dates["revision_date"].notna(), dates["death_date"].notna()],
                                  [1, 2], default=0)
dates["end_date"] = dates["revision_date"].fillna(dates["death_date"]).fillna(dates["last_seen"])
dates["followup_years"] = (dates["end_date"] - dates["surgery_date"]).dt.days / 365.25

print(dates[["patient", "event_status", "end_date", "followup_years"]])

  patient  event_status   end_date  followup_years
0      P1             1 2019-07-02        3.299110
1      P2             2 2022-01-20        3.208761
2      P3             0 2025-11-17        5.382615
3      P4             1 2017-04-18        0.271047






P1 was revised in 2019 and died in 2023. The revision came first, so P1’s follow-up ends at the revision, 3.30 years after surgery.
P2 died 3.21 years after surgery without a revision. Death ends the follow-up: P2 can never be revised. (The section on competing risks explains why that matters.)
P3 was alive and unrevised at the last visit: censored at 5.38 years.
P4 was revised at 0.27 years: 0.271 × 365.25 = 99 days after surgery.







Warning⚠️ Watch out: follow-up ends at the last visit, not today



Don’t set every unrevised patient’s end date to the date you pulled the data. A patient last seen in 2021 might have been revised elsewhere since. Censor at the last date you know the implant was in place. And check that no event date comes before the surgery date: it’s always a data-entry error.

title: 13 · Kaplan-Meier & the log-rank test
text:
The Kaplan-Meier curve
Now the practice cohort: 600 procedures, each followed from surgery to revision, death or the last visit.

RPython



cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

km <- survfit2(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ 1, data = cohort,
               conf.type = "log-log")              # the CI method lifelines uses

km |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_censor_mark(size = 1, alpha = 0.4) +         # a tick for each censored patient
  add_risktable(times = c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10)) +
  scale_ggsurvfit(x_scales = list(breaks = c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10))) +
  labs(x = "Years since surgery", y = "Revision-free survival")











from lifelines.plotting import add_at_risk_counts

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")

km = KaplanMeierFitter(label="All procedures").fit(cohort["followup_years"], event_observed=cohort["revised"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
km.plot_survival_function(ax=ax, show_censors=True,                # a tick for each censored patient
                          censor_styles={"ms": 3, "alpha": 0.4}, legend=False)
ax.set_xlabel("Years since surgery")
ax.set_ylabel("Revision-free survival")
add_at_risk_counts(km, ax=ax, xticks=[0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10], rows_to_show=["At risk", "Events"])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()











How to read it: - The steps: the curve starts at 100% and drops at each revision. The drops get bigger later on, because each revision is then a bigger share of the fewer patients still at risk. - The ticks mark censored patients. They don’t move the curve; they leave the at-risk group. - The shaded band is the 95% CI. It widens as patients leave. - The table below the plot gives the number of procedures still being followed (at risk) at each time, 600 at surgery, 332 at 4 years and 84 at 8 years in R (lifelines shows 331 and 83; the R vs Python box below explains why), and the revisions so far. Always publish the numbers at risk with the curve: they tell the reader how much to trust each part of it.






Warning⚠️ Watch out: the tail of the curve



By 10 years only 21 procedures are still followed, so each late revision moves the curve a lot. Don’t draw conclusions from the far right-hand end. A common rule of thumb is to stop drawing the curve once fewer than about 10% of procedures (here, 60) remain at risk.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: the confidence band



R’s survfit() uses a “log” CI by default; lifelines uses “log-log”. We set conf.type = "log-log" in R so the two match, as on page 4. The numbers at risk can differ by one or two: R counts the patients followed for at least 4 years, lifelines those followed for more than 4 years, so a patient censored at exactly 4.00 years is in R’s count only. Here that is one case at 4 years and one at 8 years. lifelines’ add_at_risk_counts() also adds a row of censored patients unless you choose rows with rows_to_show.

title: 13 · Kaplan-Meier & the log-rank test
text:
Survivorship at 2, 5 and 10 years
Papers report the curve at fixed times: the survivorship, the percentage of implants still unrevised.

summary(km, times = c(2, 5, 10))

Call: survfit(formula = Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ 1, data = cohort, 
    conf.type = "log-log")

   10     21      15    0.780 0.02579        0.725        0.826





for years in [2, 5, 10]:
    estimate = km.survival_function_at_times(years).iloc[0]
    ci = km.confidence_interval_survival_function_.loc[:years].iloc[-1]   # last step at or before that time
    at_risk = (cohort["followup_years"] >= years).sum()

5 0.863 [0.828, 0.892] 263
10 0.78 [0.725, 0.826] 21






survival: 0.939 at 2 years, 0.863 at 5 years and 0.780 at 10 years.
lower 95% CI / upper 95% CI: the CI around each one. The 10-year CI (0.725 to 0.826) is the widest.
n.risk: 496 procedures still followed at 2 years, 263 at 5 years and only 21 at 10 years.

Python prints the same numbers in one row per time: years, survival, [lower, upper] and the number at risk. It has no n.event.


Methods: Implant survivorship was estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method, with revision for any reason as the end point and the date of surgery as time zero. Patients were censored at death or at their last follow-up. Confidence intervals used the log-log transformation.
Results: Survivorship free of revision was 93.9% (95% CI 91.6% to 95.6%) at 2 years, 86.3% (95% CI 82.8% to 89.2%) at 5 years and 78.0% (95% CI 72.5% to 82.6%) at 10 years, when 21 procedures remained at risk.







Warning⚠️ Watch out: “86% survival” needs its time point, CI and numbers at risk



A survivorship figure means nothing without the time it refers to. Give the 95% CI, and the number still at risk at the time you quote, so readers can see how much data the estimate rests on.

title: 13 · Kaplan-Meier & the log-rank test
text:
How long were patients followed?
Every survival paper reports the median follow-up. The obvious way to calculate it is wrong:

RPython



median(cohort$followup_years)        # misleading: revisions and deaths cut follow-up short

[1] 4.365

# reverse Kaplan-Meier: treat "still followed at the end" as the event
reverse_km <- survfit(Surv(followup_years, event_status == 0) ~ 1, data = cohort)
quantile(reverse_km, probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), conf.int = FALSE)

  25   50   75 
3.52 5.62 7.93 





from lifelines.utils import qth_survival_times

print(cohort["followup_years"].median())   # misleading: revisions and deaths cut follow-up short

4.365

# reverse Kaplan-Meier: treat "still followed at the end" as the event
reverse_km = KaplanMeierFitter().fit(cohort["followup_years"],
                                     event_observed=(cohort["event_status"] == 0))
print(qth_survival_times([0.75, 0.5, 0.25], reverse_km.survival_function_))   # 25th, 50th, 75th percentiles

      KM_estimate
0.75         3.52
0.50         5.62
0.25         7.93





The plain median, 4.4 years, mixes two things: how long the study watched patients, and how soon they were revised or died. A patient revised at 1 year wasn’t “followed for 1 year” in the sense readers care about. The study would have kept watching them.
The reverse Kaplan-Meier method answers the real question: how long would patients have been followed if nothing had happened to them? It swaps the roles: being censored at the end of follow-up becomes the “event”, and revisions and deaths become the censored observations. The median follow-up is 5.62 years (IQR 3.52 to 7.93).

Methods: Median follow-up was estimated with the reverse Kaplan-Meier method.
Results: The median follow-up was 5.62 years (IQR 3.52 to 7.93).

title: 13 · Kaplan-Meier & the log-rank test
text:
Comparing groups: the log-rank test
The log-rank test asks whether two or more survival curves differ. At every revision time it compares each group’s observed revisions with the number expected if all groups had the same risk, then adds up the differences across the whole follow-up. Page 6 rebuilds the observed and expected counts by hand. It’s the same test as the Mantel-Haenszel (or Mantel-Cox) test in the decision table.
Two groups. In total hips, does the surgical approach (anterior or posterior) affect revision?

RPython



tha <- cohort |> filter(procedure == "THA")        # approach applies to hips only

survfit2(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ approach, data = tha, conf.type = "log-log") |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable() +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Years since surgery", y = "Revision-free survival")







approach_logrank <- survdiff(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ approach, data = tha)
approach_logrank

Call:
survdiff(formula = Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ approach, 
    data = tha)

                     N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
approach=anterior  145       18     20.9     0.397     0.912
approach=posterior 125       19     16.1     0.513     0.912

 Chisq= 0.9  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.3 

approach_logrank$pvalue      # the printout rounds p to one digit; this is the full value

[1] 0.33968





from lifelines.statistics import logrank_test

tha = cohort[cohort["procedure"] == "THA"]                # approach applies to hips only
anterior = tha[tha["approach"] == "anterior"]
posterior = tha[tha["approach"] == "posterior"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
km_anterior = KaplanMeierFitter(label="anterior").fit(anterior["followup_years"], anterior["revised"])
km_posterior = KaplanMeierFitter(label="posterior").fit(posterior["followup_years"], posterior["revised"])
km_anterior.plot_survival_function(ax=ax)
km_posterior.plot_survival_function(ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Years since surgery")
ax.set_ylabel("Revision-free survival")
add_at_risk_counts(km_anterior, km_posterior, ax=ax, rows_to_show=["At risk", "Events"])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







approach_logrank = logrank_test(anterior["followup_years"], posterior["followup_years"],
                                event_observed_A=anterior["revised"], event_observed_B=posterior["revised"])
print(approach_logrank.test_statistic, approach_logrank.p_value)

0.9116386659614966 0.33968000597546394






N: the number of hips in each group, 145 anterior and 125 posterior. N, Observed and Expected are in R’s table only: lifelines prints the test statistic and the p-value.
Observed / Expected: the posterior hips had 19 revisions where 16.1 were expected; the anterior hips had 18 where 20.9 were expected.
Chisq = 0.9 on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.340: R’s printout rounds p to 0.3, and the line under it gives 0.33968. Python prints the test statistic and then p. No clear evidence that the curves differ over the whole follow-up.

But look at the plot. The posterior curve drops sharply in the first months, then the two curves come together (late on they even cross, where the CIs overlap widely). The early revisions are real: by 6 months, survivorship was 88.7% after the posterior approach and 98.6% after the anterior approach.

summary(survfit(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ approach, data = tha, conf.type = "log-log"), times = 0.5)

upper 95% CI

for curve in [km_anterior, km_posterior]:

anterior 0.986 [0.945, 0.996]
posterior 0.887 [0.817, 0.932]





The log-rank test adds up the differences over the whole follow-up. A large difference in the first months gets diluted by the years after, when the groups differ little, and the test can miss a real difference. Page 14 shows how to detect this and how to model it.
Three or more groups. The same test compares any number of groups. Does revision differ between implants A, B and C?

RPython



implant_logrank <- survdiff(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ implant, data = cohort)
implant_logrank

Call:
survdiff(formula = Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ implant, data = cohort)

            N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
implant=A 246       25     34.0      2.40      4.15
implant=B 217       18     30.0      4.81      7.65
implant=C 137       38     16.9     26.17     33.18

 Chisq= 33.5  on 2 degrees of freedom, p= 5e-08 





from lifelines.statistics import multivariate_logrank_test

implant_logrank = multivariate_logrank_test(cohort["followup_years"], cohort["implant"], cohort["revised"])
print(implant_logrank.test_statistic, implant_logrank.degrees_of_freedom, implant_logrank.p_value)

33.46861907356945 2 5.399850171504637e-08






Observed / Expected (R’s table only): implant C had 38 revisions where 16.9 were expected. Implants A (25 vs 34.0) and B (18 vs 30.0) had fewer than expected.
Chisq = 33.5 on 2 degrees of freedom, p < 0.001: R prints p= 5e-08, which is scientific notation for 0.00000005. Python prints the test statistic, the degrees of freedom and p. At least one implant’s curve differs from the others. The test doesn’t say which; page 15 covers comparing pairs of groups. Page 8 gives each implant’s hazard ratio.


Methods: Revision-free survival was compared between groups with the log-rank test.
Results: The log-rank test for revision-free survival across implants gave χ² = 33.5 (df = 2, p < 0.001). In total hip arthroplasty, survivorship at 6 months was 88.7% (95% CI 81.7% to 93.2%) after the posterior approach and 98.6% (95% CI 94.5% to 99.6%) after the anterior approach (log-rank test over the whole follow-up, χ² = 0.9, df = 1, p = 0.340).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: always plot the curves before you trust the test



The log-rank test is most powerful when one group’s hazard is a steady multiple of the other’s over time (proportional hazards). When the curves cross, as with the surgical approach here, a non-significant test can hide a real difference. And don’t compare groups at one hand-picked time point to get a significant result: decide your time points before you look.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: one function or two



R’s survdiff() takes a formula and handles two groups or more. lifelines has logrank_test() for two groups, which takes each group’s data separately, and multivariate_logrank_test() for any number, which takes a grouping column. They give identical results.

title: 13 · Kaplan-Meier & the log-rank test
section: Competing risks: when patients die first
text:
Competing risks: when patients die first
So far, patients who died were treated as censored. That assumes they would have gone on to be revised at the same rate as everyone else. They can’t: a patient who has died can never be revised. Death is a competing risk.
With death treated as censored, 1 − Kaplan-Meier estimates the risk of revision in an imaginary world where nobody dies. In an older population, where many patients die during follow-up, it overstates the real proportion who will be revised. The cumulative incidence function (CIF), estimated with the Aalen-Johansen method, gives the real proportion: the chance of being revised by a given time, allowing for the chance of dying first.
Here is how the cumulative incidence is calculated. At each moment when a revision happens, take the share of cases that are still alive and unrevised just before it, and multiply it by the fraction of the cases at risk that are revised at that moment. Add these small pieces up to the time you are interested in. 1 − Kaplan-Meier is the same sum with one difference: its “still unrevised” share ignores the deaths, so it is too big, and so is every piece. A box under “Reading it” does both sums by hand.
The data need one status column with three values. In the cohort, event_status is 0 for censored, 1 for revised and 2 for died.

RPython



cohort <- cohort |>
  mutate(status = factor(event_status, levels = c(0, 1, 2),
                         labels = c("censored", "revision", "death")))   # censored must come first

# with a three-level status, survfit() estimates the cumulative incidences (Aalen-Johansen)
cif <- survfit2(Surv(followup_years, status) ~ 1, data = cohort, conf.type = "log-log")

cif |>
  ggcuminc(outcome = c("revision", "death")) +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Years since surgery", y = "Cumulative incidence")







tidy_survfit(cif, times = c(2, 5, 10)) |>
  select(outcome, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  outcome   time estimate conf.low conf.high
  <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 death        2   0.0530   0.0369    0.0733
2 death        5   0.142    0.112     0.174 
3 death       10   0.240    0.193     0.290 
4 revision     2   0.0595   0.0423    0.0806
5 revision     5   0.128    0.100     0.159 
6 revision    10   0.193    0.153     0.237 

1 - summary(km, times = c(2, 5, 10))$surv    # 1 − Kaplan-Meier, for comparison

[1] 0.06071255 0.13690651 0.21968772





from scipy.stats import norm
from statsmodels.duration.survfunc import CumIncidenceRight

# event_status: 0 = censored, 1 = revision, 2 = death
cif = CumIncidenceRight(cohort["followup_years"], cohort["event_status"])
revision = pd.DataFrame({"cif": cif.cinc[0], "se": cif.cinc_se[0]}, index=cif.times)   # event type 1
death = pd.DataFrame({"cif": cif.cinc[1], "se": cif.cinc_se[1]}, index=cif.times)      # event type 2

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.step(revision.index, revision["cif"], where="post", label="revision")
ax.step(death.index, death["cif"], where="post", label="death")
ax.set_xlabel("Years since surgery")
ax.set_ylabel("Cumulative incidence")
legend = ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







z = norm.ppf(0.975)
for outcome, table in [("revision", revision), ("death", death)]:
    for years in [2, 5, 10]:
        row = table.loc[:years].iloc[-1]                                     # last step at or before that time
        spread = np.exp(z * row["se"] / (row["cif"] * np.log(row["cif"])))   # the log-log CI, as in R
        print(outcome, years, round(row["cif"], 3), round(row["cif"] ** (1 / spread), 3), round(row["cif"] ** spread, 3))

revision 2 0.059 0.042 0.081
revision 5 0.128 0.1 0.159
revision 10 0.193 0.153 0.237
death 2 0.053 0.037 0.073
death 5 0.142 0.112 0.174
death 10 0.24 0.193 0.29

for years in [2, 5, 10]:
    print(years, round(1 - km.survival_function_at_times(years).iloc[0], 3))   # 1 − Kaplan-Meier, for comparison

2 0.061
5 0.137
10 0.22





Reading it: - The revision curve is the cumulative incidence of revision: 5.9% at 2 years (R prints 0.0595, which is 0.05949 before rounding), 12.8% at 5 years and 19.3% at 10 years. - The death curve ends higher: 24.0% of patients had died without a revision by 10 years (the death row at 10 years). - 1 − Kaplan-Meier says 22.0% by 10 years, against a cumulative incidence of 19.3%. That is 22.0 − 19.3 = 2.7 percentage points too many, because it pretends the patients who died could still have been revised. - Python’s rows read: outcome, years, cumulative incidence, lower and upper CI limit. Its last three rows are the years and 1 − Kaplan-Meier.






Note🔍 Under the hood: the cumulative incidence by hand






RPython



cif_steps <- cohort |>
  filter(event_status != 0, followup_years <= 10) |>          # the revisions and deaths in the first 10 years
  group_by(followup_years) |>                                 # one row per moment at which one happened
  summarise(revisions = sum(event_status == 1), deaths = sum(event_status == 2)) |>
  mutate(at_risk = map_int(followup_years, \(t) sum(cohort$followup_years >= t)),
         # the share neither revised nor dead just before this moment
         still_free = lag(cumprod(1 - (revisions + deaths) / at_risk), default = 1),
         revised_now = still_free * revisions / at_risk,      # the share of all cases revised at this moment
         # the same two steps, ignoring the deaths (Kaplan-Meier)
         still_unrevised = lag(cumprod(1 - revisions / at_risk), default = 1),
         revised_now_km = still_unrevised * revisions / at_risk)

cif_steps |>
  filter(revisions > 0) |>
  select(followup_years, at_risk, revisions, still_free, still_unrevised) |>
  tail(3)                                                     # the last three revisions

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  followup_years at_risk revisions still_free still_unrevised
           <dbl>   <int>     <int>      <dbl>           <dbl>
1           7.35     117         1      0.624           0.804
2           7.82      99         1      0.607           0.797
3           7.9       92         1      0.595           0.789

c(cumulative_incidence = sum(cif_steps$revised_now), one_minus_km = sum(cif_steps$revised_now_km))

cumulative_incidence         one_minus_km 
           0.1930504            0.2196877 





events = cohort[(cohort["event_status"] != 0) & (cohort["followup_years"] <= 10)]   # the revisions and deaths in the first 10 years
cif_steps = (pd.crosstab(events["followup_years"], events["event_status"])          # one row per moment at which one happened
             .rename(columns={1: "revisions", 2: "deaths"}).reset_index())
cif_steps["at_risk"] = [(cohort["followup_years"] >= t).sum() for t in cif_steps["followup_years"]]
# the share neither revised nor dead just before this moment
got_past = 1 - (cif_steps["revisions"] + cif_steps["deaths"]) / cif_steps["at_risk"]
cif_steps["still_free"] = got_past.cumprod().shift(1, fill_value=1)
cif_steps["revised_now"] = cif_steps["still_free"] * cif_steps["revisions"] / cif_steps["at_risk"]   # the share of all cases revised at this moment
# the same two steps, ignoring the deaths (Kaplan-Meier)
got_past_km = 1 - cif_steps["revisions"] / cif_steps["at_risk"]
cif_steps["still_unrevised"] = got_past_km.cumprod().shift(1, fill_value=1)
cif_steps["revised_now_km"] = cif_steps["still_unrevised"] * cif_steps["revisions"] / cif_steps["at_risk"]

columns = ["followup_years", "at_risk", "revisions", "still_free", "still_unrevised"]
print(cif_steps.loc[cif_steps["revisions"] > 0, columns].tail(3))                   # the last three revisions

event_status  followup_years  at_risk  revisions  still_free  still_unrevised
142                     7.35      117          1    0.623707         0.803807
145                     7.82       99          1    0.607270         0.796937
147                     7.90       92          1    0.594741         0.788887

print(cif_steps["revised_now"].sum(), cif_steps["revised_now_km"].sum())

0.19305042560075752 0.21968771693607914





Look at the last revision, 7.9 years after surgery: 92 cases were at risk and 1 was revised. Just before it, 59.5% of all cases were still alive and unrevised (still_free). Kaplan-Meier ignores the deaths and works with 78.9% (still_unrevised), so this revision adds more to its total. The pieces add up to 0.193 for the cumulative incidence and 0.220 for 1 − Kaplan-Meier, the two 10-year values in the output.



The gap grows with the number of deaths. It’s small at 2 years, when few patients have died, and largest in older patients (see exercise 2).
Comparing groups: Gray’s test (R only). Gray’s test is the competing-risks counterpart of the log-rank test: it compares cumulative incidence curves between groups. The tidycmprsk package runs it:

library(tidycmprsk)

cif_by_implant <- cuminc(Surv(followup_years, status) ~ implant, data = cohort)
glance(cif_by_implant) |>
  select(outcome_1, statistic_1, df_1, p.value_1, outcome_2, statistic_2, df_2, p.value_2)

# A tibble: 1 × 8
  outcome_1 statistic_1  df_1   p.value_1 outcome_2 statistic_2  df_2 p.value_2
  <chr>           <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>           <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 revision         31.5     2 0.000000142 death           0.969     2     0.616


The cumulative incidence of revision differed between implants (Gray’s test: statistic_1 is χ² = 31.5, with df = 2 and p < 0.001; the output prints p as 0.000000142); there was no clear evidence that the cumulative incidence of death differed (statistic_2: χ² = 0.97, p = 0.616).

Methods: The cumulative incidence of revision was estimated with the Aalen-Johansen method, treating death as a competing risk, and compared between implants with Gray’s test.
Results: The cumulative incidence of revision was 12.8% (95% CI 10.0% to 15.9%) at 5 years and 19.3% (95% CI 15.3% to 23.7%) at 10 years, when the cumulative incidence of death was 24.0% (95% CI 19.3% to 29.0%). Gray’s test for the cumulative incidence of revision across implants gave χ² = 31.5 (df = 2, p < 0.001).







Warning⚠️ Watch out: which number answers your question?



Both estimates are useful, but they answer different questions: - 1 − Kaplan-Meier answers “how well does the implant perform while patients are alive?” It’s the usual measure for comparing implants, and registries report it. - The cumulative incidence answers “what proportion of patients will actually be revised?” Use it to counsel patients or plan services, especially for older patients.
Say which one you report. Never call 1 − Kaplan-Meier “the proportion of patients revised” when many patients died.








Tip🔀 R vs Python: which tools




The cumulative incidence: R’s survfit() estimates it whenever the status has more than two levels. In Python, use statsmodels’ CumIncidenceRight(): it gives the estimates and their standard errors but no CI, so the code builds the same log-log CI as R. lifelines also has an AalenJohansenFitter, but it moves tied follow-up times by a small random amount, which can shift an estimate read at exactly 5 or 10 years, so we don’t use it.
Gray’s test: Python has no mature implementation of Gray’s test. Plot the curves in Python, but run the test in R. tidycmprsk’s cuminc() also gives the cumulative incidences, with a slightly different CI method.
Fine-Gray regression models the cumulative incidence with several predictors at once; it’s R only too (page 14).

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
text: A test for three or more groups asks one question: “is there any difference among them?”. When the answer is yes, the next question is which groups differ from which. Answering it means running several tests at once, and every extra test is another chance of a false positive. This page shows how to compare groups in pairs while keeping that chance under control. Most “After …” sections pick up an example from page 8, page 9 or page 13.

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
text:
Why many tests mislead
A test at the 5% level has a 5% chance of a false positive when there is truly no difference. Run several tests and those chances accumulate. The chance of at least one false positive across a set of tests is the family-wise error rate. For independent tests at the 5% level it’s 1 − 0.95k, where k is the number of tests:

RPython



library(tidyverse)
library(survival)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
trial <- read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

tests <- c(1, 3, 6, 10, 20)
false_positives <- tibble(tests, chance_of_a_false_positive = round(1 - 0.95^tests, 2))
false_positives

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  tests chance_of_a_false_positive
  <dbl>                      <dbl>
1     1                       0.05
2     3                       0.14
3     6                       0.26
4    10                       0.4 
5    20                       0.64

# four equal groups, six pairwise tests: the chance that at least one gives p < 0.05
1 - ptukey(qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(2), nmeans = 4, df = Inf)

[1] 0.2033224





import itertools
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pingouin as pg
import scikit_posthocs as sp
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd
from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import mcnemar
from lifelines import CoxPHFitter
from lifelines.statistics import multivariate_logrank_test, pairwise_logrank_test

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")
proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")
trial = pd.read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv")

tests = np.array([1, 3, 6, 10, 20])
false_positives = pd.DataFrame({"tests": tests, "chance_of_a_false_positive": (1 - 0.95**tests).round(2)})
print(false_positives)

   tests  chance_of_a_false_positive
0      1                        0.05
1      3                        0.14
2      6                        0.26
3     10                        0.40
4     20                        0.64

# four equal groups, six pairwise tests: the chance that at least one gives p < 0.05
print(1 - stats.studentized_range.cdf(stats.norm.ppf(0.975) * np.sqrt(2), 4, np.inf))

0.20332243416794726





Four groups make six pairs. Six independent tests at the 5% level give a 26% chance of at least one false alarm, even when nothing is going on; twenty tests give 64%. Pairwise comparisons aren’t independent, because each group appears in three of the six pairs, so for four groups of equal size the chance is a little lower: about 20% (the last line of the output, 0.203). That’s still four times the 5% you meant to allow. Comparing pairs therefore needs an adjustment: a stricter rule that keeps the chance of any false positive across the whole set of comparisons at 5%.






Note💡 In plain language



Buy one lottery ticket and you’ll almost certainly lose. Buy twenty and your chance of winning something goes up. Each p-value below 0.05 is a small “win”, and with enough tests one will turn up by luck alone. Adjusting the p-values makes each win harder to get, so the overall chance stays where you set it.

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
section: Adjusting p-values: Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg
text:
Adjusting p-values: Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg
Page 8 found that age differs across the four ASA classes. Here are the six pairwise comparisons, each a Welch t test, with the p-values left as they are (unadjusted) and then adjusted three ways:

RPython



age_pairs <- pairwise.t.test(cohort$age, cohort$asa, pool.sd = FALSE,      # Welch t tests
                             p.adjust.method = "none")
unadjusted <- age_pairs$p.value[lower.tri(age_pairs$p.value, diag = TRUE)]  # the six p-values, in pair order

adjusted <- tibble(pair = c("1 vs 2", "1 vs 3", "1 vs 4", "2 vs 3", "2 vs 4", "3 vs 4"),
                   unadjusted,
                   bonferroni = p.adjust(unadjusted, method = "bonferroni"),
                   holm = p.adjust(unadjusted, method = "holm"),
                   bh = p.adjust(unadjusted, method = "BH"))
adjusted |> mutate(across(-pair, \(p) round(p, 4)))

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  pair   unadjusted bonferroni   holm     bh
  <chr>       <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 1 vs 2     0.022      0.132  0.0439 0.0263
2 1 vs 3     0          0      0      0     
3 1 vs 4     0          0      0      0     
4 2 vs 3     0          0      0      0     
5 2 vs 4     0.0002     0.0013 0.0007 0.0003
6 3 vs 4     0.0298     0.179  0.0439 0.0298





asa_pairs = list(itertools.combinations([1, 2, 3, 4], 2))
unadjusted = [stats.ttest_ind(cohort.loc[cohort["asa"] == a, "age"], cohort.loc[cohort["asa"] == b, "age"],
                              equal_var=False).pvalue                    # Welch t tests
              for a, b in asa_pairs]

adjusted = pd.DataFrame({
    "pair": [f"{a} vs {b}" for a, b in asa_pairs],
    "unadjusted": unadjusted,
    "bonferroni": multipletests(unadjusted, method="bonferroni")[1],
    "holm": multipletests(unadjusted, method="holm")[1],
    "bh": multipletests(unadjusted, method="fdr_bh")[1],
})
print(adjusted.round(4))

     pair  unadjusted  bonferroni    holm      bh
0  1 vs 2      0.0220      0.1317  0.0439  0.0263
1  1 vs 3      0.0000      0.0000  0.0000  0.0000
2  1 vs 4      0.0000      0.0000  0.0000  0.0000
3  2 vs 3      0.0000      0.0000  0.0000  0.0000
4  2 vs 4      0.0002      0.0013  0.0007  0.0003
5  3 vs 4      0.0298      0.1790  0.0439  0.0298





Follow the ASA 1 vs ASA 2 comparison across the row: - Unadjusted, p = 0.022: “significant” on its own, but it’s one of six tests. - Bonferroni, p = 0.132: multiplies every p-value by the number of tests (here 6). Simple, but the strictest: it often throws away real differences. - Holm, p = 0.044: a step-down version of Bonferroni. It multiplies the smallest p-value by 6, the next smallest by 5, and so on, but an adjusted p-value can’t be smaller than the one before it in that order. ASA 1 vs 2 has the fifth smallest of the six p-values, so it’s multiplied by 2: 0.022 × 2 = 0.044. ASA 3 vs 4 has the largest unadjusted p-value (0.030), so it’s multiplied by 1, but it takes 0.044 from ASA 1 vs 2, the one before it. It controls the family-wise error rate just as well as Bonferroni and is never less powerful, so use Holm rather than Bonferroni. - Benjamini-Hochberg (BH), p = 0.026: controls something different, the false discovery rate: the expected share of false positives among the results you call significant. It’s the most lenient of the three. It suits screening many outcomes for leads, not confirming a claim. To get it, each p-value is multiplied by the number of tests and divided by its rank, counted from the smallest: here 0.022 × 6 / 5 = 0.026.






Note🔍 Under the hood: Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg by hand






RPython



by_hand <- adjusted |>
  select(pair, unadjusted) |>
  arrange(unadjusted) |>                                          # the smallest p-value first
  mutate(rank = row_number(),
         times_holm = 6 - rank + 1,                               # Holm: × 6, × 5, ... × 1
         holm = pmin(1, cummax(unadjusted * times_holm)),         # never smaller than the one before it
         times_bh = 6 / rank,                                     # BH: × 6 ÷ rank
         bh = rev(cummin(rev(pmin(1, unadjusted * times_bh)))))   # never larger than the one after it
by_hand |> mutate(across(c(unadjusted, holm, bh), \(p) signif(p, 3)))

# A tibble: 6 × 7
  pair      unadjusted  rank times_holm          holm times_bh            bh
  <chr>          <dbl> <int>      <dbl>         <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl>
1 2 vs 3 0.00000000022     1          6 0.00000000132      6   0.00000000132
2 1 vs 3 0.00000131        2          5 0.00000653         3   0.00000392   
3 1 vs 4 0.0000083         3          4 0.0000332          2   0.0000166    
4 2 vs 4 0.000217          4          3 0.000651           1.5 0.000325     
5 1 vs 2 0.022             5          2 0.0439             1.2 0.0263       
6 3 vs 4 0.0298            6          1 0.0439             1   0.0298       





by_hand = adjusted[["pair", "unadjusted"]].sort_values("unadjusted").reset_index(drop=True)        # the smallest p-value first
by_hand["rank"] = by_hand.index + 1
by_hand["times_holm"] = 6 - by_hand["rank"] + 1                                                    # Holm: × 6, × 5, ... × 1
by_hand["holm"] = (by_hand["unadjusted"] * by_hand["times_holm"]).cummax().clip(upper=1)           # never smaller than the one before it
by_hand["times_bh"] = 6 / by_hand["rank"]                                                          # BH: × 6 ÷ rank
by_hand["bh"] = (by_hand["unadjusted"] * by_hand["times_bh"])[::-1].cummin()[::-1].clip(upper=1)   # never larger than the one after it
print(by_hand.to_string(float_format=lambda p: f"{p:.3g}"))

     pair  unadjusted  rank  times_holm     holm  times_bh       bh
0  2 vs 3     2.2e-10     1           6 1.32e-09         6 1.32e-09
1  1 vs 3    1.31e-06     2           5 6.53e-06         3 3.92e-06
2  1 vs 4     8.3e-06     3           4 3.32e-05         2 1.66e-05
3  2 vs 4    0.000217     4           3 0.000651       1.5 0.000325
4  1 vs 2       0.022     5           2   0.0439       1.2   0.0263
5  3 vs 4      0.0298     6           1   0.0439         1   0.0298





The six p-values are sorted from the smallest to the largest. ASA 1 vs 2 comes fifth: Holm multiplies it by 2 (0.022 × 2 = 0.044), and Benjamini-Hochberg by 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2 (0.022 × 1.2 = 0.026). ASA 3 vs 4 comes last. Holm multiplies it by 1, which leaves 0.030, less than the 0.044 before it, so it takes 0.044. The holm and bh columns match the ones the software gave above.









Warning⚠️ Watch out: decide the adjustment before you see the p-values



Picking whichever adjustment keeps your favourite result significant is p-hacking. Choose in advance: Holm (or a method built for the test, like Tukey’s below) for comparisons you’ll report as findings, Benjamini-Hochberg only for exploratory screening. Say in the Methods which you used and how many comparisons it covered.

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
section: After ANOVA: Tukey’s HSD and Games-Howell
text:
After ANOVA: Tukey’s HSD and Games-Howell
After a one-way ANOVA, Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) compares every pair of group means. It adjusts for all the pairs at once, and gives each difference a CI that’s adjusted too. It assumes the groups have similar spreads, like the ANOVA. When they don’t (the largest SD is more than about twice the smallest), use Games-Howell, the Welch version of Tukey’s test.

RPython



cohort |> group_by(asa) |> summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(age), sd = sd(age))   # look first: group sizes, means and SDs

Four of the six pairs differ clearly (p < 0.001 or, for ASA 2 vs 4 in the Games-Howell test, p = 0.001). Two don’t: ASA 2 patients were 3.6 years older than ASA 1 patients (95% CI −0.4 to 7.7, p = 0.096), and ASA 4 patients 5.3 years older than ASA 3 patients (95% CI −0.3 to 10.9, p = 0.072). Both CIs include 0, and both comparisons involve one of the two small classes (ASA 1 with 36 patients and ASA 4 with 18). The SDs are similar (8.7 to 9.3 years: sd in R’s first table, std in Python’s), so Games-Howell reaches the same conclusions.

Methods: Age was compared across ASA classes with one-way ANOVA, followed by Tukey’s honestly significant difference test for pairwise comparisons.
Results: Across ASA classes, one-way ANOVA gave F(3, 596) = 23.9 (p < 0.001). In pairwise comparisons, the difference in mean age was 5.0 years between ASA 3 and ASA 2 (95% CI 3.0 to 6.9; p < 0.001), 3.6 years between ASA 2 and ASA 1 (95% CI −0.4 to 7.7; p = 0.096) and 5.3 years between ASA 4 and ASA 3 (95% CI −0.3 to 10.9; p = 0.072). Table 2 gives all six pairwise comparisons.







Tip🔀 R vs Python: Tukey and Games-Howell



R’s TukeyHSD() and statsmodels’ pairwise_tukeyhsd() give identical results; R writes the pairs as “2-1” (second group minus first), statsmodels as group1, group2 with meandiff = group2 − group1. For Games-Howell, R needs the rstatix package; in Python, pingouin’s pairwise_gameshowell() reports diff as A − B, so its signs are the reverse of R’s estimates. The p-values agree.

title: 15 · Post-hoc tests & multiple comparisons
text:
After Kruskal-Wallis: Dunn’s test
Dunn’s test follows a Kruskal-Wallis test. It compares the groups’ mean ranks from the Kruskal-Wallis ranking, so it measures every pair on the same scale. Use it with Holm’s adjustment. Running separate Mann-Whitney tests instead re-ranks the data for each pair and needs an adjustment of its own.
Length of stay (LOS) is skewed (most patients go home on day 0 or 1), so it belongs in the rank column. Does it differ across ASA classes?
